data.description: A congenital nonfunctioning lung segment that lacks normal communication with the tracheobronchial tree and receives systemic arterial blood supply, commonly from the descending thoracic or abdominal aorta. It may cause respiratory distress in neonates, particularly when large or associated with other lung malformations.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal systemic arterial vessel identified near the descending aorta on imaging
Abnormal lower-lung opacity or asymmetric lung appearance
Need for intubation and intensive respiratory support
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound perinatal arrest after prolonged labor
Meconium-stained fluid
Prenatal urinary tract dilatation
Gestational hypertension exposure
Maternal hepatitis C infection

data.diagnosis: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), possibly with hybrid sequestration
data.description: A developmental malformation of the lower respiratory tract characterized by cystic or solid abnormal lung tissue. Some lesions coexist with systemic arterial supply from the aorta, termed a hybrid CPAM-sequestration lesion, and can produce neonatal respiratory distress through mass effect or impaired ventilation.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal chest radiographs with focal/asymmetric pulmonary lucency or opacity
Possible abnormal systemic arterial supply to affected lung tissue
Severe respiratory compromise in the newborn period
symptoms_not_in_common: Cardiorespiratory arrest primarily associated with a difficult delivery
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Breech delivery
Prenatal right urinary tract dilatation
Maternal infectious history

data.diagnosis: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
data.description: Failure of the normal postnatal decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance, leading to right-to-left shunting through fetal circulatory pathways and severe hypoxemia. It is often associated with perinatal asphyxia, meconium aspiration, pulmonary disease, or congenital cardiopulmonary malformations.
symptoms_in_common: Severe hypoxemia and cardiorespiratory failure at delivery
Need for intubation, CPR, epinephrine, and prolonged resuscitation
Meconium-stained fluid, a risk factor for pulmonary vascular disease
Perinatal asphyxia with extremely low Apgar scores
Possible underlying congenital pulmonary vascular anomaly on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Prenatal right urinary tract dilatation
A discrete anomalous systemic vessel on imaging
Breech presentation
Maternal hepatitis C infection
Treated maternal Chlamydia trachomatis infection

data.description: Respiratory disease caused by aspiration of meconium-contaminated amniotic fluid before or during delivery. It can cause airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, hyperinflation, atelectasis, pulmonary hypertension, and severe respiratory failure.
symptoms_in_common: Apnea and severe respiratory failure at birth
Need for intubation and prolonged resuscitation
Patchy/asymmetric pulmonary abnormalities and hyperinflation that may be seen on chest radiographs
Risk of secondary persistent pulmonary hypertension
symptoms_not_in_common: Prenatal abnormal urinary tract dilatation
Apparent anomalous systemic thoracic vessel on ultrasound or CT
Possible congenital pulmonary venous drainage abnormality
Breech presentation
Maternal hepatitis C infection

data.description: 54-year-old man with a history of polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. He was afebrile, drowsy, and hypertensive (172/110 mmHg), with distended jugular veins and crackles at the lung bases. He had a family history of a sister with renal failure of unknown cause requiring dialysis at age 45. Laboratory studies showed severe renal dysfunction (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL), proteinuria, elevated LDH, rare schistocytes, and reduced C3 with normal C4; C3 hypocomplementemia persisted during hospitalization. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine and metabolites. Renal ultrasound showed echogenic kidneys measuring 9.8 cm and 10.3 cm.

data.diagnosis: Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangiopathy with malignant hypertension
data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy causing endothelial injury and small-vessel thrombosis, often triggered or worsened by cocaine-associated severe hypertension; renal biopsy may show arteriolar intimal thickening and onion-skin lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Severe acute kidney dysfunction with creatinine 16.0 mg/dL
Histologic vascular lesions compatible with thrombotic microangiopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent isolated low C3 with normal C4
Family history of renal failure at a relatively young age

data.description: A complement dysregulation disorder producing thrombotic microangiopathy, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia of variable severity, and often profound renal failure; inherited complement abnormalities can cause familial kidney disease.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent low C3 with normal C4
Family history of unexplained renal failure
Renal vascular changes consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Cocaine exposure, which provides an alternative trigger for thrombotic microangiopathy
Only rare schistocytes and relatively mild anemia
No reported thrombocytopenia
No reported diarrheal prodrome or other clear complement-amplifying illness

data.description: Severe, accelerated hypertension can injure renal arterioles and glomeruli, producing hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with onion-skin intimal thickening, ischemic kidney injury, proteinuria, and renal failure.
symptoms_in_common: Altered mental status consistent with hypertensive encephalopathy or uremia
Pulmonary crackles and jugular venous distention consistent with volume overload
Small echogenic kidneys suggesting chronic kidney damage
Vascular onion-skin-type lesions on renal pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent low C3 with normal C4
Elevated LDH and schistocytes suggesting a superimposed thrombotic microangiopathy
Family history of renal failure
Cocaine exposure may be a precipitating factor rather than primary essential hypertension

data.diagnosis: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
data.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, commonly with proteinuria, renal dysfunction, hematuria, and complement consumption; mixed cryoglobulinemia often lowers C4 prominently.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal C4 despite low C3, whereas cryoglobulinemic disease often markedly lowers C4
Severe hypertension with vascular thrombotic microangiopathy-type lesions
Elevated LDH and schistocytes
Cocaine exposure
No reported purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy, or other cryoglobulinemic manifestations

data.description: A group of complement alternative-pathway disorders causing dominant C3 deposition in glomeruli, proteinuria, hematuria, progressive renal failure, and persistent low serum C3; familial complement abnormalities may occur.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent low C3 with normal C4
Family history of unexplained renal failure
Small echogenic kidneys compatible with chronic kidney disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated LDH and schistocytes, which favor thrombotic microangiopathy
Cocaine-associated severe hypertension as a clear alternative renal insult
Predominantly arteriolar onion-skin vascular lesions rather than a primarily glomerular pattern
No reported hematuria or nephritic urinary sediment

data.description: 44-year-old Chinese woman with a 7-week history of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting, associated with 13 kg weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, distension, or diarrhea. Initial treatment for presumed functional gastrointestinal disorder with antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics for 3 weeks was ineffective. Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, absent pharyngeal reflex, reduced tendon reflexes on the right, and bilateral Babinski sign. She had no significant past medical history; prior gastroscopy and abdominal CT were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal liver, kidney, thyroid, autoimmune, and glucose-related tests; serum AQP4-IgG was negative, but cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG was positive.

data.diagnosis: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
data.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies that can cause inflammatory lesions in the area postrema and brainstem, producing otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, hiccups, and neurological deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Marked weight loss due to prolonged vomiting
Brainstem neurological signs including horizontal nystagmus and absent pharyngeal reflex
Right-sided limb paralysis and abnormal reflexes
Acute respiratory failure, compatible with medullary/brainstem involvement
Brain MRI findings involving the dorsal medulla/area postrema region
symptoms_not_in_common: Metabolic alkalosis is a complication of severe vomiting rather than a primary NMOSD manifestation
Absence of optic neuritis or myelitis symptoms at presentation

data.diagnosis: Area postrema syndrome due to AQP4-IgG-positive autoimmune brainstem encephalitis
data.description: Area postrema syndrome is a characteristic NMOSD presentation caused by inflammation of the dorsal medulla, especially the area postrema, a vomiting center with high aquaporin-4 expression.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent nausea and vomiting for several weeks
Failure to respond to antiemetics and prokinetic therapy
No gastrointestinal structural abnormality on gastroscopy or abdominal CT
Brainstem signs including nystagmus, impaired pharyngeal reflex, and respiratory failure
symptoms_not_in_common: Right-sided paralysis and bilateral Babinski signs suggest extension beyond an isolated area postrema lesion
Metabolic alkalosis is secondary to vomiting rather than a direct neurologic feature

data.description: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause brainstem lesions, eye movement abnormalities, weakness, and upper motor neuron signs.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe prolonged intractable nausea and vomiting as the dominant initial presentation is less typical
Acute respiratory failure is uncommon in typical multiple sclerosis
CSF AQP4-IgG positivity strongly favors NMOSD rather than multiple sclerosis
No history of typical relapsing neurologic episodes, optic neuritis, or sensory symptoms

data.description: MOGAD is an inflammatory demyelinating disorder that may involve the optic nerves, spinal cord, brain, or brainstem and can occasionally mimic NMOSD.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal pyramidal signs including Babinski responses
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF AQP4-IgG positivity is more characteristic of NMOSD than MOGAD
Persistent isolated vomiting due to area postrema involvement is much more typical of AQP4-positive NMOSD
No reported optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, or encephalopathy
Acute respiratory failure is not a common presenting manifestation

data.diagnosis: Brainstem encephalitis (rhombencephalitis), including autoimmune or infectious causes
data.description: Rhombencephalitis is inflammation of the hindbrain, including the pons and medulla, and may be caused by autoimmune disorders or infections such as Listeria, leading to cranial nerve, motor, respiratory, and autonomic dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Acute respiratory failure due to medullary involvement
Nausea and vomiting can occur with dorsal medullary involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever, headache, altered consciousness, or systemic infectious symptoms
Seven weeks of isolated nausea and vomiting before neurological deficits is less typical for infectious rhombencephalitis
CSF AQP4-IgG positivity supports NMOSD rather than a nonspecific infectious encephalitis

data.description:
47-year-old male with 2-month history of fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. History of inguinal hernia repair surgery 10 years ago and cardiac disease. On admission, body temperature was 37.3°C. Physical examination revealed aortic valve diastolic murmurs at the precordium. --- Imagen documental 1: 01.jpg --- # Antibiotics # Minimal inhibitory concentrations (ug/ml)
Ampicillin 1.5
Penicillin 0.5
Cefazolin > 256
Cefuroxime > 256
Ceftriaxone > 256
Meropenem 16
Imipenem 1
Vancomycin > 256
Levofloxacin 1

A subacute bacterial infection of a cardiac valve caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive rod that is characteristically resistant to vancomycin and often causes destructive aortic-valve endocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: Echocardiographic abnormality involving the aortic valve with aortic regurgitant flow
Antibiotic profile with penicillin/ampicillin activity and marked vancomycin resistance
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported occupational or animal exposure, such as contact with fish, swine, poultry, or meat
No reported localized erysipeloid skin lesion
Temperature of 37.3°C on admission is lower than the high fever often seen in active bacterial endocarditis

data.description: Infection of the native aortic valve, usually bacterial, producing valvular inflammation, vegetations, regurgitation, and potentially periannular extension or abscess formation.
symptoms_in_common: New or abnormal aortic diastolic murmur
Cardiac disease as a predisposing condition
Echocardiographic evidence of significant aortic-valve structural abnormality and regurgitant flow
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported peripheral stigmata such as petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, or Janeway lesions
No reported embolic neurologic, renal, or pulmonary manifestations
No documented positive blood cultures in the provided information

data.diagnosis: Aortic root abscess complicating infective endocarditis
data.description: A localized suppurative infection around the aortic valve annulus or aortic root, usually occurring as a complication of infective endocarditis and often associated with severe aortic regurgitation.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute constitutional symptoms including fever and malaise
Aortic diastolic murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation
Echocardiographic appearance concerning for destructive peri-aortic or aortic-root involvement
Long duration of illness, which can allow local extension of valve infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported conduction abnormality, such as new atrioventricular block
No reported chest pain or heart-failure symptoms
No documented persistent high-grade fever or hemodynamic instability

data.description: An uncommon form of infective endocarditis caused by Lactobacillus species, which can occur in patients with underlying cardiac disease and may show intrinsic resistance to vancomycin.
symptoms_in_common: Aortic diastolic murmur suggesting valvular regurgitation
Potential vancomycin resistance with relative susceptibility to penicillin or ampicillin
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported gastrointestinal disease, probiotic exposure, dental source, or immunosuppression
No reported heart-failure symptoms
Marked resistance to multiple cephalosporins is not a defining clinical feature

data.description: A subacute, often blood-culture-negative infective endocarditis caused by Bartonella species, commonly involving the aortic valve and presenting with prolonged nonspecific constitutional symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Aortic-valve murmur and echocardiographic valve abnormality
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported cat exposure, flea exposure, body lice exposure, homelessness, or exposure to farm animals
The provided antimicrobial susceptibility pattern suggests a cultured bacterium rather than typical culture-negative Bartonella infection
No reported hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or vascular skin lesions

data.description: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.

data.diagnosis: Paradoxical arterial air embolism through a patent foramen ovale
data.description: Venous air introduced during venesection can cross a patent foramen ovale into the arterial circulation, causing embolic obstruction of cerebral and coronary arteries.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden onset during venesection with a gurgling sensation in the arm
Severe crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm
Raised troponin and inferior T-wave inversion
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal baseline right-heart pressures

data.description: Air entering the venous circulation during an invasive vascular procedure can obstruct pulmonary vessels, producing abrupt hypoxia, dyspnoea, chest pain, and cardiovascular instability.
symptoms_in_common: Gurgling sensation travelling up the arm
Oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
Pulmonary vascular abnormality on CT imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient left-sided hemiplegia
Dysphasia
Coronary ischemic ECG changes and elevated troponin are not typical unless air crosses into the systemic arterial circulation

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary air embolism causing myocardial ischemia
data.description: Air entering the coronary arteries can transiently obstruct coronary blood flow and cause acute myocardial ischemia or infarction, often with chest pain, ECG changes, and troponin elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden severe crushing central chest pain
Pain radiating to the jaw and left arm
Abrupt onset during a procedure capable of introducing air
Patent foramen ovale allowing arterial passage of venous air
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe hypoxia is not usually prominent in isolated coronary air embolism
Transient hemiplegia and dysphasia suggest simultaneous cerebral embolization rather than isolated coronary involvement

data.diagnosis: Transient ischemic attack due to cerebral air embolism
data.description: An embolus of air reaching the cerebral arterial circulation can produce sudden focal neurological deficits that may resolve rapidly if the obstruction is transient.
symptoms_in_common: Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunting
Temporal association with venesection and suspected intravascular air entry
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw and arm
Elevated troponin and inferior T-wave inversion
Marked dyspnoea and hypoxia

data.diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism, including pulmonary arterial air embolism
data.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by embolic material can cause sudden dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, chest pain, and secondary right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale.
symptoms_in_common: Hypoxia with oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
Potential pulmonary arterial filling abnormality on CT imaging
Right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale
symptoms_not_in_common: Gurgling sensation in the arm during venesection favors direct air entry rather than thrombotic pulmonary embolism
Transient focal neurological deficits are unusual without paradoxical embolization
Normal baseline right-heart pressures
Jaw and left-arm radiation with elevated troponin more strongly suggests coronary involvement

data.description: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.
A rare, usually superficial astrocytic tumor that commonly affects younger patients, often presents with seizures, and is frequently associated with BRAF V600E mutation. It may recur after resection.
symptoms_in_common: Long history of seizures beginning in early adulthood
Prior pathology confirming WHO grade 2 PXA
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly documented focal neurologic deficits
No reported cognitive or personality changes
No reported visual-field deficit

data.description: An anaplastic PXA is a higher-grade, more aggressive form of PXA that can arise through recurrence or malignant transformation of a previously lower-grade PXA and may show more infiltrative imaging features.
symptoms_in_common: BRAF V600E mutation, which is common in PXA and can persist in anaplastic transformation
Progressive or recurrent temporal lobe lesion on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported rapidly progressive neurologic decline
No reported marked focal weakness or sensory loss
No reported altered consciousness

data.description: A diffusely infiltrating lower-grade glioma that commonly arises in the cerebral hemispheres of younger to middle-aged adults and often presents with longstanding seizures. It typically appears as a nonenhancing or minimally enhancing T2/FLAIR-hyperintense lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Adult onset with a prolonged clinical course
Temporal lobe FLAIR signal abnormality on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior pathology specifically identified PXA rather than diffuse astrocytoma
BRAF V600E mutation is less typical than in PXA
No IDH mutation information is provided

data.description: A generally slow-growing glioneuronal tumor, often located in the temporal lobe, that is strongly associated with chronic focal seizures. Some gangliogliomas harbor BRAF V600E mutations.
symptoms_not_in_common: Previous tissue diagnosis was PXA rather than ganglioglioma
No described cyst-with-mural-nodule pattern or calcification
No documented mixed neuronal and glial pathology

data.diagnosis: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype or high-grade diffuse glioma
data.description: A highly aggressive infiltrating astrocytic malignancy that can produce enhancing mass lesions, edema, headache, seizures, and neurologic deficits. It is less likely than recurrent/anaplastic PXA in this clinical setting but may be considered if there is malignant transformation or rapid radiographic progression.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very long seizure history and indolent course are less typical of de novo glioblastoma
Prior WHO grade 2 PXA pathology favors recurrent or transformed PXA
No reported rapid onset focal deficits, severe cognitive decline, or major mass-effect symptoms

data.description: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous rash and progressive muscle weakness. The rash began on the eyelids, elbows, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and knees, followed 1 week later by severe generalized myalgia and weakness with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Exam showed heliotrope rash, periungual edema/erythema, erythematous papules on the fingertips and extensor surfaces of the fingers, elbows, and knees, pitting edema of the arms and legs, and marked proximal muscle weakness with inability to lift the arms, legs, or head against gravity. Muscle tone, reflexes, and sensation were normal. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier; he did not smoke or use illicit drugs.
An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal skeletal-muscle weakness.
symptoms_in_common: Violaceous heliotrope rash on the eyelids
Papules over metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints consistent with Gottron papules
Rash on extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees
Progressive severe symmetric proximal muscle weakness
Difficulty rising from a squat, climbing stairs, and walking
Difficulty lifting the arms, legs, and head against gravity
Normal sensation and reflexes despite severe weakness

data.description: A systemic autoimmune inflammatory myopathy syndrome that can cause myositis, inflammatory arthritis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, mechanic's hands, and sometimes dermatomyositis-like rash.
symptoms_in_common: Marked difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a squat
symptoms_not_in_common: Classic heliotrope rash
Classic Gottron papules on the finger joints
No reported cough, dyspnea, or other evidence of interstitial lung disease
No reported Raynaud phenomenon
No mechanic's hands
No inflammatory polyarthritis

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing subacute, symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes, but without the characteristic skin findings of dermatomyositis.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a squat
Inability to lift the limbs and head against gravity
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope eyelid rash
Gottron papules over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints
Rash on the elbows and knees
Periungual edema and erythema
Pitting edema of the arms and legs

data.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy, often associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies, that produces rapidly progressive proximal weakness and myalgia with muscle necrosis; cutaneous findings are generally absent.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty standing from a squat, walking, and climbing stairs
Difficulty lifting the arms, legs, and head
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash
Gottron papules on the fingers
Rash over elbows and knees
Periungual edema and erythema
Pitting peripheral edema
No reported statin exposure or other typical medication trigger

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory myositis overlap
data.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus can rarely overlap with inflammatory myositis, causing proximal weakness, myalgia, skin eruptions, and periungual vascular changes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Highly characteristic heliotrope rash of dermatomyositis
Gottron papules over the finger joints
Extensor-surface papules over elbows and knees
No reported photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis, renal symptoms, or cytopenia-related symptoms
Severity of isolated proximal weakness is more typical of dermatomyositis

data.description: 59-year-old woman with a longstanding history of epilepsy with complex partial seizures treated with phenytoin for >20 years, presenting with a 3-year history of progressive proximal muscle weakness and generalized bone and muscle pain, worsening over time and limiting daily activities. Physical examination showed normal renal and liver function. Radiographs revealed bilateral Looser’s zones in the femoral necks. Laboratory tests showed hypophosphatemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term phenytoin use, often through increased vitamin D breakdown, impaired calcium/phosphate balance, and defective mineralization of osteoid.
symptoms_in_common: Long-term phenytoin treatment for more than 20 years
Bilateral Looser's zones in the femoral necks

data.description: Defective mineralization of bone due to inadequate vitamin D availability, causing bone pain, muscle weakness, insufficiency fractures, and biochemical evidence of increased bone turnover.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very long history of phenytoin use suggests a medication-associated cause rather than simple nutritional vitamin D deficiency
No reported poor diet, malabsorption, limited sun exposure, or low vitamin D measurement

data.description: A rare paraneoplastic syndrome, usually caused by a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor producing excess FGF23, which leads to renal phosphate wasting and osteomalacia.
symptoms_not_in_common: No identified phosphaturic tumor is described
Long-term phenytoin exposure provides a more direct explanation
No documented renal phosphate wasting, elevated FGF23, or low calcitriol level

data.description: A proximal renal tubular disorder causing urinary losses of phosphate, glucose, bicarbonate, uric acid, and amino acids; chronic phosphate wasting can produce osteomalacia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal renal function without reported tubular dysfunction
No glucosuria, metabolic acidosis, aminoaciduria, or urinary phosphate wasting is reported
Long-term phenytoin exposure is a more likely explanation

data.description: Excess parathyroid hormone secretion causes increased bone turnover and renal phosphate loss; severe longstanding disease can cause skeletal pain, weakness, fractures, and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
symptoms_not_in_common: Looser's zones are more characteristic of osteomalacia than primary hyperparathyroidism
No hypercalcemia or elevated parathyroid hormone level is reported
Long-term phenytoin treatment strongly favors anticonvulsant-associated osteomalacia

data.description: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

data.diagnosis: Acute infective endocarditis of the mitral valve due to group A Streptococcus
data.description: A bacterial infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, with formation of valvular vegetations. The echocardiographic image is consistent with a mitral-valve vegetation, and blood cultures identify group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus.
symptoms_in_common: Positive blood culture for group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus
New or prominent grade 4/6 systolic murmur at the apex
Echocardiographic valvular mass consistent with vegetation
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal troponin T, CK, and CK-MB levels are not specifically diagnostic of endocarditis
Acute respiratory distress is possible with severe valve dysfunction but is not present in every case

data.diagnosis: Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke from infective endocarditis
data.description: An ischemic cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected valvular vegetation into the cerebral circulation. The brain image is compatible with an acute cortical infarct, likely from septic embolism.
symptoms_in_common: Poor performance on right-hand alternating movement testing
Focal brain lesion on imaging consistent with ischemic infarction
Mitral-valve vegetation as a potential embolic source
Fever and bacteremia supporting septic embolism
symptoms_not_in_common: Respiratory distress is not a typical primary manifestation of an ischemic stroke
Apical systolic murmur is not caused by stroke itself
Elevated NT-pro-BNP is not a usual direct feature of stroke

data.diagnosis: Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to infective mitral-valve destruction
data.description: Backward leakage of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole, potentially caused by infected mitral-valve leaflet damage or perforation. Color Doppler imaging appears consistent with substantial mitral regurgitation.
symptoms_in_common: Grade 4/6 systolic murmur maximal at the apex
Displaced apex beat in the sixth intercostal space outside the midclavicular line
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute dysarthria is not a typical direct manifestation of mitral regurgitation
Positive group A Streptococcus blood culture indicates the underlying infection rather than mitral regurgitation alone
Neutrophilic leukocytosis and elevated ESR are not caused by isolated noninfectious mitral regurgitation

data.diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure due to valvular infective endocarditis
data.description: Acute heart failure can occur when infective endocarditis causes severe valvular regurgitation, impaired forward cardiac output, and pulmonary congestion. In this case, mitral-valve involvement and severe regurgitation are likely contributors.
symptoms_in_common: Displaced apex beat suggesting cardiac enlargement or volume overload
Lethargy, which may reflect reduced perfusion or severe systemic illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever and positive blood cultures are not typical of heart failure alone
Acute focal neurologic deficits are not typical of uncomplicated heart failure
Neutrophilic leukocytosis and elevated ESR suggest infection rather than isolated heart failure

data.diagnosis: Group A streptococcal sepsis with septic embolization
data.description: A systemic infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes that can produce fever, tachycardia, inflammatory-marker elevation, organ dysfunction, and—in the setting of endocarditis—septic emboli to the brain or other organs.
symptoms_in_common: Heart rate of 116 beats per minute
Positive blood culture for group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus
Acute neurologic deficit potentially caused by septic cerebral embolism
symptoms_not_in_common: A focal grade 4/6 apical systolic murmur is more specifically explained by mitral-valve involvement
Displaced apex beat is not a typical primary feature of sepsis
Elevated NT-pro-BNP may reflect associated cardiac dysfunction rather than sepsis alone

data.description: 3.5-year-old male with normal birth history and unremarkable family history. Proteinuria, hematuria, and glycosuria were noted in the early neonatal period. He had a UTI at 12 months and developed bronchopneumonia with elevated creatinine at 3 years. Ongoing findings included persistent proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, reduced eGFR, elevated creatinine, uric acid, urea, total cholesterol, and triglycerides, with normal CBC, blood glucose, albumin, thyroid, and liver tests. Renal ultrasound showed increased cortical echogenicity and decreased corticomedullary differentiation. Physical features at 3 years 6 months included dolichocephaly, craniosynostosis, frontal bossing, full cheeks, broad nasal bridge, long philtrum, flat philtrum columns, narrow upper lip, everted lower lip, low-set/protruding ears, narrow chest, pectus excavatum, short ribs, wide ribs, rhizomelic limb shortening, short humeri, short fibulae, flattened epiphyses, brachydactyly, overlapping toes, joint laxity, fine sparse hair, small teeth, thin/short nails, and protuberant abdomen. Ophthalmologic findings included hyperopia, strabismus, and nystagmus. Motor development was normal.

A rare ciliopathy characterized by sagittal craniosynostosis/dolichocephaly, distinctive facial appearance, ectodermal abnormalities involving hair, teeth and nails, skeletal dysplasia with narrow thorax and short limbs, and progressive kidney disease.
symptoms_in_common: Frontal bossing, full cheeks, broad nasal bridge, long philtrum and narrow upper lip
Narrow chest, pectus excavatum, short/wide ribs
Rhizomelic limb shortening, short humeri, short fibulae and brachydactyly
Proteinuria and reduced eGFR with elevated creatinine and urea
Abnormal renal ultrasound with increased cortical echogenicity and reduced corticomedullary differentiation
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematuria beginning in the neonatal period
Marked glycosuria with normal blood glucose
Hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia
Urinary tract infection

data.diagnosis: Short-rib thoracic dysplasia with or without polydactyly (Jeune syndrome spectrum)
data.description: A group of ciliopathies causing a narrow thorax with short ribs, limb shortening, skeletal abnormalities, and variable renal disease that can progress to chronic kidney failure.
symptoms_in_common: Short ribs and abnormal rib shape
Progressive renal dysfunction with proteinuria and elevated creatinine
symptoms_not_in_common: Craniosynostosis and dolichocephaly
Fine sparse hair
Small teeth and thin/short nails
Long philtrum with narrow upper lip and everted lower lip
Hematuria and glycosuria from the neonatal period
No polydactyly reported

data.description: A ciliopathy usually featuring renal tubulointerstitial disease or nephronophthisis, retinal degeneration, cone-shaped epiphyses, and variable short stature or skeletal dysplasia.
symptoms_in_common: Early-onset chronic kidney disease with proteinuria and reduced eGFR
Ophthalmologic abnormalities including nystagmus and refractive error
symptoms_not_in_common: Craniosynostosis and marked dolichocephaly
Narrow thorax with short ribs
Fine sparse hair, small teeth and nail hypoplasia
Characteristic craniofacial appearance with long philtrum and everted lower lip
Hematuria and glycosuria in the neonatal period
No retinal dystrophy has been described

data.description: A multisystem disorder caused by SMARCAL1-related disease, characterized by steroid-resistant nephropathy, progressive renal failure, disproportionate short stature/spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, and often immune deficiency.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive renal insufficiency with elevated creatinine and reduced eGFR
Short stature pattern with limb and epiphyseal skeletal abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Craniosynostosis and dolichocephaly
Short ribs and narrow thorax
Fine sparse hair, dental abnormalities and thin nails
Typical Sensenbrenner-like facial features
Normal CBC without evidence of lymphopenia or immune deficiency
Glycosuria and hematuria from the neonatal period

data.description: A skeletal dysplasia characterized by short limbs, short ribs and narrow thorax, ectodermal abnormalities of hair, teeth and nails, and frequent congenital heart defects; renal disease is not a usual major feature.
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive chronic kidney disease with proteinuria and reduced eGFR
Hematuria and glycosuria beginning in the neonatal period
Abnormal renal cortical echogenicity
Craniosynostosis and dolichocephaly
No polydactyly reported
No congenital heart defect reported

data.description: A 58-year-old man presented with a six-week history of muscle weakness, dysphagia, and a symmetrical widespread rash on the face, torso, and limbs. Laboratory testing revealed elevated creatine kinase of 7070 u/L (reference range 30-175). An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed and showed abnormal findings, and a PET CT scan was arranged.
An inflammatory autoimmune myopathy causing characteristic skin lesions and proximal muscle weakness; in adults it may be associated with an underlying malignancy, including gastrointestinal cancer.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia due to involvement of pharyngeal/oesophageal muscles
Scaly erythematous papules over the knuckles consistent with Gottron papules
Abnormal oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and PET CT investigation suggesting possible associated malignancy

data.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, and possible dysphagia, but without the characteristic dermatomyositis rash.
symptoms_not_in_common: Symmetrical widespread rash
Papules and scaling over the knuckles consistent with Gottron papules
Facial rash

data.description: A severe autoimmune muscle disease causing rapidly progressive proximal weakness and marked creatine kinase elevation; it can occur with malignancy, statin exposure, or anti-SRP/anti-HMGCR antibodies.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia can occur in severe disease
Possible association with an underlying malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Characteristic widespread inflammatory skin rash
Gottron-like papules over the knuckles
Facial rash

data.description: A subtype of inflammatory myositis associated with antisynthetase antibodies, commonly causing myositis, inflammatory arthritis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and hyperkeratotic 'mechanic's hands.'
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia may occur with inflammatory myositis
Hand skin changes may be seen in myositis syndromes
symptoms_not_in_common: Gottron-like papules rather than mechanic's hands
Widespread facial, torso, and limb rash
No reported interstitial lung disease
No reported arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, or fever

data.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic inflammatory myopathy due to oesophageal malignancy
data.description: An inflammatory muscle syndrome triggered by an underlying cancer. Dermatomyositis is the most common paraneoplastic inflammatory myopathy and may precede discovery of oesophageal or other gastrointestinal malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: New-onset inflammatory muscle weakness at age 58
Characteristic dermatomyositis-type rash including knuckle lesions
PET CT findings prompting malignancy evaluation
symptoms_not_in_common: No confirmed tumour histology or specific cancer diagnosis is provided
No reported weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding, or odynophagia

data.description: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.

Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, causing fragmentation, flattening, and possible collapse of the capital femoral epiphysis. It most often affects boys aged 4 to 10 years.
symptoms_in_common: Hip pain with reduced internal rotation

data.description: Displacement of the femoral head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, usually occurring in adolescents during periods of rapid growth and often associated with obesity.
symptoms_in_common: Leg pain that may be referred from the hip
Painful limitation of hip internal rotation
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 8 years is younger than the typical adolescent presentation
No reported obesity or rapid growth history
Occasional mild pain rather than more persistent hip, groin, thigh, or knee pain

data.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip effusion, often occurring after a viral illness, that causes acute hip pain and a limp in children.
symptoms_not_in_common: No preceding viral illness is described
Reduced internal rotation and abduction with radiographic structural femoral-head abnormality would be atypical
The presentation appears more consistent with a chronic mechanical hip disorder than an acute self-limited episode

data.description: A bacterial infection of the hip joint that can rapidly damage cartilage and bone; it is an orthopedic emergency and commonly causes severe pain, fever, and inability to bear weight.
symptoms_in_common: Painful restricted hip range of motion
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
Otherwise healthy and well appearance
Only occasional leg pain rather than severe acute pain
No systemic illness described
No reported refusal or inability to bear weight

data.diagnosis: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the hip
data.description: A chronic inflammatory arthritis beginning before age 16 that may cause joint pain, stiffness, reduced range of motion, and gait disturbance; isolated hip involvement is less common.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced hip abduction and internal rotation
symptoms_not_in_common: No prolonged morning stiffness reported
No swelling or inflammatory symptoms in other joints reported
No recurrent fevers, rash, fatigue, or other systemic inflammatory features
Imaging appearance of femoral-head fragmentation or collapse would be less typical than in Perthes disease

data.description: A 62-year-old fit and well Romanian man presented with a two-week history of worsening acute localized pain in the upper abdomen and vomiting. His surgical history included an open appendectomy as a child and laparoscopic cholecystectomy 20 years ago. On presentation, he had fever (39°C) and tachycardia (104 beats/min), with blood pressure of 125/73 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, worse in the right upper quadrant, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 16 × 10⁹/L (reference range 4-10 × 10⁹/L) and a C reactive protein concentration of 277 mg/L (reference value <9 mg/L). A frontal projection erect chest radiograph was initially reported as showing pneumoperitoneum, but showed a normal bowel gas pattern under the left hemidiaphragm.

A bacterial abscess within the liver, sometimes caused by gas-producing organisms such as Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, or anaerobes. Gas within a hepatic abscess can mimic free intraperitoneal air on radiography.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper-quadrant and upper abdominal pain
Generalized abdominal tenderness with right upper-quadrant guarding
Imaging appearance of gas associated with the liver
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported jaundice
No reported diarrhoea
No reported weight loss or prolonged constitutional symptoms

data.diagnosis: Ruptured or perforated pyogenic liver abscess with perihepatic gas
data.description: A liver abscess may enlarge, rupture into the subcapsular or peritoneal space, and cause localized peritonitis, sepsis, and an apparent pneumoperitoneum.
symptoms_in_common: High white cell count and C-reactive protein
Apparent free air beneath the right hemidiaphragm on chest radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure is preserved rather than showing septic shock
No reported diffuse rigid abdomen
No reported jaundice

data.description: A gastric or duodenal ulcer can perforate, releasing air and gastrointestinal contents into the peritoneal cavity and producing acute peritonitis with pneumoperitoneum.
symptoms_in_common: Initial chest radiograph interpreted as pneumoperitoneum
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is most pronounced in the right upper quadrant rather than epigastrium
Two-week progressive course is less typical than sudden onset severe pain
CT appearance suggests gas related to the liver rather than uncomplicated free intraperitoneal gas
No history of dyspepsia, peptic ulcer disease, NSAID use, or gastrointestinal bleeding is reported

data.diagnosis: Acute cholangitis due to biliary obstruction
data.description: Bacterial infection of an obstructed biliary system, commonly from choledocholithiasis or biliary stricture, causes fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and systemic inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: History of prior gallbladder disease treated with cholecystectomy
symptoms_not_in_common: No jaundice is reported
No abnormal liver-function tests or biliary dilatation are provided
Localized guarding and apparent subdiaphragmatic gas are not typical primary features
Generalized peritoneal tenderness is less typical without perforation or abscess formation

data.diagnosis: Perforated hollow viscus from small-bowel obstruction or adhesional complication
data.description: Prior abdominal operations can cause adhesions leading to bowel obstruction; bowel ischemia or perforation can then produce vomiting, peritonitis, sepsis, and free intraperitoneal gas.
symptoms_in_common: Previous open appendectomy and laparoscopic abdominal surgery
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal bowel gas pattern on the chest radiograph
Pain is predominantly right upper-quadrant rather than diffuse or colicky
No reported abdominal distension, obstipation, or reduced bowel movements
Imaging appearance is more suggestive of a hepatic/perihepatic gas-containing process

data.description: A 1-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted for evaluation of psychomotor retardation and an operation for exotropia. She was born at term (gestational age: 40 weeks) by cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, and was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The family history was unremarkable. On admission, she presented with a characteristic high-pitched cry and microcephaly. She showed delayed motor functions and crawling, was able to sit unassisted but unable to stand, with developmental characteristics lagging behind for normal chronologic age. On neurologic examination, she had left leg hypotonia, with normal tendon reflexes and normal cranial nerve signs. When she was 6 months old, ventricular septal defect was detected by echocardiography. Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (5) (p15.2) one month after delivery.

A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and possible congenital heart defects. The documented 5p15.2 deletion is diagnostic.
symptoms_in_common: Global psychomotor and motor developmental delay
Delayed crawling and inability to stand at 16 months
Brain imaging abnormalities compatible with neurodevelopmental involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal tendon reflexes are possible but not a defining feature
Unilateral left-leg hypotonia is less typical than generalized hypotonia

data.description: A chromosomal deletion syndrome caused by loss of material from chromosome 4p. It commonly causes severe developmental delay, growth restriction, microcephaly, hypotonia, seizures, eye abnormalities, and congenital heart defects.
symptoms_not_in_common: High-pitched cat-like cry is not characteristic
No seizures reported
No prenatal or postnatal growth restriction reported
Chromosomal testing shows a 5p deletion rather than a 4p deletion
No typical 'Greek warrior helmet' facial appearance described

data.description: A chromosome deletion disorder involving the distal short arm of chromosome 1, associated with developmental delay or intellectual disability, hypotonia, microcephaly, visual problems, seizures, brain abnormalities, and congenital cardiac defects.
symptoms_in_common: Possible structural brain abnormalities on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: High-pitched cat-like cry is not a typical hallmark
No seizures reported
No feeding difficulty or hearing loss reported
Chromosomal analysis identifies deletion of chromosome 5p rather than 1p36

data.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder usually caused by deletion of chromosome 22q13 involving the SHANK3 gene. It is characterized by severe speech and developmental delay, neonatal hypotonia, reduced pain perception, autistic features, and sometimes minor dysmorphic or cardiac findings.
symptoms_not_in_common: Microcephaly is less typical; normal or accelerated head growth is more common
High-pitched cat-like cry is not characteristic
No absent or severely delayed speech specifically reported
No autistic behaviors or reduced pain sensitivity reported
Chromosomal analysis shows a 5p deletion rather than a 22q13 deletion

data.description: A congenital viral infection that can cause microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia or motor impairment, intracranial abnormalities, hearing loss, visual abnormalities, and growth restriction.
symptoms_not_in_common: High-pitched cat-like cry is not typical
Ventricular septal defect is not a classic manifestation
No hearing loss, seizures, petechiae, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, or growth restriction reported
Uneventful pregnancy and term birth do not support a typical symptomatic congenital infection presentation
The confirmed chromosome 5p deletion provides a more direct explanation

data.description: A 7-year-old girl with no past medical history presented with intermittent abdominal pain for about 1 month, unrelieved by anti-inflammatory treatment. Abdominal CT showed peritoneal effusion and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was elevated at 1,210 ng/mL. Ultrasonography revealed multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal hypoechoic lymph nodes; the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina were unremarkable. Surgical resection found a 4 cm full-thickness jejunal mass with a grey-white cut surface. Histology showed a highly mitotic tumor with microcystic, reticular, macrocystic, papillary, solid, and tubule-glandular patterns. Lymph nodes showed reactive hyperplasia.

data.diagnosis: Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of the jejunum
data.description: A malignant germ-cell tumor showing yolk-sac differentiation, typically associated with markedly elevated AFP and diverse histologic patterns including microcystic/reticular, papillary, solid, and glandular areas. Primary gastrointestinal involvement is exceptionally rare.
symptoms_in_common: Macrocystic, papillary, solid, and tubule-glandular histologic patterns
No ovarian or other genital tract mass, supporting an extragonadal primary site
symptoms_not_in_common: Reactive rather than metastatic lymph nodes

data.description: An aggressive nonseminomatous germ-cell tumor that can produce AFP when associated with yolk-sac differentiation. Histology often shows primitive epithelial cells in solid, glandular, papillary, or tubular patterns.
symptoms_in_common: Solid, papillary, and tubule-glandular architectural patterns
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominant microcystic and reticular pattern is more characteristic of yolk sac tumor
A primary jejunal location is very unusual
No gonadal mass was identified
Macrocystic pattern is less typical

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from intestinal mucosal glands, usually occurring in adults and capable of invading through the bowel wall and producing obstruction, pain, or peritoneal spread.
symptoms_in_common: Jejunal mass involving the full bowel wall
symptoms_not_in_common: Age of 7 years is highly atypical
Marked AFP elevation is not typical
Microcystic and reticular tumor pattern is not typical
Very high mitotic activity with mixed yolk-sac-like patterns is unusual
Retroperitoneal lymph nodes were reactive rather than metastatic

data.description: A rare aggressive pediatric and young-adult malignancy that usually arises in the peritoneal cavity and commonly presents with abdominal masses, ascites, and peritoneal dissemination.
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked serum AFP elevation is not typical
A discrete primary full-thickness jejunal mass is less typical than multifocal peritoneal disease
Microcystic, reticular, papillary, and tubule-glandular morphology is not characteristic
No desmoplastic stromal pattern was described
Female sex is less common than male sex

data.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small intestine
data.description: Pediatric non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve the ileum or jejunum and cause abdominal pain, bowel-wall masses, ascites, and abdominal lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked AFP elevation is not typical
Lymph nodes showed reactive hyperplasia rather than lymphoma involvement
Microcystic, reticular, macrocystic, papillary, and glandular histology is not typical of lymphoma
The described tumor is epithelial/germ-cell-patterned rather than a lymphoid neoplasm

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

data.description: 6-month-old boy with 2 days of intermittent nocturnal abdominal pain causing crying, leg-drawing, and abdominal rigidity, followed by three bowel movements with progressively increasing red blood, the last nearly all blood with a large clot. History includes infantile colic and gastroesophageal reflux treated with ranitidine; recently started pureed foods and was on low-lactose cow milk-based formula. On presentation he was tachycardic and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right, without masses or anal fissures; later developed pallor with persistent tachycardia and low blood pressure. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.7 g/dl, hematocrit 17.5%), leukocytosis, elevated reticulocyte count, and low serum iron.

data.diagnosis: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
data.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ileal ulceration and sometimes massive painless or painful lower gastrointestinal bleeding. The scan appearance is consistent with ectopic gastric mucosa in the right lower abdomen.
symptoms_in_common: Progressively bloody stools with a large clot
Focal right lower abdominal uptake on technetium-99m pertechnetate imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent colicky abdominal pain with leg-drawing
Abdominal rigidity
Leukocytosis

data.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, most often ileocolic in infants, causing episodic colicky pain, obstruction, ischemia, and bloody mucus-containing stool.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent severe abdominal pain with crying and leg-drawing
Abdominal tenderness, worse on the right
Tachycardia and hypotension in severe disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Massive hemorrhage with stool nearly entirely composed of blood
Severe anemia with hemoglobin of 5.7 g/dl after only 2 days
No palpable abdominal mass
Focal uptake suggestive of ectopic gastric mucosa on nuclear imaging

data.diagnosis: Enteric duplication cyst with ectopic gastric mucosa
data.description: A rare congenital duplication of the gastrointestinal tract that can contain ectopic gastric mucosa, resulting in ulceration, bleeding, abdominal pain, or obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal pain and right-sided abdominal tenderness
Severe anemia and pallor from blood loss
Possible uptake on technetium-99m pertechnetate imaging due to ectopic gastric mucosa
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal mass was detected
Leg-drawing episodic colic is less characteristic
Large-volume abrupt rectal bleeding is less common than with a bleeding Meckel diverticulum

data.description: A non-IgE-mediated food allergy in young infants that causes colonic inflammation and small amounts of rectal bleeding, often related to cow's milk protein exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Recent dietary changes with introduction of pureed foods
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe intermittent abdominal pain with leg-drawing
Abdominal rigidity and marked right-sided tenderness
Massive bloody stools with a large clot
Profound anemia with hemoglobin of 5.7 g/dl
Pallor, persistent tachycardia, and hypotension
Focal ectopic gastric-mucosa-type uptake on nuclear imaging

data.description: Inflammation of the intestine caused by bacterial or viral infection, which can produce abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and bloody stools in infants.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported fever or diarrhea
Intermittent nocturnal colicky episodes with leg-drawing
Massive acute gastrointestinal blood loss with severe anemia
Hypotension from hemorrhagic blood loss
Focal right lower abdominal uptake on technetium-99m pertechnetate imaging

data.description: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.
Abnormal direct connections between pulmonary arteries and veins that create right-to-left shunting; CT typically shows well-defined enhancing vascular nodules with feeding and draining vessels.
symptoms_in_common: CT appearance of multiple vascular pulmonary nodules with apparent feeding/draining vessels
Normal transthoracic echocardiogram does not exclude pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe obstructive spirometry with a small-airway disease flow-volume loop is not typical of pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
No reported cyanosis, hypoxemia, clubbing, hemoptysis, migraine, or neurologic complications

data.diagnosis: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
data.description: An inherited vascular disorder characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations, commonly involving the lungs, nose, gastrointestinal tract, liver, and brain.
symptoms_in_common: Breathlessness that may result from pulmonary right-to-left shunting
Multiple pulmonary vascular lesions compatible with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
Female sex and presentation in later adulthood are compatible
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported recurrent epistaxis
No reported mucocutaneous telangiectasias
No reported family history of HHT
Severe small-airway obstruction is not a usual primary manifestation of HHT

data.description: An obstructive small-airway disorder caused by inflammatory and fibrotic narrowing of bronchioles, producing progressive and often fixed airflow limitation; CT may show mosaic attenuation and air trapping.
symptoms_in_common: Flow-volume loop suggesting severe small-airway disease
Normal echocardiogram, supporting a noncardiac cause of dyspnea
symptoms_not_in_common: The prominent rounded enhancing vascular lesions on CT are not typical of bronchiolitis obliterans
No reported history of transplantation, inhalational injury, severe respiratory infection, autoimmune disease, or drug exposure

data.diagnosis: Asthma with severe fixed airflow obstruction
data.description: A chronic inflammatory airway disease causing episodic or persistent airflow obstruction, breathlessness, wheeze, and cough; longstanding disease can produce partially fixed small-airway obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Small-airway disease pattern on the flow-volume loop
Nonsmoking status is compatible with asthma
symptoms_not_in_common: New presentation at 69 years without a prior respiratory history is less typical

data.description: 27-year-old man with a few days of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. History notable for left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement that had intermittently enlarged and regressed since age 15. On examination, he was thin, had low-grade fever (37.6°C), mild hypoxemia (SpO₂ 94% on room air), crackles in the left upper lung field, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures for bacteria, acid-fast organisms, and fungi were negative; autoimmune serologies, HIV antibody, and tumor markers were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identified pathogens.

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary sarcoidosis with concomitant unicentric Castleman disease
data.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, often involving the lungs and lymph nodes. Negative bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, HIV, and autoimmune testing

Unilateral upper-lobe destructive/cystic change is less typical than bilateral hilar and mediastinal adenopathy

symptoms_not_in_common: Repeatedly negative sputum and tissue studies for acid-fast organisms

data.description:
A 31-year-old Caucasian man with multiple sclerosis who had received 24 natalizumab infusions and was switched to fingolimod due to persistent high anti-JCPyV antibody index (3.61). After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs. He presented with leukopenia (0.83 × 10^9/L) at hospital admission.

data.description: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

data.description: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

data.description: A severe sterile pustular drug eruption characterized by abrupt onset of numerous small nonfollicular pustules, neutrophilic inflammation, and frequent neutrophilia. Iodinated contrast media can rarely trigger it within hours to days.

data.description: 54-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to cardiology clinic for follow-up 20 months since her most recent office visit. She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. The patient was in her usual state of health and asymptomatic without changes in her exercise tolerance, weight, or energy levels. She did not have any gross hematuria or flank pain.

45-year-old man with acute illness after dog bites. He was well until the day before admission, when he developed nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting. Three days earlier, he had been bitten on the hands and forearms while bathing his dog. He also reported head trauma from a rusty nail a few days earlier and dental extractions 1–2 weeks prior. Past history included asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse, with recent intake up to 18 beers daily, stopped 3 days before admission. On examination, he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic, with hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and delayed capillary refill. He had numerous lacerations with necrotic edges and scratch marks on the hands and forearms, including a larger purplish lesion on the right forearm.

Purplish skin lesion and widespread purpuric/necrotic skin changes

data.description: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body in the rectum
Endoscopic finding of a gallstone in the rectum
symptoms_not_in_common: Known Crohn's disease is not required for gallstone ileus

data.description: Crohn's disease can cause chronic inflammation and scarring of the anus or rectum, resulting in narrowing of the bowel lumen and obstructed defecation.
symptoms_not_in_common: A gallstone visualized in the rectum is not typical of a Crohn-related stricture

data.description: Fecal impaction is accumulation of hardened stool in the rectum that can cause obstructed defecation, pressure, and minor mucosal bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body in the rectum
symptoms_not_in_common: Endoscopic identification of a gallstone rather than impacted stool
Known Crohn's disease is not a typical cause in itself

data.description: A retained object in the rectum can produce rectal pressure, impaired stool passage, mucosal trauma, and bleeding. In this case, the gallstone functioned as an intraluminal foreign body.
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body in the rectum
Endoscopically detected object in the rectum
symptoms_not_in_common: The object was a migrated gallstone rather than a typical externally inserted foreign body
Known Crohn's disease is not typical of rectal foreign body presentation

data.diagnosis: Rectal or colorectal malignancy causing partial obstruction
data.description: A rectal or colorectal tumor can narrow the bowel lumen and cause altered stool passage, rectal pressure, and bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of rectal fullness or a foreign body
symptoms_not_in_common: A gallstone found and removed from the rectum provides an alternative mechanical cause
No rectal mass or tumor was described on endoscopy
Known Crohn's disease is a risk context but does not establish malignancy

data.description: 15-year-old boy presented after injuring his left knee while carrying a tray of food at a fast food restaurant. He felt his knee 'wobble' and fell to the floor, unable to bear weight due to pain. Medical history included chronic fatigue syndrome. Had a Beighton score of 6 (indicating joint laxity) but no history of joint dislocations. On examination: laterally dislocated patella, moderate effusion, pain on palpation around medial patellofemoral ligament, range of movement reduced to extension-flexion of 0/10/60 degrees, ligamentous tests unremarkable. Two weeks later: complained of intermittent locking in left knee, had joint effusion and palpable loose body under patella.
Displacement of the patella to the outside of the knee, commonly occurring in adolescents with ligamentous laxity and often causing injury to the medial patellofemoral ligament.
symptoms_in_common: Knee felt unstable or 'wobbled' before the fall
Tenderness around the medial patellofemoral ligament
Generalized joint laxity with Beighton score of 6
symptoms_not_in_common: Palpable loose body beneath the patella two weeks later
Intermittent locking after the injury

data.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, often from the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after a lateral patellar dislocation; the fragment may detach and become a loose body.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to bear weight immediately after injury
Palpable loose body under the patella
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic fatigue syndrome
Generalized joint laxity is not itself a typical consequence of an osteochondral fracture

data.diagnosis: Intra-articular loose body of the knee
data.description: A free fragment of cartilage, bone, or osteochondral tissue within the knee joint, commonly resulting from trauma such as patellar dislocation and capable of causing mechanical locking.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable loose body beneath the patella
symptoms_not_in_common: Observed lateral patellar dislocation at the initial presentation
Medial patellofemoral ligament tenderness
Generalized joint laxity

data.diagnosis: Medial patellofemoral ligament injury or tear
data.description: Sprain or tearing of the main ligament that restrains lateral patellar movement, typically occurring during an acute lateral patellar dislocation.
symptoms_in_common: Tenderness around the medial patellofemoral ligament
Acute knee pain after a patellar instability event
Generalized joint laxity increasing risk of patellar instability
symptoms_not_in_common: Palpable loose body beneath the patella
Intermittent locking is less typical unless there is an associated osteochondral injury

data.description: A tear of the medial or lateral meniscus, usually from a twisting knee injury, which may cause pain, swelling, catching, and mechanical locking.
symptoms_not_in_common: Laterally dislocated patella on examination
Medial patellofemoral ligament tenderness
Palpable loose body under the patella is more suggestive of an osteochondral fragment
Generalized joint laxity is not a typical feature of an isolated meniscal tear

data.description: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

A rare follicular variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring loss of axillary and pubic hair, and widespread keratotic follicular papules (lichen spinulosus-like lesions).
symptoms_in_common: Long-standing intensely pruritic papular spiny follicular eruption on trunk and limbs
Scalp alopecia developing after the body papules
Clinical and dermoscopic appearance of keratotic follicular plugs
Histologic lichenoid perifollicular inflammation compatible with lichen planopilaris
symptoms_not_in_common: Family history of psoriasis in a sister
Lack of response to topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines

data.description: A lymphocyte-mediated inflammatory disorder that destroys hair follicles and causes permanent scarring alopecia; follicular keratotic papules and perifollicular scale may occur.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent generalized papular eruption preceding scalp alopecia by years
Marked axillary and pubic hair loss
Truncal and limb lesions as the dominant initial manifestation
Family history of psoriasis

data.description: An uncommon follicular keratosis producing groups of rough, spiny keratotic papules, often on the trunk and extremities; it can resemble keratosis pilaris.
symptoms_in_common: Spiny follicular papules on the trunk and limbs
symptoms_not_in_common: Scarring alopecia of the scalp
Pubic alopecia
Axillary alopecia
Lichenoid perifollicular inflammation suggestive of lichen planopilaris
Very prolonged 13-year course with progressive multi-site hair loss

data.description: A common benign disorder of follicular keratinization causing rough, small keratotic papules, usually on the upper arms, thighs, buttocks, or cheeks.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe pruritus
Extensive involvement of trunk and limbs with prominent follicular plugs
Scalp alopecia
Pubic and axillary hair loss
Lichenoid inflammatory infiltrate around hair follicles
Failure to improve with topical corticosteroids

data.description: A papulosquamous keratinization disorder that may cause follicular hyperkeratotic papules, reddish-orange scaling plaques, palmoplantar keratoderma, and sometimes alopecia.
symptoms_in_common: Alopecia may occur in severe or chronic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported orange-red scaly plaques
No reported palmoplantar keratoderma
Selective pubic and axillary alopecia is not typical
Scarring alopecia pattern is not typical
Lichenoid perifollicular inflammation is not the characteristic histology
