data.description: 35-year-old woman with severe hypertension, edema, and renal failure. History of preeclampsia 12 months earlier requiring Caesarean delivery at 29 weeks, followed by poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria >1 g/day. Over the preceding 6 months, she developed fatigue, headaches, severe hypertension, and facial/pedal edema. She denied fever, neurologic symptoms, and diarrheal prodrome. Exam showed pallor, hydration, and blood pressure 151/103 mmHg. Labs revealed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked renal dysfunction, proteinuria 4.9 g/24 h with hematuria, elevated reticulocytes, schistocytes, high LDH, elevated bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and negative Coombs test; liver enzymes, immunologic tests, viral screening, and antiphospholipid antibodies were normal.

A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period and characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and prominent kidney injury.
symptoms_in_common: Ulcerative/necrotic skin lesions compatible with thrombotic vasculopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: No neurologic symptoms
No fever

data.description: Severe uncontrolled hypertension can damage small vessels, producing endothelial injury, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and mechanical hemolytic anemia; it may also cause ischemic skin lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Cutaneous ulceration/necrosis suggestive of small-vessel injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Preeclampsia preceding the illness by 12 months
Severe anemia and thrombocytopenia may be more pronounced than in hypertension alone
No hypertensive neurologic manifestations such as confusion, seizures, or visual disturbance

data.description: A severe thrombotic microangiopathy, usually due to marked ADAMTS13 deficiency, causing thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with variable kidney, neurologic, and systemic involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Renal failure is unusually severe and dominant for classic TTP
No neurologic symptoms apart from headache
No fever
Long course of progressive hypertension and proteinuria following preeclampsia

data.diagnosis: Pregnancy-associated thrombotic microangiopathy related to preeclampsia/HELLP-spectrum disease
data.description: Preeclampsia and related pregnancy-associated endothelial injury can cause hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, and renal injury; persistent or delayed disease may reveal an underlying complement-mediated TMA.
symptoms_in_common: History of severe preeclampsia requiring preterm Caesarean delivery
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation is 12 months after delivery rather than during pregnancy or immediately postpartum
Normal liver enzymes
Persistent severe renal failure long after pregnancy
Ulcerative/necrotic ankle skin lesions are not typical features

data.diagnosis: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) or antiphospholipid-associated thrombotic vasculopathy
data.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder causing widespread small-vessel thrombosis, which may lead to renal thrombotic microangiopathy, thrombocytopenia, hypertension, skin necrosis, and pregnancy complications.
symptoms_in_common: Cutaneous ulcerative or necrotic lesions compatible with thrombotic vasculopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Antiphospholipid antibody testing was negative
No reported large-vessel thrombosis
No multiorgan acute thromboses described
No fever or systemic inflammatory presentation

data.description: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).

data.diagnosis: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the ileum
data.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursors. Most GISTs express KIT (CD117), and activating KIT exon 11 mutations are characteristic and support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Ileal wall mass in the right lower quadrant
Syncope likely related to acute or chronic blood-loss anemia
Resected localized tumor without metastatic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative colonoscopy is not unusual but does not directly characterize GIST

data.description: A neuroendocrine neoplasm that commonly arises in the distal ileum and may present as an enhancing small-bowel mass, sometimes with bleeding, obstruction, or metastatic mesenteric and liver disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 deletion mutation is not typical
Severe bleeding with hemoglobin of 6 g/dL is less typical than occult bleeding or obstruction
No carcinoid syndrome symptoms such as flushing, diarrhea, or wheezing
No mesenteric mass, desmoplastic reaction, or liver metastases reported

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can cause gastrointestinal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, abdominal pain, obstruction, or weight loss.
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 deletion is not characteristic of adenocarcinoma
A discrete enhancing mass arising from the bowel wall is more suggestive of a mesenchymal tumor in this context
No bowel obstruction, abdominal pain, weight loss, or metastatic lymphadenopathy reported

data.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the small intestine that may produce bowel-wall thickening or a mass and can present with bleeding, anemia, pain, obstruction, or systemic symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 deletion is not typical of lymphoma
Solitary, well-defined contrast-enhancing ileal mass is less typical than diffuse thickening or bulky nodal disease
No lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, fever, night sweats, or weight loss reported
No metastatic or disseminated disease seen on CT

data.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise from the intestinal wall and may cause bleeding, anemia, abdominal pain, or a mass. It can resemble GIST morphologically but generally lacks the characteristic KIT molecular alterations of GIST.
symptoms_in_common: Mass arising from the ileal wall
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 activating deletion strongly favors GIST rather than leiomyosarcoma
No metastatic disease, whereas leiomyosarcoma may present with hematogenous spread
No reported smooth-muscle immunophenotype such as diffuse desmin or smooth-muscle actin positivity

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

data.description: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

data.diagnosis: Solid serous adenoma of the pancreas
data.description: A rare solid variant of pancreatic serous cystadenoma, a generally benign epithelial neoplasm composed of glycogen-rich clear cells and a prominent capillary network. It can mimic hypervascular solid pancreatic tumors on imaging.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion from mass effect on adjacent pancreas or gastrointestinal structures
Normal laboratory results apart from pre-existing hyperglycemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Diabetes mellitus is not a specific presenting feature of this tumor
Hypertension is unrelated to the tumor

data.description: A neoplasm arising from pancreatic endocrine cells. Nonfunctioning tumors may become large before detection and can present with abdominal mass effect, whereas functioning tumors produce hormone-related syndromes.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion or early gastrointestinal symptoms due to a large pancreatic mass
Normal routine laboratory findings in a nonfunctioning tumor
Diabetes or hyperglycemia can occur with pancreatic endocrine dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: No hormone-excess syndrome such as hypoglycemia, flushing, diarrhea, or peptic-ulcer symptoms
No abdominal pain or tenderness
No jaundice

data.description: A rare malignant pancreatic epithelial tumor with acinar differentiation. It often forms a large, well-circumscribed solid mass and may cause nonspecific abdominal symptoms or pancreatic exocrine dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Large palpable epigastric or intra-abdominal mass
Possible association with diabetes or hyperglycemia
symptoms_not_in_common: No weight loss reported
No abdominal pain or tenderness
No lipase-hypersecretion manifestations such as subcutaneous fat necrosis or polyarthritis
No abnormal liver tests or jaundice

data.diagnosis: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
data.description: A low-grade malignant pancreatic neoplasm that is typically encapsulated and contains solid and degenerative or hemorrhagic areas. It occurs predominantly in young women but can rarely occur in older men.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion or nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms from mass effect
symptoms_not_in_common: Patient is a 73-year-old man, whereas this tumor usually occurs in young women
No abdominal pain or tenderness
No reported nausea, vomiting, or weight loss

data.description: The most common primary pancreatic malignancy, usually arising from pancreatic ducts. It often causes obstructive jaundice, weight loss, abdominal or back pain, and progressive decline, especially when located in the pancreatic head.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion that may reflect pancreatic insufficiency
Palpable epigastric mass in advanced disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal or back pain
No jaundice
No weight loss reported
No abnormal liver-function tests or other laboratory abnormalities
No tenderness on examination

data.description: A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

An autosomal dominant acantholytic skin disorder caused by impaired keratinocyte adhesion, producing recurrent painful, erosive, crusted plaques in flexural areas that worsen with heat, sweating, and friction.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic recurrent rash in the axillae
Maceration, erosions, and malodorous crusting in a skin fold
Family history of a similar axillary rash in a sister
Normal oral and other mucosal membranes
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation
Numerous acrochordons
Pseudofolliculitis barbae

data.description: A rare vegetating variant of pemphigus vulgaris characterized by flaccid blisters that evolve into painful, eroded, verrucous plaques, often in axillae, groin, and other intertriginous sites.
symptoms_in_common: Painful, crusted lesions in the axilla
symptoms_not_in_common: Five-year recurrent course that is specifically worse in summer
Family history of a similar rash
Normal oral mucosa
No other mucosal involvement
Prominent hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation
Multiple acrochordons
Mild rather than severe pruritus

data.description: An inherited disorder of keratinization and epidermal adhesion causing greasy, crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic and flexural areas; heat, sweating, and friction commonly exacerbate it.
symptoms_in_common: Worsening with summer heat and sweating
symptoms_not_in_common: Disease confined predominantly to the axillae
Large macerated erosive plaques rather than widespread keratotic papules
No nail abnormalities
No mucosal lesions
No reported seborrheic distribution involving scalp, forehead, chest, or back
Multiple acrochordons

data.description: Psoriasis affecting skin folds, where lesions are often smooth, red or hyperpigmented, painful, and prone to maceration because of moisture and friction.
symptoms_in_common: Maceration and erosions may occur in severe fold disease
Overweight status, which increases friction in skin folds
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent blisters
Family history of an identical axillary blistering eruption
Marked malodorous crusting
Multiple acrochordons within the lesion
Histologic acantholysis rather than psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia
Summer-triggered recurrent erosive flares are less characteristic

data.description: Acanthosis nigricans causes velvety hyperpigmented thickening of flexural skin, commonly associated with obesity and insulin resistance; moisture and friction can lead to secondary intertrigo with odor, maceration, and erosion.
symptoms_in_common: Maceration, odor, and erosions compatible with superimposed intertrigo
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent blister formation
Painful erosive rash worsening in summer as the principal presentation
Similar familial blistering rash suggesting an inherited acantholytic disorder
Hypopigmented areas
Histologic acantholysis
Mild pruritus as a prominent symptom

data.description: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

A benign reactive process in which bone forms within soft tissue or muscle, often after trauma but sometimes without a recognized injury. Imaging commonly shows a well-circumscribed mass with peripheral mature ossification (zonal pattern).
symptoms_in_common: Gradually enlarging tender pelvic soft-tissue mass
Peripheral mineralization/ossification of the mass on CT
Heterogeneous MRI appearance compatible with evolving ossification
Increased uptake on bone scintigraphy and FDG-PET, which can occur in active myositis ossificans
No fever or systemic infectious symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of preceding trauma, although nontraumatic myositis ossificans can occur

data.description: A rare malignant mesenchymal tumor that produces osteoid or bone in soft tissues without originating from bone. It usually presents as an enlarging calcified soft-tissue mass.
symptoms_in_common: Calcified or ossified soft-tissue pelvic mass
Heterogeneous soft-tissue appearance on CT and MRI
Increased radiotracer uptake on bone scintigraphy
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 22 years, as extraskeletal osteosarcoma is more typical in older adults
Short 1-month clinical history
No imaging evidence described of aggressive invasion or destruction of adjacent bone

data.description: A low-grade bone-forming osteosarcoma arising from the outer cortical surface of bone, often producing a densely ossified mass adjacent to the pelvis or long bones.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly enlarging painful or tender mass
Mineralized mass adjacent to the iliac bone
Bone-scan uptake within an ossified lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: The imaging appearance suggests a primarily soft-tissue mass rather than a lesion clearly attached to the cortex
No described cortical thickening, cortical erosion, or marrow continuity with the iliac bone
Rapid symptom development over only 1 month

data.description: A malignant soft-tissue sarcoma that commonly occurs in adolescents and young adults and may contain punctate or peripheral calcifications. It can arise near joints, including the hip and pelvic region.
symptoms_in_common: Calcifications within a heterogeneous soft-tissue mass
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear relationship to a joint or tendon sheath is described
Extensive mature peripheral ossification is less typical than small focal calcifications
No evidence described of invasive local behavior or metastases

data.description: A benign cartilaginous tumor arising in soft tissues, sometimes with calcification or ossification. It is usually slow growing and may be painful because of local mass effect.
symptoms_in_common: Soft-tissue lesion with calcified or ossified components
Lack of fever or systemic illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Pelvic location is less common than the hands and feet
Rapid enlargement over 1 month is less typical
Marked bone-scan and FDG-PET activity may be more concerning for active ossification or malignancy than a typical benign chondroma

data.description: 36-year-old female with no past medical history who developed progressive lower-limb and paraspinal muscle spasms over 3 months, worsening to wheelchair dependence 6 months later. She became severely disabled, required regular IVIG every 12 days, diazepam 30 mg/day, and morphine up to 60 mg/day for pain. Examination showed brisk reflexes and severe clonus, and spasms were severe enough to impair breathing, requiring intermittent oxygen.

A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and limb muscle rigidity, painful stimulus-sensitive spasms, and continuous motor-unit activity on electromyography; commonly associated with anti-GAD65 or amphiphysin antibodies.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive paraspinal and lower-limb muscle stiffness and spasms
Severe painful spasms requiring diazepam and morphine
Marked functional decline progressing to wheelchair dependence
Continuous involuntary muscle activity on the displayed electrophysiology
Improvement/need for ongoing IVIG is consistent with immune-mediated SPS
Spasms involving truncal/respiratory muscles causing breathing difficulty
symptoms_not_in_common: Brisk reflexes and severe clonus are less typical in classic SPS, in which reflexes may be normal or difficult to assess because of rigidity
Very severe respiratory compromise is uncommon in classic SPS, although it can occur in severe disease

data.diagnosis: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
data.description: A severe autoimmune stiff-person-spectrum disorder, often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, producing rigidity, painful spasms, exaggerated reflexes, myoclonus, and potentially brainstem or respiratory involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Rapidly progressive severe rigidity and spasms
Respiratory impairment due to severe spasms
Electrophysiologic evidence of abnormal continuous muscle activation
symptoms_not_in_common: No myoclonus is specifically described
No encephalopathy, confusion, seizures, eye-movement abnormalities, or other brainstem signs are reported
No autonomic instability is described

data.description: An autoimmune form of stiff-person spectrum disease caused by antibodies targeting glutamic acid decarboxylase 65, resulting in impaired inhibitory GABAergic signaling and severe muscle hyperexcitability.
symptoms_in_common: Adult onset of progressive stiffness and painful spasms
Need for high-dose diazepam, which enhances GABAergic inhibition
Use of IVIG, a common immunotherapy for anti-GAD65 SPS
Continuous motor-unit activity during apparent rest on electrophysiologic testing
Severe spasms sufficient to limit mobility and breathing
symptoms_not_in_common: No anti-GAD65 antibody result is provided
No associated autoimmune diabetes, thyroid disease, or other autoimmune disease is reported
Marked clonus and hyperreflexia may suggest a more severe SPS-spectrum phenotype rather than uncomplicated classic anti-GAD65 SPS

data.description: A group of inherited upper-motor-neuron disorders causing slowly progressive bilateral leg spasticity, weakness, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses, sometimes with additional neurologic features.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent painful paraspinal and generalized muscle spasms are not typical
Severe truncal spasms impairing breathing are unusual
Continuous motor-unit activity on electrophysiology is not characteristic
The relatively rapid progression over months is less typical
Need for frequent IVIG suggests an autoimmune process rather than a hereditary spastic paraplegia

data.description: An acute toxin-mediated neurologic illness caused by Clostridium tetani, producing painful generalized muscle rigidity, stimulus-induced spasms, and potentially life-threatening respiratory muscle involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Hyperreflexia-like increased muscle excitability may be observed clinically
symptoms_not_in_common: The illness progressed over many months rather than the usual acute onset over days to weeks
No wound, infection, trismus, dysphagia, risus sardonicus, or autonomic instability is reported
Long-term dependence on IVIG is not typical treatment for tetanus
Continuous motor-unit activity and the chronic course are more consistent with stiff-person-spectrum disease

data.description: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.
A chronic large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, typically in younger women, causing arterial stenosis, occlusion, cerebral hypoperfusion, and ischemic complications.
symptoms_in_common: Age under 50 years and female sex
Frequent collapse, compatible with cerebral hypoperfusion
Previous ischemic stroke at an unusually young age
History of carotid arterial disease requiring endarterectomy
Scalp ischemia/ulceration consistent with severe extracranial arterial insufficiency
Imaging evidence of major neck-vessel stenosis or occlusive disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypercholesterolaemia is not a typical manifestation, although it may coexist
No reported constitutional symptoms such as fever, fatigue, weight loss, or limb claudication

data.diagnosis: Premature atherosclerotic carotid and great-vessel disease
data.description: Atherosclerotic plaque formation can cause narrowing or occlusion of the carotid and subclavian arteries, producing transient cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemic stroke, and rarely scalp ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse that may reflect cerebrovascular insufficiency
Scalp lesion that may result from severe arterial ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe carotid disease and stroke occurring in her thirties are unusually early for uncomplicated atherosclerosis
Scalp necrosis is an uncommon manifestation of atherosclerotic carotid disease
Multifocal great-vessel disease in a 46-year-old woman may suggest vasculitis rather than isolated atherosclerosis

data.diagnosis: Giant cell arteritis with large-vessel involvement
data.description: A granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries that can cause scalp ischemia or necrosis, stroke, and stenosis of the carotid or subclavian arteries.
symptoms_in_common: Large-vessel stenosis involving branches of the aortic arch
Collapse potentially related to cerebral hypoperfusion
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 46 years is atypical because giant cell arteritis almost exclusively occurs after age 50
No reported new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, polymyalgia symptoms, or systemic inflammatory symptoms
Carotid disease requiring endarterectomy at approximately age 35 is unusual for giant cell arteritis

data.description: Hemodynamically significant subclavian artery stenosis can reverse vertebral artery flow, reducing posterior cerebral circulation and causing presyncope, syncope, or neurologic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging showing stenosis involving a proximal great vessel/subclavian arterial region
symptoms_not_in_common: Scalp ulceration or necrosis is not typical
Prior right hemispheric stroke and carotid endarterectomy are not explained solely by subclavian steal
No reported arm-exertional symptoms, arm claudication, or blood-pressure difference between arms

data.diagnosis: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the cervical arteries
data.description: A non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arterial disorder, more common in women, that may affect carotid and vertebral arteries and predispose to stenosis, dissection, transient ischemic attacks, and stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Cerebrovascular event at a relatively young age
Frequent collapse that could reflect cerebrovascular insufficiency
symptoms_not_in_common: Scalp ischemic ulceration is not a typical feature
Proximal great-vessel/subclavian stenosis is less characteristic than mid-to-distal carotid or renal artery involvement
Hypercholesterolaemia does not specifically support fibromuscular dysplasia

data.description: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and adalimumab, admitted after a burn from an electric heater. Four months earlier she developed pain and stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli, with anemia, leukopenia, neutropenia, elevated rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinemia, positive ANA, low C4, low-level anti-dsDNA, and positive cryoglobulins. On admission she had fever and pancytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, CMV PCR, tuberculin skin test, and viral serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. She had traveled to Athens seven months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

A systemic infection caused by Leishmania parasites, transmitted by sandflies and associated with dog reservoirs in Mediterranean regions. Immunosuppression from anti-TNF therapy can predispose to severe or atypical disease. The blood/bone-marrow image is compatible with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia including anemia, leukopenia, and neutropenia
Positive ANA and low-level anti-dsDNA, which can occur as infection-related autoantibodies
Travel to Athens, an area where Mediterranean leishmaniasis occurs
Exposure to multiple dogs, an important reservoir for Leishmania infantum
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of hepatosplenomegaly
Absence of lymphadenopathy
Livedo reticularis and purpuric malleolar lesions are less typical than fever and pancytopenia

data.description: A complication of longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, splenomegaly, and increased susceptibility to infection; anemia and thrombocytopenia may also occur.
symptoms_in_common: Fever that could reflect infection in the setting of neutropenia
Leg ulcers or purpuric skin lesions can occur in rheumatoid vasculitis-associated disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No hepatosplenomegaly
Pancytopenia is more extensive than the typical isolated neutropenia
Travel-associated dog exposure
Hypergammaglobulinemia with positive cryoglobulins
Intracellular organisms seen on the hematologic specimen

data.diagnosis: T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia associated with rheumatoid arthritis
data.description: An indolent clonal lymphoproliferative disorder often associated with rheumatoid arthritis and characterized by chronic neutropenia, anemia, splenomegaly, and sometimes thrombocytopenia.
symptoms_in_common: Fever may occur because of recurrent infections during neutropenia
symptoms_not_in_common: No splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy
No described increase in circulating large granular lymphocytes
Positive cryoglobulins and low complement are not characteristic findings
Dog exposure and travel to a Mediterranean endemic area are not relevant to this disorder
The marrow/blood image suggesting intracellular parasites is not typical

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis-systemic lupus overlap syndrome
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory arthritis, fever, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, autoantibodies, and immune-complex skin vasculitis. Anti-TNF therapy can also induce lupus-like autoimmunity.
symptoms_not_in_common: Travel to Athens and exposure to dogs do not support lupus
Marked hypergammaglobulinemia with profound pancytopenia is less specific for lupus
No typical malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, nephritis, or serositis is described
Intracellular organisms in the hematologic specimen would not be explained by lupus alone

data.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins, commonly associated with hepatitis C, autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disorders, or chronic infections. It often causes purpura, arthralgia, low complement, and elevated rheumatoid factor.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe pancytopenia is not a typical primary manifestation
Persistent fever is less typical unless there is an underlying infection
Negative hepatitis C serology removes the most common cause
No renal involvement, peripheral neuropathy, or other classic vasculitic organ involvement is described
The intracellular parasitic morphology is not explained by cryoglobulinemia alone

data.description: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

A chronic granulomatous inflammatory skin disorder, strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, that typically forms yellow-brown, atrophic, indurated plaques with violaceous or erythematous borders on the pretibial shins.
symptoms_in_common: Tenderness can occur, particularly with active inflammation or ulceration
Image shows a yellow-brown atrophic plaque with an erythematous border
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age of 25 years is less typical, as necrobiosis lipoidica more often presents in middle adulthood
Initial presentation as a very small macule is less characteristic than a papule or plaque

data.description: A benign granulomatous skin condition that usually causes firm papules arranged in annular plaques, often on the hands, feet, elbows, or ankles. Generalized forms may be associated with diabetes.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic course without fevers or chills
Can occur in patients with diabetes
Granulomatous histologic pattern may overlap with necrobiosis lipoidica
symptoms_not_in_common: Pretibial shin location is less typical
Central atrophy or indentation is not typical
Yellow-brown waxy appearance is not typical
Tenderness is uncommon because granuloma annulare is usually asymptomatic
The image does not show a classic ring of papules with central clearing

data.description: A common diabetes-associated microvascular skin manifestation characterized by multiple small, round or oval, light-brown, slightly atrophic macules on the shins, often called diabetic shin spots.
symptoms_in_common: Brown hyperpigmented lesion on the shin
Gradual development of an atrophic or indented appearance
symptoms_not_in_common: Diabetic dermopathy is usually multiple rather than a single enlarging lesion
Lesions are typically small and do not progressively enlarge over 3 years
Tenderness is not typical
Prominent erythematous border and yellow central plaque are not typical
Diabetic dermopathy usually has minimal inflammation and no substantial induration

data.description: An inflammatory dermatitis caused by chronic venous insufficiency, usually affecting the lower legs and causing edema, erythema, scaling, pruritus, and brown hemosiderin pigmentation.
symptoms_in_common: Erythema and surface scale visible in the lesion
Tenderness may occur with marked inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: The patient is young and has no reported chronic venous insufficiency
No leg edema, varicosities, or bilateral lower-leg involvement is described
A solitary slowly enlarging indented plaque is atypical
Central yellow-brown atrophy with a raised erythematous border is not the usual pattern
Stasis dermatitis is often pruritic rather than focally tender

data.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disease that can cause papules, plaques, nodules, or scars in the skin; histology typically shows noncaseating granulomas. Skin disease may occur with or without systemic sarcoidosis.
symptoms_in_common: Lack of fever or chills does not exclude the condition
symptoms_not_in_common: The strong association with diabetes and the classic pretibial yellow atrophic plaque favor necrobiosis lipoidica instead
Central atrophy with a yellow waxy appearance is less typical
Tenderness is not a common presenting symptom
No pulmonary, ocular, constitutional, or other systemic sarcoidosis features are reported
A solitary shin lesion is less characteristic than common sarcoid distributions such as the face, scars, or upper body

data.description: 14-year-old boy with 2 days of acute fear of choking while swallowing after choking on chicken at dinner, followed by refusal/fear of eating, vomiting after trying ice cream, and markedly reduced fluid intake. Mother also reported episodes of inspiratory stridor during sleep over the preceding few weeks. On presentation he had drooling, persistent involuntary burping, dry oral mucosa, and was anxious but alert; neurologic and gait examination were normal. On subsequent exam he had hypertonic leg muscles and a mildly positive left Chvostek's sign. Past history included infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, keratosis pilaris, eczema, sensory-integration training in childhood, incomplete immunizations after age 2.5 years, and no current medications.

A disorder of parathyroid hormone resistance, usually caused by abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus. It leads to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite elevated parathyroid hormone levels. The abnormal GNAS methylation pattern in the patient strongly supports this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Inspiratory stridor consistent with hypocalcemia-related laryngospasm
Anxiety and fear associated with neuromuscular symptoms
Normal neurologic and gait examination between episodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset immediately after choking on chicken
Persistent involuntary burping
History of eczema, keratosis pilaris, and milk-protein allergy

data.description: Low serum calcium can cause increased neuromuscular excitability, including muscle stiffness, tetany, dysphagia, laryngospasm, stridor, and positive Chvostek's sign. In this case, it may be caused by parathyroid hormone resistance.
symptoms_in_common: Fear of choking and swallowing difficulty
symptoms_not_in_common: Choking event involving chicken as the apparent trigger
Persistent involuntary burping
Childhood sensory-integration training

data.description: Deficient parathyroid hormone secretion causes hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, producing tetany, paresthesias, muscle cramps, dysphagia, and laryngospasm. It is a key alternative cause of hypocalcemic symptoms, although the abnormal GNAS methylation favors pseudohypoparathyroidism rather than primary hypoparathyroidism.
symptoms_not_in_common: Abnormal GNAS methylation pattern, which is more characteristic of pseudohypoparathyroidism
Symptoms temporally beginning after choking on food
Persistent burping

data.diagnosis: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), fear of aversive consequences subtype
data.description: ARFID can develop after a frightening choking or vomiting event, leading to avoidance of eating or drinking because of fear of choking, vomiting, or other harmful consequences. It can rapidly cause dehydration and weight or nutritional compromise.
symptoms_in_common: Acute fear of choking after a choking event
Vomiting after attempting to eat ice cream
Dry oral mucosa consistent with dehydration
symptoms_not_in_common: Inspiratory stridor during sleep preceding the choking event
Hypertonic leg muscles
Positive Chvostek's sign
Drooling and possible laryngospasm
Abnormal GNAS methylation findings

data.description: A chronic allergic inflammatory disease of the esophagus that commonly occurs in children with atopic conditions and can cause dysphagia, food impaction, vomiting, and avoidance of eating.
symptoms_in_common: Choking sensation while eating solid food
Fear of swallowing and food avoidance
History of milk-protein allergy and atopic tendencies
symptoms_not_in_common: Inspiratory stridor during sleep
Hypertonic leg muscles
Positive Chvostek's sign
Dry mouth from reduced intake rather than chronic esophageal symptoms
Abnormal GNAS methylation pattern

data.description: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with recurrent fever. Four months before admission, she developed bleeding from a right scalp lesion; evaluation showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months before admission, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which showed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 lymph nodes; BRAF V600E mutation was identified. One month before admission, she started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib, after which fever and nausea began within 1 day and improved when the drugs were temporarily stopped. Fever recurred 2 weeks before admission. On presentation, she was febrile to 40.2°C, hypotensive (85/53 mm Hg), tachycardic, diaphoretic, ill appearing, with mild right upper quadrant tenderness and no rash.

A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, which can involve the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and reticuloendothelial system. Tissue may show granulomatous inflammation with small intracellular yeasts highlighted by fungal stains.
symptoms_in_common: Hypotension and tachycardia consistent with severe systemic infection
Granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms on tissue staining
symptoms_not_in_common: Temporal onset of fever within 1 day of starting dabrafenib and trametinib
Prior bleeding scalp melanoma lesion
History of metastatic regional melanoma lymph nodes

data.description: A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy, characterized by recurrent high fever, chills, dehydration, hypotension, nausea, and sometimes renal or hepatic dysfunction. Symptoms often improve after temporary drug interruption.
symptoms_in_common: Fever beginning soon after initiation of dabrafenib and trametinib
Recurrent fever after restarting or continuing therapy
Improvement when the drugs were temporarily stopped
symptoms_not_in_common: Granulomatous tissue inflammation containing fungal organisms
Hepatic and splenic lesions suggestive of disseminated infection
Pulmonary abnormalities consistent with infectious involvement
Right upper quadrant tenderness is not a defining feature

data.description: Hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause fever, constitutional illness, granulomatous hepatitis, hepatosplenic lesions, and diffuse pulmonary disease; acid-fast organisms may be demonstrable in tissue.
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt fever onset within 1 day of dabrafenib-trametinib initiation
Prompt improvement with temporary interruption of anticancer therapy
Fungal organisms demonstrated by fungal staining rather than acid-fast bacilli
Acute hypotensive shock is less typical of untreated disseminated tuberculosis

data.description: Severe bacterial infection, such as acute cholangitis, hepatic abscess, or another intra-abdominal source, can produce fever, hypotension, tachycardia, diaphoresis, nausea, and right upper quadrant abdominal discomfort.
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent episodes temporally linked to dabrafenib and trametinib exposure
Pulmonary abnormalities and splenic lesions suggesting disseminated disease
Granulomatous inflammation with fungal forms on pathology
No stated jaundice or biliary obstruction symptoms

data.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma with hepatic, splenic, and pulmonary involvement
data.description: Melanoma can recur or disseminate to the lungs, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, bone, brain, and other organs. Extensive tumor burden can cause constitutional symptoms and abdominal discomfort.
symptoms_in_common: History of stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma
Prior metastatic melanoma in cervical lymph nodes
Fever and ill appearance can occur with advanced malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever beginning immediately after dabrafenib and trametinib treatment
Improvement in fever when the medications were stopped
Severe acute hypotension and tachycardia suggestive of sepsis
Granulomatous inflammation containing fungal organisms rather than melanoma cells

data.description: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. In August 2011, presented to emergency room with abdominal pain. Lab tests showed elevated lipase (874 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (289 IU/L), and ALT (222 IU/L), with normal bilirubin. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase of 357 IU/L and normal serum lipase.

data.diagnosis: Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma involving the gallbladder
data.description: Rare metastatic spread of prostate cancer to the gallbladder, potentially causing gallbladder enlargement, biliary-type pain, and cholecystitis-like symptoms. The histologic and immunohistochemical appearance is consistent with metastatic prostatic carcinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Known history of metastatic prostate cancer
Gallbladder mass or infiltrative lesion on imaging
Prior abdominal pain with elevated liver enzymes
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal bilirubin despite biliary-region symptoms
Initial markedly elevated lipase
Absence of fever

data.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly caused by cystic-duct obstruction from gallstones, although malignant obstruction or infiltration can also produce cholecystitis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
No reported leukocytosis
No documented gallstones
Normal bilirubin
Prior markedly elevated lipase is not typical of isolated cholecystitis

data.description: A primary malignant epithelial tumor of the gallbladder that may cause abdominal pain, gallbladder distention, cholestatic liver-test abnormalities, and local invasion or biliary obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Possible malignant cells on cytology or tissue examination
symptoms_not_in_common: Known metastatic prostate cancer provides a more likely source for a metastatic lesion
Normal bilirubin
No reported jaundice
Acute presentation with positive Murphy's sign is more suggestive of superimposed inflammation

data.diagnosis: Malignant biliary obstruction from metastatic lymphadenopathy or periportal metastatic disease
data.description: Compression or invasion of the biliary tract by metastatic lymph nodes or tumor deposits can cause cholestatic enzyme elevation, abdominal pain, gallbladder distention, and sometimes pancreatitis.
symptoms_in_common: History of metastatic cancer with periaortic lymph-node involvement
Elevated ALT during the initial presentation
Initial episode of elevated lipase, which can occur with obstructive pancreatobiliary disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal bilirubin
No reported jaundice
No documented dilated common bile duct
Positive Murphy's sign suggests gallbladder inflammation rather than isolated extrahepatic obstruction

data.diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis due to transient pancreatobiliary obstruction
data.description: Inflammation of the pancreas, often caused by transient obstruction at the ampulla from gallstones, sludge, tumor, or metastatic compression of the biliary-pancreatic outflow tract.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly elevated serum lipase of 874 U/L
Elevated ALT and alkaline phosphatase during the initial episode
Potential pancreatobiliary obstructive process on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Later lipase was normal
Later pain was localized to the right upper quadrant rather than typical epigastric pain
Positive Murphy's sign is more typical of gallbladder disease
Palpable gallbladder is not typical of uncomplicated pancreatitis
No persistent pancreatic findings were described

data.description: 13-year-old boy with Addison’s disease, dysphagia since age 11, muscle weakness, marked fatigue, and recent gait ataxia. He had normal early development but later global developmental delay with mild intellectual disability, and a history of poor tear production since infancy. At age 2 he developed recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, and progressive hyperpigmentation; at age 4 he had recurrent hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia leading to diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Birth history was notable for bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and hypospadias. Examination showed severe hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles, facial dysmorphism with malar hypoplasia and prognathism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal upper-limb weakness and wasting, milder pyramidal weakness in the legs, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Labs showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin, consistent with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency.

data.diagnosis: Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome; AAAS-related disorder)
data.description: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by alacrima, achalasia/dysphagia, ACTH-resistant isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, and progressive neurologic/autonomic dysfunction; the neurologic form is often called 4A syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia beginning in childhood, suggestive of achalasia
Isolated glucocorticoid deficiency with markedly elevated ACTH and preserved aldosterone/renin
Recurrent vomiting, hypoglycemia, hypotonia, hypothermia, and failure to thrive during childhood
Hyperreflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses
Abnormal eye movements, nystagmus, poorly reactive pupils, and optic atrophy
Developmental delay and mild intellectual disability
Possible cervical spinal cord atrophy on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral cryptorchidism
Hypospadias
Inguinal hernia
Facial dysmorphism with malar hypoplasia and prognathism
Marked hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles

data.description: An inherited ACTH-resistance disorder causing isolated cortisol deficiency, elevated ACTH, hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, and recurrent adrenal crises while mineralocorticoid function is generally preserved.
symptoms_in_common: Hypothermia and hypotonia during adrenal crises
Vomiting, failure to thrive, fatigue, and muscle weakness
symptoms_not_in_common: Poor tear production since infancy
Childhood-onset dysphagia/possible achalasia
Progressive gait ataxia
Dysarthria, nasal speech, and nystagmus
Dilated pupils with poor light response
Optic atrophy
Distal muscle wasting with pyramidal signs
Global developmental delay and mild intellectual disability
Hyperkeratosis
Cryptorchidism and hypospadias

data.description: A peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 variants that can produce primary adrenal insufficiency and progressive neurologic disease, including spasticity, ataxia, cognitive decline, and peripheral neuropathy.
symptoms_in_common: Male patient with childhood-onset adrenal insufficiency
Visual pathway involvement can occur in neurologic forms
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal mineralocorticoid-related laboratory values may be less typical in overt adrenal involvement
Poor tear production since infancy
Dysphagia caused by childhood achalasia
Recurrent vomiting and hypoglycemia beginning in early childhood as the dominant presentation
Dilated poorly light-reactive pupils
Congenital cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and inguinal hernia
Facial dysmorphism and marked knuckle/elbow hyperkeratosis

data.description: An autosomal-recessive autoimmune disease caused by AIRE variants, classically featuring chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency, with possible ectodermal and neurologic complications.
symptoms_in_common: Vomiting and failure to thrive during adrenal insufficiency
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
No reported hypoparathyroidism or hypocalcemic symptoms
Normal aldosterone and renin with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency
Poor tear production from infancy
Dysphagia suggestive of achalasia
Progressive upper motor neuron signs, muscle wasting, and gait ataxia
Abnormal pupils, nystagmus, and optic atrophy
Congenital genital anomalies including cryptorchidism and hypospadias

data.diagnosis: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita (NR0B1/DAX1-related adrenal insufficiency)
data.description: An X-linked developmental disorder of the adrenal cortex causing childhood primary adrenal insufficiency; affected males may later develop hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and reproductive abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Vomiting, failure to thrive, hypoglycemia, hypotonia, and fatigue
Cryptorchidism or other genital/reproductive abnormalities can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Preserved aldosterone and renin are less typical because adrenal hypoplasia commonly causes mineralocorticoid deficiency
Poor tear production since infancy
Dysphagia/possible achalasia
Progressive gait ataxia and pyramidal signs
Distal upper-limb wasting
Nystagmus, poorly reactive pupils, and optic atrophy
Developmental delay with facial dysmorphism
Marked hyperkeratosis of elbows and knuckles

data.description: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, now stage IV with metastases to bone, lungs, and liver, status post mastectomy, multiple systemic therapies, and stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier. After 3 months on anastrozole and paracetamol for pain, she developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion over several days, rapidly worsening to unresponsiveness. On admission, she was found disoriented on the floor, with lower leg weakness and inability to follow basic instructions. She was awake but unresponsive and uncooperative on examination, with no focal neurologic deficits initially, normal blood pressure, mild tachycardia, and no fever. Brain MRI had been normal 2 weeks earlier.

Neurologic injury from fat or marrow emboli entering the cerebral circulation, causing multifocal microinfarcts and petechial hemorrhages. It may occur with extensive bone disease or marrow necrosis even without a recent fracture.
symptoms_in_common: Susceptibility-sensitive MRI appearance consistent with small petechial hemorrhages
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported recent long-bone fracture or orthopedic procedure
No reported respiratory distress or hypoxemia
No reported petechial skin rash

data.description: Multiple acute ischemic strokes caused by malignancy-related hypercoagulability, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, or tumor-associated embolic disease.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple lesions with diffusion restriction on MRI
Initially absent or subtle focal neurologic findings can occur with numerous small bilateral infarcts
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented cardiac murmur, valvular vegetation, or atrial fibrillation
No clear focal cortical stroke syndrome
Petechial microhemorrhagic MRI changes are less typical than in fat embolism

data.diagnosis: Cerebral intravascular tumor embolism from metastatic breast carcinoma
data.description: Tumor cells or tumor emboli occlude small cerebral vessels in disseminated cancer, producing multifocal ischemic lesions, hemorrhagic microvascular injury, and rapidly progressive encephalopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Long history of invasive ductal breast carcinoma
Stage IV disease with lung, liver, and bone metastases
Multifocal cerebral lesions involving more than one vascular territory
Possible small hemorrhagic lesions on susceptibility MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No established focal mass lesion or contrast-enhancing brain metastasis described
No pathologic confirmation of intravascular tumor cells
This is an uncommon complication of breast cancer

data.description: A vasogenic edema syndrome causing seizures, altered mental status, headache, or visual symptoms, often associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, cytotoxic therapy, or endothelial injury from malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: Acute to subacute confusion and reduced responsiveness
Posterior-predominant cerebral abnormalities may be present on MRI
Underlying malignancy and prior systemic cancer therapies are risk factors
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure was reported as normal rather than markedly elevated
No seizures, headache, or visual disturbance were reported
Prominent multifocal diffusion restriction suggests cytotoxic ischemic injury rather than typical vasogenic edema
Petechial hemorrhagic microlesions are not the classic dominant imaging finding

data.description: A JC-virus demyelinating infection of the central nervous system occurring in immunosuppressed patients, typically causing progressive cognitive, motor, and visual deficits with multifocal white-matter MRI lesions.
symptoms_in_common: History of significant immunosuppression from metastatic cancer and prior stem-cell transplantation
Confusion and inability to follow instructions
Multifocal brain white-matter abnormalities can occur on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Clinical deterioration over several days is faster than the usual course of PML
Rapid progression to unresponsiveness is less typical
Multifocal acute diffusion-restricting lesions with petechial hemorrhagic features are not classic for PML
A normal brain MRI two weeks earlier would be less typical for advanced symptomatic PML

data.description: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 1 month of progressive weakness in all four extremities, sensory changes, and urinary difficulty. Exam showed hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, bilateral Hoffmann and Tromner signs, and asymmetric weakness (MRC 2 on the right, MRC 4 on the left). Sensory loss included decreased pinprick and temperature below C4, mainly on the left, and decreased vibration and proprioception, mainly on the right. Serologic autoimmune testing and cerebrospinal fluid studies were normal; ACE was mildly elevated. Brain MRI, chest and abdominal CT, and nerve conduction study showed no other organ involvement.
Sarcoidosis involving the spinal cord without detectable systemic disease. It commonly produces an enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive weakness in all four extremities
Upper motor neuron signs including hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, Hoffmann sign, and Tromner sign
Loss of pain and temperature sensation

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder that can cause longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, often with severe motor, sensory, and autonomic deficits.
symptoms_not_in_common: Asymmetric loss of vibration and proprioception is less characteristic than the often severe bilateral deficits of NMOSD
No optic neuritis or other typical NMOSD-associated visual symptoms are reported

data.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that may cause focal spinal cord lesions with weakness, sensory deficits, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Rapid progression to severe quadriparesis over 1 month is less typical for a first MS presentation
A distinct cervical sensory level with marked pain and temperature loss is less typical of a small focal MS lesion
No prior relapsing neurologic episodes, optic neuritis, or brain lesions are reported

data.diagnosis: Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (ependymoma or astrocytoma)
data.description: A primary tumor arising within the spinal cord that can enlarge the cord and progressively disrupt corticospinal, spinothalamic, and dorsal-column pathways.
symptoms_in_common: Dissociated sensory deficits involving pain/temperature and proprioception/vibration
symptoms_not_in_common: The relatively rapid 1-month progression is faster than many intramedullary tumors
No chronic focal neck pain or radicular pain is reported

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can form granulomatous inflammatory lesions within the spinal cord, causing subacute compressive or inflammatory myelopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Cervical spinal cord syndrome with hyperreflexia and Babinski signs
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, or other systemic tuberculosis symptoms are reported
No pulmonary or other systemic organ involvement is identified on chest and abdominal imaging

data.description: 33-year-old male with 20 days of cough and sputum production starting after a cold, with small amounts of yellow-white sticky sputum. No hemoptysis, fever, chills, chest pain, or dyspnea initially. He received unspecified intravenous treatment at a local clinic without improvement. Seven days before admission, the cough worsened, especially at night, causing sleep disturbance, and was sometimes associated with right-sided chest pain. Previously healthy; no significant medical history. Smoked about 10 cigarettes/day for over 10 years; no alcohol use. Physical exam: T 36.2℃, P 112/min, R 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg; symmetric chest, equal respiratory movement, symmetric vocal fremitus, clear percussion, coarse breath sounds bilaterally, and a small amount of wet rales in the right lung.

data.diagnosis: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lung abscess
data.description: A severe bacterial infection causing consolidation and tissue necrosis, sometimes forming cavitary lesions or abscesses in the lung.
symptoms_in_common: Wet rales in the right lung
Right lower-lung consolidation and cavitary-appearing changes on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or chills
No initial dyspnea
Only a relatively short 20-day illness course

data.description: A chronic lung infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that may produce cough, sputum, chest discomfort, consolidation, and cavitary lung lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Failure to improve after nonspecific intravenous treatment
Cavitary or destructive-appearing pulmonary lesion on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt onset after a cold
No fever or chills
No hemoptysis
No reported weight loss, night sweats, or fatigue
Predominantly right lower-lobe involvement rather than typical upper-lobe predominance

data.description: An inflammatory lung disorder in which granulation tissue plugs fill small airways and alveoli, often causing persistent cough and consolidative opacities that do not respond to antibiotics.
symptoms_in_common: Lack of improvement with prior presumed anti-infective treatment
Histologic appearance compatible with inflammatory/organizing alveolar injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Yellow-white sputum suggesting airway infection
Cavitary-appearing changes, which are less typical
Localized right-sided chest pain

data.description: A chronic bacterial infection caused by Actinomyces species that can cause mass-like consolidation, abscess formation, cavitation, and chest pain; it may mimic cancer or tuberculosis.
symptoms_in_common: Chest pain on the affected side
Poor response to brief nonspecific treatment
Mass-like or consolidative lesion with possible cavitation in the right lower lung
symptoms_not_in_common: Very short duration of symptoms
No reported poor dentition, aspiration risk, or dental infection
No fever or systemic constitutional symptoms

data.diagnosis: Endobronchial obstruction with post-obstructive pneumonia, including bronchial carcinoid or other lung tumor
data.description: A lesion obstructing a bronchus can impair drainage and cause recurrent or persistent localized pneumonia, mucus retention, collapse, or abscess-like changes distal to the obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Failure to improve after initial treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age of 33 years
Acute onset after a cold
No hemoptysis
No reported weight loss or other cancer-related systemic symptoms

data.description: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

data.diagnosis: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
data.description: A zoonotic filarial nematode infection transmitted by mosquitoes, commonly affecting dogs and occasionally causing solitary or migrating subcutaneous nodules in humans in Mediterranean Europe. Histology typically shows a thick-cuticled nematode within an inflammatory nodule.
symptoms_in_common: Migrating nodules in the brachial region
Dog ownership, a relevant reservoir exposure
Outdoor exposure in forests and islands where mosquitoes may occur
Residence in Istria/Croatia, a Mediterranean region where Dirofilaria repens can occur
Normal blood counts and inflammatory markers, which are common in localized human infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical symptoms are strongly discordant; localized human dirofilariasis is often asymptomatic apart from the nodule
Normal ultrasonography may be less typical because a moving worm can sometimes be visualized

data.description: Infection with larval Taenia solium cysts, which can form painless mobile subcutaneous or intramuscular nodules. It is usually acquired through ingestion of parasite eggs and may occur with or without neurologic disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative cysticercosis serology
Migrating nodules are not typical because cysticerci are generally fixed in tissue
No travel to or epidemiologic history suggesting exposure in a highly endemic area
Histologic appearance is more suggestive of a nematode than a cystic larval cestode

data.description: A tissue-invasive nematode infection caused by Gnathostoma species. Larval migration can cause intermittent or migratory subcutaneous swellings, often after eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish, amphibians, or other intermediate hosts.
symptoms_in_common: Possible painless or minimally symptomatic soft-tissue swelling
Nematode infection can produce a subcutaneous lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel outside Croatia, whereas most cases occur in endemic regions of Asia or Latin America
No reported ingestion of raw or undercooked freshwater fish or other high-risk foods
No eosinophilia reported
Gnathostomiasis lesions are often painful, itchy, erythematous, or associated with edema rather than a stable painless firm nodule

data.description: A larval tapeworm infection caused by Spirometra species. It may produce slowly growing or migrating subcutaneous nodules after ingestion of contaminated water or raw intermediate-host meat.
symptoms_in_common: Normal routine inflammatory markers may occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported exposure to contaminated water or raw frog, snake, or other intermediate-host meat
Sparganosis is uncommon in Croatia and more often reported in Asia
The histologic image appears more compatible with a nematode than a plerocercoid tapeworm larva
No eosinophilia reported

data.description: A filarial infection caused by Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by blackflies. Adult worms may reside in subcutaneous nodules, while microfilariae cause pruritic dermatitis and ocular disease.
symptoms_in_common: Filarial nematodes can be identified in excised nodules
Outdoor exposure could involve biting insects
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel to endemic areas in sub-Saharan Africa or limited endemic foci in Latin America/Yemen
No pruritic dermatitis
No eye symptoms
Migrating brachial nodules are less typical than fixed onchocercomas
Croatia is not an endemic setting for onchocerciasis
