data.description: 66-year-old man with progressive neurologic symptoms since around 2000, beginning with recurrent unexplained falls while riding a motorcycle. By 2003 he developed blurred vision, photophobia, and worsening imbalance/unsteadiness. He had prior bilateral lens implantation in 2000 for cataracts/presbyopia without benefit. Over time he developed frequent falls, gait instability requiring a cane, retrocollis, slurred speech, inability to look down, and dysphagia. On examination, pupils were irregular with sluggish direct light responses; vertical and horizontal voluntary eye movements were slow and limited, with bilateral adduction paresis, but passive head movements could elicit full ocular movements initially. He was slow on rapid alternating movements and tended to fall backward. By March 2007 he was admitted for dysphagia with repeated aspiration; eye movements were severely restricted with absent vertical and medial gaze, inability to converge, absent Bell’s phenomenon, optokinetic nystagmus, caloric nystagmus, and doll’s eye movements. He also had severe nuchal rigidity, retrocollis, inability to sit unsupported, marked postural instability, axial rigidity, symmetric minimally brisk reflexes, and bilateral flexor plantar responses.

A rapidly progressive tauopathy causing early falls, axial-predominant parkinsonism, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and frontal-subcortical dysfunction. Midbrain atrophy may produce the "hummingbird" sign on sagittal MRI.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive gait instability and backward falls
Vertical gaze slowing and eventual vertical gaze palsy, especially impaired downward gaze
Initially preserved eye movements with passive head movement, consistent with a supranuclear ocular motor disorder
Slow and limited horizontal eye movements
Postural instability and inability to sit unsupported
symptoms_not_in_common: Photophobia and blurred vision as prominent early symptoms
Irregular pupils with sluggish direct light response
Complete loss of vestibulo-ocular responses, caloric nystagmus, and doll's eye movements late in the course
Marked bilateral adduction paresis resembling internuclear ophthalmoplegia

data.description: A synucleinopathy characterized by poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism with autonomic failure; cerebellar dysfunction, dysarthria, dysphagia, and dystonia may occur.
symptoms_not_in_common: Early prominent vertical supranuclear gaze palsy
Inability to look downward as a major early feature
No reported autonomic failure such as orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention/incontinence, or erectile dysfunction
No reported cerebellar ataxia
Severe loss of voluntary and reflex eye movements is unusual
Early recurrent backward falls are more characteristic of PSP

data.diagnosis: Corticobasal syndrome (often due to corticobasal degeneration)
data.description: A progressive neurodegenerative syndrome, frequently caused by a tauopathy, that produces asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, dystonia, myoclonus, and sometimes supranuclear gaze impairment.
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms are described as largely symmetric rather than markedly asymmetric
No limb apraxia
No alien-limb phenomenon
No cortical sensory loss
No focal cortical myoclonus
Early severe vertical gaze palsy and backward falls favor PSP over corticobasal syndrome

data.description: A lysosomal lipid-trafficking disorder that can present in adulthood with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and neuropsychiatric or cognitive symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with impaired downward gaze
symptoms_not_in_common: Late age of onset at approximately 60 years
No reported psychiatric symptoms, cognitive decline, or psychosis
No reported hepatosplenomegaly or systemic storage-disease features
Severe axial parkinsonism with early backward falls is more typical of PSP
Complete loss of vestibulo-ocular reflexes is not a classic feature

data.diagnosis: Whipple disease with central nervous system involvement
data.description: A rare infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that can involve the brainstem and cause supranuclear gaze palsy, oculomasticatory myorhythmia, cognitive changes, ataxia, and systemic gastrointestinal or joint symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Supranuclear gaze palsy and progressive ophthalmoplegia
symptoms_not_in_common: Very long, slowly progressive course over many years without systemic illness
No chronic diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal symptoms, fever, or arthralgia
No cognitive or behavioral decline described
No oculomasticatory myorhythmia reported
Severe axial rigidity, retrocollis, and early backward falls more strongly support PSP

data.description: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

Subacute fungal meningitis caused most often by Cryptococcus neoformans in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS. The images show encapsulated budding yeasts with prominent clear halos, characteristic of Cryptococcus on India ink preparation.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute 2-week course of fever and headache
Markedly elevated CSF opening pressure (29 cm water)
Advanced HIV infection with CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL
Encapsulated yeast appearance on CSF microscopy
symptoms_not_in_common: No major atypical symptoms are described

data.description: A subacute or chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, commonly producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated protein, reduced glucose, and raised intracranial pressure; risk is increased in advanced HIV.
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF glucose is relatively preserved at 46 mg/dL rather than markedly low
No pulmonary tuberculosis symptoms or known tuberculosis exposure are reported
Microscopy shows encapsulated yeasts rather than acid-fast bacilli

data.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as HSV, VZV, enteroviruses, or HIV itself. CSF usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose.
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated opening pressure is less typical for routine viral meningitis
Severe advanced HIV immunosuppression strongly favors opportunistic infection
CSF protein elevation and prolonged subacute course are more suggestive of fungal or mycobacterial meningitis
Encapsulated budding yeasts on microscopy are not consistent with viral infection

data.description: Central nervous system infection with Treponema pallidum that can cause chronic or subacute meningitis, headache, cranial neuropathies, and lymphocytic CSF inflammation. Coinfection is common among people with HIV.
symptoms_in_common: Sexual risk factors and newly diagnosed HIV infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Very low CD4+ count and high opening pressure more strongly suggest cryptococcal meningitis
No rash, genital lesion history, cranial neuropathy, or other syphilis manifestations are reported
Encapsulated yeasts on CSF microscopy are not compatible with neurosyphilis

data.description: Rapid-onset infection of the meninges caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis. It generally produces fever, severe headache, meningismus, altered mental status, neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose.
symptoms_not_in_common: Two-week subacute course is less typical than abrupt presentation
CSF is predominantly lymphocytic rather than neutrophilic
CSF glucose is not markedly reduced
Encapsulated budding yeast morphology supports Cryptococcus rather than bacterial meningitis

data.description: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute left medial longitudinal fasciculus infarction causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
data.description: A small acute ischemic stroke affecting the left medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons, disrupting coordination between the left medial rectus and right lateral rectus muscles. This produces left internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to adduct the left eye
Nystagmus of the right eye during attempted leftward gaze
Atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation, increasing embolic stroke risk
Diffusion-restricted focal brainstem lesion on MRI consistent with acute infarction
Otherwise normal neurological examination, compatible with a small focal pontine infarct
symptoms_not_in_common: Diplopia reported only when looking through the right eye, which can suggest a monocular visual phenomenon rather than classic binocular diplopia

data.description: An acute ischemic stroke involving the vertebrobasilar circulation, affecting a small area of the dorsal pons or midbrain responsible for horizontal eye movement coordination.
symptoms_in_common: MRI appearance of an acute focal brainstem ischemic lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: No limb weakness or sensory loss
No dysarthria
No ataxia or vertigo reported
No facial weakness
No altered consciousness

data.description: Multiple sclerosis can cause demyelinating plaques in the medial longitudinal fasciculus, producing internuclear ophthalmoplegia with impaired adduction of one eye and abducting nystagmus of the other.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to adduct the left eye
Nystagmus of the right eye on attempted conjugate gaze
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 83 years, which is highly atypical for new-onset multiple sclerosis
Sudden onset over hours rather than a typical inflammatory demyelinating course
Atrial fibrillation with substantial stroke risk
MRI lesion described as diffusion-restricted and consistent with acute infarction
No prior neurological episodes suggestive of demyelination

data.description: A third cranial nerve palsy causes impaired eye adduction and may produce diplopia, often with additional deficits in elevation, depression, eyelid elevation, or pupillary function depending on the cause.
symptoms_in_common: Acute onset may occur with ischemic cranial neuropathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Right eye abducting nystagmus is not typical of an isolated oculomotor nerve palsy
No ptosis reported
No pupil abnormality reported
No impaired left eye elevation or depression reported
Brainstem diffusion-restricted lesion favors a central medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion rather than peripheral cranial nerve palsy

data.description: Ocular myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that can cause fluctuating diplopia and variable ocular muscle weakness, sometimes mimicking cranial nerve palsies or internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
symptoms_in_common: Ocular movement weakness may occur without other neurological deficits
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden fixed onset over three hours is less typical than fluctuating fatigable symptoms
Right eye nystagmus during attempted gaze is not typical
A unilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia pattern strongly suggests a central brainstem lesion
No ptosis reported
MRI evidence of an acute focal brainstem lesion is not explained by myasthenia gravis
No fatigability or symptom variation reported

data.description: 35-day-old male infant, born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation, previously healthy and feeding breast milk plus formula, presented with 2 days of increasing fussiness, pallor, fever, vomiting, mottled skin, tachycardia, and respiratory distress. On examination he was pale, listless, fussy, and mottled with cool extremities, temperature 39.1°C, heart rate 176 bpm, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, oxygen saturation 97% on 1 L/min nasal cannula, a grade 2/6 holosystolic-flow murmur, and splenomegaly 2–3 cm below the costal margin. Urinalysis showed dark red cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, elevated AST, and abnormal blood smear with numerous intracellular ring forms; cerebrospinal fluid also showed intraerythrocytic ring forms.

Malaria acquired transplacentally or around delivery, causing febrile hemolytic illness in the first weeks of life. P. falciparum commonly produces multiple delicate ring forms within erythrocytes and can cause severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, hemoglobinuria, and shock.
symptoms_in_common: Dark red urine with blood and protein, consistent with hemoglobinuria
Numerous intraerythrocytic ring forms on blood smear
Intraerythrocytic ring forms reported in cerebrospinal fluid

data.description: Babesiosis is a protozoal infection of red blood cells that can rarely be transmitted congenitally. It causes hemolytic anemia, fever, thrombocytopenia, and intraerythrocytic ring forms; some species may form tetrads known as Maltese crosses.
symptoms_in_common: Dark red urine compatible with hemoglobinuria
Intraerythrocytic ring forms on peripheral blood smear
symptoms_not_in_common: Intracellular ring forms reported in cerebrospinal fluid
Very young age with severe illness is less typical than congenital malaria
No described Maltese-cross tetrads on smear

data.diagnosis: Neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
data.description: Serious bacterial infection in a young infant can cause fever, shock, respiratory distress, thrombocytopenia, anemia, organ injury, and abnormal urine findings. Disseminated intravascular coagulation may contribute to thrombocytopenia and bleeding or hematuria.
symptoms_in_common: Poor systemic perfusion with mottled skin and cool extremities
Abnormal urinalysis with blood and protein
symptoms_not_in_common: Numerous intraerythrocytic ring forms on blood smear
Intraerythrocytic ring forms in cerebrospinal fluid
Marked hemolytic anemia with elevated LDH and dark red urine is more suggestive of a hemoparasitic infection
Splenomegaly is less typical in acute neonatal bacterial sepsis

data.diagnosis: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection with hepatitis
data.description: Disseminated neonatal HSV can present during the first weeks of life with fever, irritability, respiratory compromise, hepatitis, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and shock; skin vesicles may be absent.
symptoms_not_in_common: Numerous intraerythrocytic ring forms on blood smear
Intraerythrocytic ring forms in cerebrospinal fluid
Severe hemolytic anemia with elevated LDH
Dark red urine suggestive of hemoglobinuria
Splenomegaly is not a dominant feature

data.diagnosis: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency with acute hemolytic crisis
data.description: G6PD deficiency is an inherited red-cell enzymatic disorder in which oxidative stress, including infection or medication exposure, can precipitate acute intravascular hemolysis with anemia, jaundice, elevated LDH, and dark urine.
symptoms_in_common: Dark red urine compatible with hemoglobinuria
Elevated AST can occur with hemolysis or systemic illness
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever is not caused by G6PD deficiency itself
Thrombocytopenia is not typical
Splenomegaly is not usually prominent in an acute episode
Respiratory distress and shock are not typical unless anemia is extreme
Numerous intraerythrocytic ring forms on blood smear
Intraerythrocytic ring forms in cerebrospinal fluid

data.description: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

data.diagnosis: Recurrent metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma with pelvic/rectal involvement
data.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after radical prostatectomy, with local pelvic recurrence and distant metastases such as lung and liver lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Pelvic mass near the rectum on imaging
Pulmonary nodules and liver lesion concerning for metastatic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Several years without known prostate cancer recurrence
Predominant rectal symptoms rather than urinary symptoms

data.diagnosis: Neuroendocrine/small-cell transformation of recurrent prostate cancer
data.description: An aggressive, poorly differentiated prostate cancer phenotype that may develop after prior prostate adenocarcinoma and can spread rapidly to visceral organs such as the liver and lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Liver lesion suspicious for visceral metastasis
Multiple pulmonary nodules suspicious for metastases
Pelvic/rectal pain from local tumor extension
symptoms_not_in_common: Tenesmus is less characteristic than systemic and metastatic symptoms
No reported urinary obstruction or neurologic symptoms

data.diagnosis: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease
data.description: Cancer arising from the rectum that commonly causes tenesmus and rectal pain and may metastasize to the liver and lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Liver lesion compatible with metastatic spread
Pulmonary nodules compatible with metastatic spread
symptoms_not_in_common: History of high-grade prostate cancer, which raises concern for recurrent prostate malignancy instead
No reported rectal bleeding
No reported change in stool caliber or bowel habit

data.diagnosis: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or prostatic urethra
data.description: An aggressive urinary tract malignancy that can invade pelvic structures and metastasize to lymph nodes, liver, lungs, and bone.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe tenesmus is not a usual presenting symptom
No hematuria
No dysuria or other urinary tract symptoms
Prior prostate cancer provides a more direct explanation for the pelvic findings

data.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma with extranodal pelvic and visceral involvement
data.description: A lymphoid malignancy that can involve abdominal or pelvic tissues and may produce systemic symptoms with liver and lung involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe focal rectal pain and tenesmus are less typical
No reported fever
No reported night sweats
History of high-grade prostate cancer makes recurrent metastatic prostate cancer more likely

data.description: 27-year-old man presented with 3 days of progressive myalgias in the upper legs followed by acute worsening weakness on the day of presentation, with inability to lift his legs or stand and associated arm weakness. For several months আগে he had difficulty sleeping, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremor. He had started an herbal supplement 4 days before presentation. On examination, he had bilateral conjunctival injection, mild proximal limb weakness (4/5 upper extremities, 3/5 lower extremities), brisk patellar reflexes, and fine hand tremor. Labs showed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L), mild transaminitis and cholestatic enzyme elevation, mild hyperbilirubinemia, elevated creatine kinase and aldolase, and venous pH 7.29.

data.diagnosis: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Graves disease
data.description: An acute hypokalemic paralysis caused by intracellular potassium shift during thyrotoxicosis, most commonly from Graves disease. Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid disorder with diffuse thyroid enlargement and increased vascularity.
symptoms_in_common: Acute proximal muscle weakness progressing to inability to stand
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid appearance on ultrasound
Elevated creatine kinase and aldolase from hypokalemic muscle injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral conjunctival injection is not a classic feature unless related to thyroid eye disease
Mild cholestatic liver enzyme elevation and hyperbilirubinemia are not core manifestations
Recent herbal supplement use is not required for the diagnosis, although it could precipitate an episode

data.description: A genetic skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder causing recurrent episodes of weakness due to potassium shifting into cells, often triggered by carbohydrate intake, rest after exercise, stress, or medications.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden severe limb weakness, especially affecting the legs
Proximal weakness greater than distal weakness
Elevated creatine kinase can occur during severe attacks
Preserved or brisk reflexes can be present early in an attack
symptoms_not_in_common: Several months of tremor, weight loss, loose stools, and insomnia
Clinical features suggesting hyperthyroidism
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid enlargement on ultrasound
Conjunctival injection
Mild cholestatic liver abnormalities

data.diagnosis: Toxic multinodular goiter with thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
data.description: Autonomously functioning thyroid nodules can cause hyperthyroidism and, rarely, hypokalemic periodic paralysis. It is more common in older adults and usually has a nodular rather than diffuse thyroid pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Hypokalemic paralysis with acute leg-predominant weakness
Possible mild liver enzyme abnormalities during thyrotoxicosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age is less typical
Diffuse thyroid hypervascularity rather than a multinodular gland
No described palpable thyroid nodules
Conjunctival injection is not typical
Herbal supplement exposure does not specifically support this diagnosis

data.description: Inflammatory thyroid disorders can release preformed thyroid hormone and produce transient thyrotoxicosis. Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is much less common than with Graves disease.
symptoms_in_common: Acute weakness associated with severe hypokalemia
Diffuse thyroid abnormalities may be seen on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked diffuse thyroid hypervascularity is more characteristic of Graves disease than destructive thyroiditis
No neck pain or thyroid tenderness was reported
No preceding viral syndrome was reported
Conjunctival injection is not typical
Brisk reflexes are less diagnostically characteristic than the biochemical hyperthyroid features

data.description: An acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy that typically causes progressive symmetric weakness, often beginning in the legs and potentially involving the arms and respiratory muscles.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe hypokalemia strongly favors a metabolic paralysis instead
Brisk patellar reflexes; Guillain-Barre syndrome usually causes reduced or absent reflexes
Tremor, weight loss, loose stools, and insomnia suggest thyrotoxicosis rather than Guillain-Barre syndrome
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid findings are not explained
Elevated creatine kinase and aldolase are not typical primary findings
No preceding infection, sensory symptoms, or autonomic dysfunction was reported

data.description: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.
A benign, slow-growing bony exostosis of the midline hard palate, often nodular or lobulated and usually asymptomatic.
symptoms_in_common: Long-standing lesion reportedly present since birth
symptoms_not_in_common: No symptoms strongly inconsistent with torus palatinus

data.description: A benign localized overgrowth of mature bone on the palate; it may resemble a torus but can be less classically midline or more focal.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty with oral hygiene around the lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported presence since birth is less typical because many exostoses become apparent later in life
The broad symmetric midline lobulated appearance is more typical of torus palatinus

data.description: A benign tumor composed of mature bone that usually presents as a slow-growing, firm, painless mass; oral osteomas are uncommon.
symptoms_in_common: Painless slow-growing or long-standing oral mass
Possible interference with cleaning and food retention
symptoms_not_in_common: Presence since birth is uncommon for osteoma
Multiple broad lobules centered on the midline are less typical than a solitary focal lesion
Food-related halitosis is not a usual primary feature

data.diagnosis: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
data.description: A benign salivary-gland tumor that commonly occurs on the palate as a painless, slowly enlarging, firm submucosal mass.
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported presence since birth is very atypical
Broad bilateral/midline lobulated appearance is less typical, as pleomorphic adenoma is often unilateral
Difficulty cleaning and food entrapment are not typical presenting features
The lesion appears more consistent with a bony prominence than a soft-tissue salivary tumor

data.description: A malignant salivary-gland tumor that may present as a painless palatal swelling, sometimes with a bluish or ulcerated surface and gradual enlargement.
symptoms_in_common: Can have a slow clinical course in low-grade tumors
symptoms_not_in_common: Presence since birth is not typical
Lack of recent growth, ulceration, bleeding, pain, or numbness is less suggestive
Symmetric midline lobulated appearance is unusual
Food entrapment and hygiene difficulty are not typical primary symptoms

data.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Lumbar disc herniation with left-sided radiculopathy
data.description: Protrusion or extrusion of lumbar disc material can compress a lumbar nerve root, causing acute radiating leg pain and motor weakness. The MRI appearance is compatible with degenerative lower-lumbar disc disease and possible canal/nerve-root compression.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating into the left leg
Left leg weakness with reduced power (3/5)
symptoms_not_in_common: Otherwise normal neurological examination despite marked 3/5 leg weakness

data.description: An enlarged or thrombosed epidural vein can form a mass-like lesion in the spinal canal and compress a nerve root, often mimicking a lumbar disc prolapse on MRI. It may produce abrupt radicular pain and weakness.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral pain radiating into the left leg
Possible lower-lumbar epidural compressive lesion on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported symptoms of venous disease, such as leg swelling or known venous thrombosis

data.description: A synovial cyst is a fluid-containing outpouching from a degenerated facet joint. In the lower lumbar spine, particularly at L4-L5, it can narrow the canal or neural foramen and compress nerve roots.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic back pain suggesting degenerative spinal disease
Lower-lumbar extradural compressive appearance on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Very abrupt onset over only two days is less typical than a more gradually progressive course

data.description: Bleeding into the epidural space can rapidly compress the cauda equina or lumbar nerve roots, causing acute back pain, radicular symptoms, and motor weakness. MRI signal varies with the age of blood products.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid development of left leg weakness
Radiating leg pain due to possible nerve-root compression
Potential epidural mass effect on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported trauma

data.description: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

data.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with eosinophilic cardiac involvement and cerebral embolic infarctions

Pulmonary nodular abnormalities that may reflect eosinophilic or thromboembolic organ involvement

data.description: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.
A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly affecting hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with high FDG uptake
Negative tuberculosis skin test and tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon-gamma testing
Mild leukopenia and anemia can occur in systemic sarcoidosis

data.description: 78-year-old woman with 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue, referred for anemia and elevated ESR. Past history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination showed normal cardiac, respiratory, and neurologic findings, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status was 1. Blood tests showed hemoglobin 99 g/L, normal white cell and platelet counts, ESR 120 mm/h, mildly elevated creatinine and LDH, and hypercalcemia (2.81 mmol/L). Further studies revealed IgG kappa paraprotein 32 g/L, elevated β₂-microglobulin, markedly increased free kappa light chains with a kappa/lambda ratio of 280, and urinary Bence-Jones protein (kappa). Vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase were normal.
A malignant clonal proliferation of plasma cells in bone marrow that produces a monoclonal immunoglobulin and/or free light chains, causing anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, and bone disease.
symptoms_in_common: Mild renal impairment with elevated creatinine

Skeletal imaging compatible with myeloma-related bone involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported bone pain

data.description: 20-year-old male with 3 years of bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. He also reported decreased facial hair growth, small testicles, blurred vision corrected with glasses, occasional post-exertional headaches, recent constipation, and a history of increased thirst and urination beginning 4 years earlier that had recently improved. Past history included generalized nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures and focal right leg seizures from ages 6–13, treated with carbamazepine until age 14, and a chronic pilonidal cyst. Examination showed minimal facial hair, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, BMI 26.5, bilateral breast enlargement without retraction, masses, or discharge, small testes, a small posterior anal fissure, and a small coccygeal lump with central punctum.

data.diagnosis: Intracranial germinoma (multifocal/bifocal pineal and suprasellar germinoma)

data.description: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic anemia and leukocytosis, with blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

data.diagnosis: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus native aortic valve infective endocarditis
data.description: A severe bacterial infection of the native aortic valve caused by MRSA, producing valvular vegetations, systemic inflammation, and embolic complications.

New early diastolic decrescendo murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation
Digital infarct of the left third toe
Recent discitis and psoas abscess, which may represent metastatic staphylococcal infection

Reduced level of consciousness is not typical unless there is central nervous system embolization or sepsis-related encephalopathy

data.diagnosis: Aortic root abscess complicating infective endocarditis

Fever and MRSA bacteremia indicating an infectious cause of valve damage
Possible periannular infection affecting the aortic valve

symptoms_not_in_common: An early diastolic murmur specifically suggests aortic valve involvement rather than nonspecific disseminated infection

data.description: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

data.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal glycogen-storage disorder caused by deficient acid alpha-glucosidase activity, resulting in glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle. No macroglossia

data.description: 6-year-old girl with a 1-year history of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain after a fall on the left hand, including rib pain, right knee pain with limping, and left flank pain radiating to the left leg. Six days before admission, she developed back pain, worsening limp, and intermittent fever up to 39.8°C. The day before admission, she developed periorbital swelling/discoloration, abdominal distention, and periumbilical discoloration. On examination, she was febrile, had bilateral periorbital discoloration, slight limping, and pain with external rotation of the right hip; abdomen was soft and nontender. Past history includes infant gastroesophageal reflux and pollen allergy with allergic rhinitis. Family history is notable for rheumatoid arthritis in the paternal grandmother.

data.description: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

data.diagnosis: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (sclerodermatous cutaneous chronic GVHD)
data.description: A late complication of allogeneic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Cutaneous chronic GVHD may cause lichenoid or sclerotic skin changes, reduced joint mobility, and autoimmune-like laboratory findings.
symptoms_in_common: History of allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation 2 years earlier
Diffuse nonpruritic rash involving face, trunk, and extremities
Skin tightening with impaired wrist dorsiflexion and positive prayer sign
Mild elevation of AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly described dry eyes, dry mouth, oral ulcers, or genital involvement
No reported diarrhea or other gastrointestinal GVHD symptoms

data.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive photosensitive cutaneous eruptions, including facial erythema, Gottron papules, and shawl-sign rash.
symptoms_in_common: Rash on upper trunk and extremities
Mild transaminase elevation, which can occur with muscle inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Impaired wrist dorsiflexion with prayer sign suggests skin sclerosis or contracture rather than typical dermatomyositis
No specifically described proximal muscle weakness
No heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, nail-fold changes, dysphagia, or elevated creatine kinase reported
Prior allogeneic transplant more strongly favors chronic GVHD

data.diagnosis: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), including scleroderma-like chronic GVHD
data.description: An autoimmune connective-tissue disease causing progressive skin thickening and fibrosis, joint contractures, and possible internal-organ involvement. A very similar scleroderma-like syndrome may occur with chronic GVHD after transplantation.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced wrist extension with positive prayer sign
Possible skin thickening/tightening of the hands
Muscle pain and weakness can occur in overlap connective-tissue disease
Mild liver-enzyme abnormalities may occur in systemic autoimmune disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute photosensitive diffuse rash and fever are less typical of classic systemic sclerosis
No Raynaud phenomenon reported
No digital ulcers, telangiectasias, calcinosis, dysphagia, reflux, or pulmonary symptoms reported
The onset after allogeneic transplantation favors sclerodermatous chronic GVHD over primary systemic sclerosis

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disorder that can cause photosensitive skin eruptions, constitutional symptoms, musculoskeletal complaints, cytopenias, renal disease, and positive antinuclear antibodies.
symptoms_in_common: Positive ANA at high titer with speckled pattern
symptoms_not_in_common: Prayer sign and restricted wrist mobility from skin tightening are not typical features of SLE
No arthritis, oral/nasal ulcers, serositis, nephritis, neurologic symptoms, or cytopenias reported
Male sex and post-transplant timing make primary SLE less likely
No anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-Smith antibody, complement, or urine abnormalities provided

data.diagnosis: Drug-induced photosensitive eruption or subacute cutaneous lupus-like reaction
data.description: A medication-associated immune or phototoxic skin reaction that develops on sun-exposed areas and may occasionally be associated with positive ANA and systemic symptoms. Acyclovir is an uncommon cause, but medication-related photosensitivity remains a consideration.
symptoms_in_common: Rash began after substantial sun exposure
Nonpruritic erythematous rash on face, trunk, and extremities
Positive ANA can be present in lupus-like drug reactions
Mild liver-enzyme elevation can occur in drug reactions
Intermittent fever and myalgias can accompany systemic drug hypersensitivity
symptoms_not_in_common: Only chronic daily acyclovir is reported, without a newly introduced medication
Prayer sign and restricted wrist movement are not explained by a simple photosensitive drug eruption
Muscle weakness is not typical of uncomplicated phototoxicity
The allogeneic transplant history strongly raises concern for chronic GVHD instead

data.description: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

data.diagnosis: Multiple eruptive keratoacanthomas (generalized eruptive keratoacanthoma of Grzybowski type)
data.description: A rare disorder characterized by the repeated eruption of numerous keratoacanthomas, which are rapidly growing crateriform keratinizing tumors considered to lie on the squamous-cell-carcinoma spectrum. Lesions may be intensely pruritic and occur on sun-exposed skin.
symptoms_in_common: Numerous papules and crateriform keratotic nodules on sun-exposed extremities
Clinical response to topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod
No evidence of metastatic disease on computed tomography
symptoms_not_in_common: Terminal kidney disease requiring long-term hemodialysis is not a defining feature
Some lesions were histologically verrucae vulgares rather than keratoacanthomas
Disease limited predominantly to the upper extremities rather than generalized body involvement

data.diagnosis: Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle disease or acquired reactive perforating collagenosis)
data.description: An intensely pruritic perforating skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes and chronic kidney disease/dialysis. It causes umbilicated hyperkeratotic papules and excoriations, usually on the extremities.
symptoms_in_common: End-stage kidney disease with long-term dialysis
Hyperkeratotic papules and excoriated/crusted lesions on the extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Histology demonstrated keratoacanthomas and verrucae rather than transepidermal elimination of collagen or elastin
Predominantly sun-exposed distribution is less characteristic
Large crateriform tumor-like lesions are less typical
Improvement with imiquimod and 5-fluorouracil is not standard for perforating dermatosis

data.diagnosis: Multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, keratoacanthoma type
data.description: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a keratinocyte malignancy that may present as hyperkeratotic papules, nodules, ulcers, or crateriform keratoacanthoma-like lesions. Risk is increased by prior immunosuppression, transplantation, ultraviolet exposure, and chronic skin injury.
symptoms_in_common: Histologic keratoacanthomas, which are closely related to well-differentiated squamous proliferations
History of two kidney transplants and prior transplant-related immunosuppression exposure
Use of topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod, which can be used for selected superficial keratinocytic neoplasms
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe generalized pruritus is not a typical presenting feature of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Numerous eruptive lesions developing in a relatively short period favor an eruptive keratoacanthoma syndrome
No metastases or lymphadenopathy were identified
Some biopsied lesions were common warts rather than carcinoma

data.description: A chronic itch-scratch disorder causing multiple intensely pruritic, firm, excoriated papules or nodules, commonly on accessible areas of the arms and legs. Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus can contribute to this condition.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple excoriated, crusted papules and nodules on the extremities
Chronic kidney disease, which can cause or worsen pruritus
Scarring and post-inflammatory skin changes from chronic lesions and scratching
symptoms_not_in_common: Histology showed keratoacanthomas rather than the typical lichenified and fibrotic changes of prurigo nodularis
Crateriform keratin-filled lesions are not typical
The sun-exposed predominance is less characteristic than a distribution on scratch-accessible sites
Response to antineoplastic topical agents such as 5-fluorouracil is not typical

data.description: Common warts are benign human-papillomavirus-associated epidermal proliferations that appear as rough hyperkeratotic papules. They may be numerous in people with impaired immune function.
symptoms_in_common: Papular hyperkeratotic lesions on the hands and extremities
Three lesions were histologically diagnosed as verrucae vulgares
Prior kidney transplantation and chronic severe systemic illness may predispose to extensive viral warts
Some lesions may be persistent and recur after local treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: The majority of biopsied lesions were keratoacanthomas rather than warts
Severe widespread pruritus is not typical of common warts
Ulcerated crateriform tumors are atypical for uncomplicated verruca vulgaris
Rapid progressive development of many keratoacanthoma-like lesions is not explained by warts alone

data.description: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst, initially presenting with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later she developed acute lower back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission she had mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, no fever or meningism, and GCS 15. Laboratory tests showed mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia. By day 2 she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffman signs. CSF studies and electromyography were normal.
An inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord causing acute or subacute motor weakness, sensory-level deficits, pain, and autonomic dysfunction. MRI commonly shows intramedullary T2 hyperintensity.
symptoms_in_common: Loss of temperature sensation with a defined sensory level
Bilateral Hoffman signs suggesting corticospinal tract involvement
Intramedullary spinal cord signal abnormality on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Frontal headaches
Conjunctival hyperaemia
Initial isolated left arm pain before spinal symptoms

data.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, that can cause severe longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and optic neuritis. Spinal attacks may produce weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Hemiparesis progressing to more extensive weakness
Sensory level with impaired temperature sensation
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctival hyperaemia without visual loss
Frontal headaches
No reported optic neuritis or persistent visual symptoms
Initial isolated arm pain

data.diagnosis: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) with myelitis
data.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease that can cause acute transverse myelitis, often in children and adolescents, with motor, sensory, and autonomic spinal cord dysfunction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctival hyperaemia
Frontal headaches without encephalopathy
No reported optic neuritis
No reported encephalopathy or seizures

data.description: Ischemic injury to the spinal cord, usually with sudden severe back or limb pain followed by weakness, loss of pain and temperature sensation, and bladder dysfunction. Cerebrospinal fluid is often normal early in the illness.
symptoms_in_common: Pain in the left arm and leg
Loss of temperature sensation below a spinal sensory level
Normal electromyography early in the course
Spinal cord signal abnormality on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms evolving over several days rather than reaching maximum severity immediately
Frontal headaches
Conjunctival hyperaemia
Mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia

data.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis presenting with partial transverse myelitis
data.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can initially present with a spinal cord lesion causing asymmetric weakness, sensory symptoms, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Upper motor neuron signs including bilateral Hoffman signs
Sensory deficit with a spinal level
Intramedullary cervical/thoracic spinal cord lesion on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked acute lower back and limb pain
Rapid progression to urinary retention over one to two days
Conjunctival hyperaemia
Frontal headaches
No reported prior neurologic episodes or brain lesions

data.description: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

An aggressive neoplasm of immature T-cell precursors that commonly presents with circulating blasts, marrow involvement, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and high LDH. The immunophenotype is typically positive for T-cell markers such as cytoplasmic/surface CD3, CD2, CD5, and CD7.
symptoms_in_common: Headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting that may reflect leukostasis or central nervous system involvement
Blasts positive for CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
Negative B-cell markers (CD10, CD19, CD20, CD22)
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of TdT expression, because most T-ALL cases express TdT
Absence of CD34 expression, although CD34 can be negative in more mature T-ALL
No mediastinal mass reported
No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly

data.diagnosis: Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ETP-ALL)
data.description: A high-risk subtype of T-ALL arising from very early thymic progenitors. It often has an immature phenotype with weak or absent CD5, expression of stem-cell or myeloid markers, and frequent CD34 and TdT positivity.
symptoms_in_common: Acute leukemia presentation with very high circulating blast percentage
T-lineage marker expression including CD2, CD3, and CD7
symptoms_not_in_common: Strong CD5 positivity, whereas ETP-ALL usually has absent or weak CD5
Negative CD34
Negative TdT
Negative myeloid-associated markers CD13 and CD33
No reported expression of typical ETP-associated markers such as CD117, CD34, HLA-DR, CD11b, or CD65
No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly

data.description: A mature post-thymic T-cell leukemia characterized by marked lymphocytosis and expression of mature T-cell markers, usually CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. It is often associated with chromosome 14 rearrangements involving T-cell receptor loci.
symptoms_in_common: Expression of mature T-cell markers CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
Negative TdT and CD34, supporting a mature rather than precursor T-cell phenotype
Chromosomal rearrangement involving chromosome 14/T-cell receptor region suggested by the imaging findings
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 27 years, because T-PLL usually occurs in older adults
Blast-like morphology with 95% blasts, rather than typical prolymphocytes
Severe thrombocytopenia at presentation is less characteristic
No splenomegaly
No hepatomegaly or lymphadenopathy

data.description: A mature peripheral T-cell neoplasm caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). Leukemic ATLL typically expresses CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, and CD25, often with hypercalcemia, lymphadenopathy, skin disease, and characteristic multilobated 'flower' cells.
symptoms_in_common: Peripheral blood involvement by malignant T cells
Expression of mature T-cell markers CD2, CD3, and CD5
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age, because ATLL usually develops after a long latency period in adults
No HTLV-1 infection or exposure history provided
No hypercalcemia reported
No lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or skin lesions
No reported CD4 or CD25 expression
Blast morphology rather than characteristic multilobated flower cells
Severe thrombocytopenia is not a defining typical feature

data.diagnosis: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including minimally differentiated AML
data.description: An acute leukemia caused by clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts in bone marrow and blood. AML commonly presents with leukocytosis or leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, high LDH, and symptoms related to leukostasis.
symptoms_in_common: Acute onset of headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting, which can occur with leukostasis
Very high percentage of peripheral blood blasts
No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy can occur in AML
symptoms_not_in_common: Blasts are negative for myeloid markers CD13 and CD33
Blasts strongly express multiple T-cell markers: CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
No reported myeloperoxidase positivity or Auer rods
Negative CD34 and TdT do not establish AML but are less helpful for an immature myeloid-blast phenotype
Chromosomal findings involving T-cell receptor-associated chromosome 14 rearrangements favor a T-cell neoplasm

data.description: 36-year-old Chinese man with 1 month of persistent fever. Previously healthy, with no significant past medical history, no prior TB, chronic disease, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, immune disease, or recent travel. On admission, he was acutely ill with fever, tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and bilateral pulmonary rales. He had persistent fever with pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, and clinical deterioration to acute respiratory failure. Initial labs: WBC 1.25 ×10^9/L, hemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 41 ×10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.79 g/L, ferritin 375,554 ng/mL.

A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, producing fever, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, extreme hyperferritinemia, and hemophagocytosis in bone marrow or other tissues.
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly atypical patient features; hypotension and severe lung involvement are complications rather than core diagnostic features

data.description: Widespread Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the lungs, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow. In severe cases it triggers secondary HLH, with hemophagocytosis, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, and multiorgan failure.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia consistent with bone-marrow involvement or HLH
Extreme ferritin elevation compatible with TB-triggered HLH
Bone-marrow histology compatible with granulomatous/inflammatory disease and hemophagocytosis
No prior tuberculosis is required for new disseminated TB
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt hypotensive shock is not a usual early presentation of tuberculosis
No reported chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, or known tuberculosis exposure
Very rapid respiratory decompensation is less typical of uncomplicated pulmonary tuberculosis

data.diagnosis: Severe viral infection with secondary HLH, such as Epstein-Barr virus-associated HLH
data.description: EBV and other viruses can provoke secondary HLH, particularly with persistent fever, cytopenias, hemophagocytosis, coagulopathy, and markedly elevated ferritin.
symptoms_in_common: Respiratory failure can occur in severe viral infection or HLH
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, hepatosplenomegaly, or atypical lymphocytosis
No reported viral prodrome or known EBV infection
Diffuse pulmonary imaging abnormalities are not specific for EBV-associated HLH

data.description: Disseminated Histoplasma infection can involve the reticuloendothelial system and bone marrow, causing prolonged fever, cytopenias, pulmonary infiltrates, very high ferritin, and secondary HLH.
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel or exposure history suggesting an endemic fungal exposure
Previously healthy and apparently immunocompetent status is less typical for severe disseminated histoplasmosis
No reported oral lesions, skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly

data.diagnosis: Hematologic malignancy-associated HLH, especially lymphoma-associated HLH
data.description: Lymphoma, leukemia, and other hematologic malignancies can trigger HLH through immune dysregulation and marrow involvement, resulting in fever, cytopenias, coagulopathy, hyperferritinemia, and organ failure.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid clinical decline and respiratory failure can occur in malignancy-associated HLH
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of malignancy
No reported lymphadenopathy, mass lesions, hepatosplenomegaly, or malignant cells in peripheral blood
Diffuse lung infiltrates and acute septic-shock physiology favor severe infection over isolated lymphoma

data.description: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.

data.diagnosis: West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease with cerebral vasculitis
data.description: Mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis that can cause fever, rash, coma, acute flaccid or asymmetric weakness, and occasionally cerebral vasculitis with ischemic brain lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel in Pacific regions where mosquito-borne flaviviruses may occur
CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and relatively preserved glucose
MRI findings compatible with multifocal ischemic/inflammatory brain lesions and vascular involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly polymorphonuclear leukocytes in CSF is less typical than lymphocytic pleocytosis
Marked focal hemiplegia is less common than diffuse encephalopathy or flaccid paralysis

data.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection causing severe encephalitis, often with altered consciousness, movement abnormalities, focal neurologic deficits, and inflammatory CSF findings.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel in regions with potential mosquito exposure
Focal neurologic deficits including hemiplegia and upper-limb paresis
CSF pleocytosis and elevated protein with preserved CSF glucose
Brain MRI abnormalities involving inflammatory or ischemic-appearing lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient rash is not a typical prominent feature
Cerebral arterial vasculitis is not a classic imaging feature
Predominantly neutrophilic CSF is less typical than lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis

data.diagnosis: Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy
data.description: Reactivation or primary infection with varicella-zoster virus can cause encephalitis and granulomatous vasculopathy, resulting in multifocal cerebral infarctions and focal neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Focal deficits including left hemiplegia, right arm paresis, and Babinski sign
Imaging suggestive of cerebral vascular inflammation and ischemic lesions
CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and normal or near-normal glucose
Rash can occur with varicella-zoster infection
symptoms_not_in_common: The rash was transient and not described as vesicular or dermatomal
Recent cruise travel and tropical exposure are not specifically suggestive of varicella-zoster infection
Predominantly polymorphonuclear CSF leukocytes are less characteristic

data.diagnosis: Dengue encephalitis or dengue-associated cerebral vasculopathy
data.description: Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection that may rarely cause encephalitis, encephalopathy, rash, and cerebrovascular complications including ischemic or hemorrhagic lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to tropical Pacific islands with mosquito exposure
Altered mental status progressing to coma
CSF inflammatory findings with elevated protein
Possible multifocal brain lesions on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No thrombocytopenia, bleeding, shock, myalgia, or severe systemic dengue manifestations are described
Cerebral arteritis/vasculitis is uncommon
CSF neutrophil predominance is not typical for viral dengue encephalitis

data.description: Tick-, mite-, or flea-borne rickettsial infections can cause fever, rash, meningoencephalitis, small-vessel vasculitis, cerebral infarction, and severe neurologic dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to areas where rickettsial infections can occur
Focal neurologic deficits and upper motor neuron signs
CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and preserved glucose
Vasculitic or ischemic-appearing lesions on neuroimaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No eschar, tick or mite bite, lymphadenopathy, or systemic multiorgan involvement is reported
The CSF leukocyte count is relatively low for severe bacterial-like meningoencephalitis
Large-vessel-appearing cerebral vascular abnormalities are less typical than small-vessel vasculitis

data.description: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved on weekly adalimumab over the past 3 years. Presented with 2 days of worsening cramping left calf pain and swelling extending to the foot, plus a purpuric/erythematous rash on the dorsum of both feet. Symptoms followed a 3-week history of sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, and chills, and occurred 2 weeks after travel for backpacking. He reported multiple prior self-limited episodes of similar upper respiratory symptoms. Exam showed left ankle synovitis, intact nasal septum, normal peripheral pulses, and discomfort from left leg pain.

An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by palpable purpura, arthritis or arthralgia, gastrointestinal involvement, and possible kidney disease. Skin biopsy typically shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA and C3 deposition.
symptoms_in_common: Recent upper respiratory illness with sore throat, cough, rhinorrhea, and chills
Skin findings consistent with small-vessel vasculitis and IgA deposition on immunofluorescence
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly unilateral left calf swelling extending to the foot
History of Crohn's disease
Long-term adalimumab treatment
No reported abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, hematuria, or renal symptoms

data.description: A drug-associated immune-complex vasculitis in which anti-TNF therapy, including adalimumab, can rarely trigger IgA-mediated leukocytoclastic vasculitis. It may present with palpable purpura and joint symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Adalimumab exposure for the past 3 years
Biopsy pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis with vascular IgA deposition
symptoms_not_in_common: A preceding upper respiratory illness is more characteristic of infection-triggered IgA vasculitis than purely drug-induced disease
Symptoms began after years of stable weekly adalimumab treatment rather than shortly after treatment initiation
Unilateral severe calf swelling is not a classic presentation

data.description: An inflammatory small-vessel vasculitis of the skin that produces palpable purpura, usually on dependent areas of the legs. It may be triggered by infections, medications, autoimmune disease, or inflammatory bowel disease.
symptoms_in_common: Purpuric rash affecting the lower extremities
Use of a medication capable of provoking immune-mediated reactions
Crohn's disease as an associated systemic inflammatory condition
Histologic appearance consistent with small-vessel neutrophilic vasculitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent IgA deposition favors the more specific diagnosis of IgA vasculitis
Ankle synovitis suggests systemic involvement rather than skin-limited disease
Severe focal left calf pain and swelling are not typical of uncomplicated cutaneous-only vasculitis

data.description: Inflammatory bowel disease can be associated with immune-mediated skin and joint manifestations, including leukocytoclastic vasculitis, peripheral arthritis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum.
symptoms_in_common: Peripheral joint inflammation with left ankle synovitis
Painful inflammatory skin lesions on the lower extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: The purpura following an upper respiratory illness and vascular IgA deposition more specifically support IgA vasculitis
No reported active gastrointestinal flare, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or weight loss
Unilateral calf swelling is not a typical Crohn's extraintestinal manifestation

data.description: A systemic necrotizing small- and medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, skin, and joints. It can cause purpura and arthralgia or arthritis, but usually has more destructive sinonasal, pulmonary, or renal features.
symptoms_not_in_common: Intact nasal septum without destructive sinus or nasal disease
No hemoptysis, pulmonary infiltrates, hematuria, or renal symptoms reported
IgA-predominant vascular deposition is not typical; GPA is usually pauci-immune
Rhinorrhea and a self-limited URI-like illness are more consistent with infection preceding IgA vasculitis

data.description: A 47-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with a six-month history of left-sided sore throat, ipsilateral otalgia, and a six-week history of a left-sided neck mass. He had never smoked and drank less than 5 units of alcohol per week. On examination in the ENT clinic, a firm fixed lymph node was palpable in the upper anterior triangle.

data.diagnosis: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil with cervical lymph-node metastasis
data.description: A malignant tumor arising in the palatine tonsil or adjacent oropharynx, commonly associated with high-risk human papillomavirus in nonsmokers and often presenting with metastatic upper-neck lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent unilateral sore throat for six months
Unilateral upper anterior cervical neck mass
Imaging showing an oropharyngeal/tonsillar mass with an enlarged ipsilateral cervical node
No smoking history, which is compatible with HPV-associated disease

data.description: Squamous cell cancer of the tonsil, base of tongue, or other oropharyngeal mucosa, traditionally associated with tobacco and heavy alcohol exposure and capable of spreading to cervical lymph nodes.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging evidence of a primary oropharyngeal lesion and regional nodal disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Never smoked
Consumes less than 5 units of alcohol per week

data.description: A lymphoma involving Waldeyer's ring, including the palatine tonsil, which may cause tonsillar enlargement and cervical lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Neck mass due to cervical lymph-node enlargement
Possible sore throat from tonsillar/oropharyngeal involvement
Imaging-visible oropharyngeal mass and cervical lymphadenopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Six-month unilateral sore throat with referred ipsilateral otalgia
Firm fixed lymph node, which is more suggestive of metastatic carcinoma
No reported constitutional symptoms such as fever, drenching night sweats, or weight loss

data.description: A carcinoma arising in the nasopharynx that can present with painless cervical lymph-node metastases and may cause referred ear symptoms through Eustachian-tube dysfunction or local nerve irritation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Imaging appears to identify an oropharyngeal/tonsillar-region primary lesion rather than a nasopharyngeal lesion
No reported nasal obstruction, epistaxis, hearing loss, or middle-ear effusion

data.diagnosis: Deep neck infection or suppurative cervical lymphadenitis
data.description: Bacterial infection of the pharynx or deep neck spaces that can produce painful sore throat, enlarged cervical lymph nodes, and occasionally a neck abscess.
symptoms_in_common: Ear pain can occur with pharyngeal infection
Cervical neck mass due to lymph-node enlargement
Imaging may show an enlarged node or inflammatory neck lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: Six-month duration of sore throat
Firm fixed lymph node rather than a tender inflammatory node
No reported fever, acute systemic illness, erythema, or leukocytosis
PET-avid primary oropharyngeal lesion and nodal lesion are more concerning for malignancy

data.description: 72-year-old white woman with 10-year history of recurrent cystitis. No systemic symptoms. Physical exam showed slight anemia. Urine cultures were positive for Escherichia coli. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy detected by CT and ultrasound. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and subsequent biopsies were negative for both pathologic lymphoid infiltrate and Helicobacter pylori. Otolaryngologic examination and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Serology for hepatitis C virus and hepatitis B virus was negative. No monoclonal component found in serum protein electrophoresis.

data.diagnosis: Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) of the urinary bladder
data.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, rarely involving the bladder. It is often associated with chronic cystitis and may show an API2-MALT1 rearrangement such as t(11;18).
symptoms_in_common: Localized bladder lesion on cystoscopic imaging
Histology showing a dense lymphoid infiltrate beneath urothelium
symptoms_not_in_common: None strongly atypical; hepatitis C negativity and lack of serum monoclonal protein do not exclude this diagnosis

data.description: A benign chronic inflammatory bladder condition characterized by lymphoid follicle formation, usually caused by recurrent bacterial urinary tract infections or chronic bladder irritation.
symptoms_in_common: Possible bladder mucosal irregularity or nodular lesions
Absence of generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly
symptoms_not_in_common: Slight anemia is not a typical feature
Dense monomorphic lymphoid infiltrate with features suggestive of lymphoma is not typical
Possible MALT-associated chromosomal rearrangement on fluorescence testing would not be expected

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
data.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can rarely arise primarily in the bladder or occur through secondary involvement. It generally consists of large atypical lymphoid cells and may cause a bladder mass.
symptoms_not_in_common: Long indolent history of recurrent cystitis favors MALT lymphoma rather than aggressive lymphoma
No systemic symptoms
No lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or bone marrow involvement
Histology does not appear dominated by sheets of large transformed cells

data.diagnosis: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with prominent inflammatory infiltrate
data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bladder that can present as a mucosal lesion and may be accompanied by chronic inflammation. It is more commonly associated with hematuria than recurrent infection alone.
symptoms_in_common: Visible bladder mucosal lesion on cystoscopic imaging
Mild anemia can occur in malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent culture-proven Escherichia coli cystitis is not the usual presenting feature
No reported hematuria
Histology is dominated by lymphoid cells rather than malignant urothelial cells
No systemic or metastatic findings

data.diagnosis: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving the urinary bladder
data.description: A usually bone-marrow-based indolent B-cell lymphoma composed of small lymphocytes, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and plasma cells; extranodal bladder involvement is uncommon and usually occurs with systemic disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: No monoclonal component on serum protein electrophoresis
Negative bone marrow biopsy
No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy
Localized bladder disease with chronic cystitis is more characteristic of bladder MALT lymphoma
No reported hyperviscosity symptoms, neuropathy, or other IgM-related manifestations

data.description: 95-year-old woman admitted after a fall. Medical history includes Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin). Laboratory findings showed elevated white cell count and C reactive protein levels. Urine culture revealed Klebsiella pneumoniae infection. Blood cultures were negative.

A complicated urinary tract infection caused by gas-forming organisms, producing gas within the bladder wall and/or lumen. It occurs most often in older patients with diabetes and can be caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae.
symptoms_in_common: Pelvic radiograph appearance suggestive of gas outlining the urinary bladder
symptoms_not_in_common: Fall

data.diagnosis: Complicated acute bacterial cystitis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae
data.description: Infection of the urinary bladder caused by bacteria; diabetes, advanced age, and impaired functional status increase the likelihood of complicated infection.
symptoms_in_common: Positive urine culture for Klebsiella pneumoniae
symptoms_not_in_common: Fall
Bladder-wall gas on imaging is not typical of uncomplicated cystitis

data.description: A severe gas-forming infection of the renal parenchyma and surrounding tissues, usually occurring in patients with diabetes and often caused by gram-negative organisms such as Klebsiella.
symptoms_not_in_common: Fall
Imaging abnormality appears centered in the pelvis/bladder rather than the kidneys
Negative blood cultures

data.description: An upper urinary tract infection involving the kidney, commonly caused by gram-negative urinary pathogens and associated with systemic inflammatory-marker elevation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Fall
No flank pain, fever, or costovertebral-angle tenderness is reported
Gas in the bladder wall is not a typical finding of ordinary pyelonephritis

data.description: An abnormal communication between the colon and urinary bladder that can introduce gas and enteric bacteria into the bladder, leading to recurrent urinary infections and intravesical gas.
symptoms_in_common: Possible gas in or around the urinary bladder on pelvic imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Klebsiella pneumoniae alone is more suggestive of a typical urinary pathogen than an enteric fistula
No pneumaturia or fecaluria is reported
No history of diverticular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or colorectal malignancy is provided
Fall

data.description: 22-year-old athletic male presented with swelling and locking of the left knee. He had no recent trauma but had several football injuries as a child. Two years prior, he had experienced disabling knee pain.

data.diagnosis: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle with a detached osteochondral loose body
data.description: A focal area of subchondral bone and cartilage injury, usually involving a femoral condyle, that may become unstable and detach into the joint as an osteochondral fragment. Detached fragments can cause intermittent locking and effusions.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent or prior disabling knee pain
Possible intra-articular ossified or osteochondral loose body on radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: History of several childhood football injuries is not necessary for osteochondritis dissecans, although repetitive athletic loading may contribute

data.diagnosis: Osteochondral fracture with retained intra-articular loose body
data.description: A cartilage-and-bone fragment may separate after prior knee trauma, often following patellar dislocation, twisting injury, or direct impact. A chronic retained fragment can produce recurrent pain, swelling, and locking.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent intra-articular bony/osteochondral fragment on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No recent trauma
Symptoms are occurring years after the reported sports injuries rather than immediately after an acute injury

data.description: A benign proliferative synovial disorder in which cartilage nodules form within the joint and may detach, calcify, or ossify into loose bodies. It commonly causes recurrent effusion, pain, restricted motion, and locking.
symptoms_in_common: Possible ossified intra-articular body on radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: A solitary visible loose body is less typical than the multiple similarly sized bodies often seen in synovial chondromatosis
Age 22 is younger than the usual presentation age

data.diagnosis: Meniscal tear, especially a bucket-handle tear
data.description: A displaced meniscal tear can mechanically block knee motion and cause true locking, joint-line pain, and recurrent effusion. Chronic tears may arise after remote athletic twisting injuries.
symptoms_not_in_common: An apparent calcified or ossified intra-articular fragment on radiographs is not typical of an isolated meniscal tear
No recent twisting injury is reported

data.diagnosis: Para-articular osteochondroma or solitary intra-articular osteocartilaginous loose body
data.description: A benign ossified/cartilaginous mass adjacent to or within the knee joint can impinge on joint movement and produce recurrent swelling and mechanical symptoms. It may be primary or represent an old detached osteochondral fragment.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent solitary ossified body near or within the knee joint on radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: Remote football injuries are not necessarily associated with a primary para-articular osteochondroma
This condition is less common than osteochondritis dissecans or a post-traumatic osteochondral loose body in this clinical setting

data.description: 48-year-old male presented with 1-week history of jaundice, dark brown urine, pale stools, and nausea. Medical history and physical exam were unremarkable.
