Laboratory findings showed hepatic panel in cholestatic pattern: total bilirubin 117 μmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 66.8 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 173 IU/L, γ-Glutamyltransferase 380 IU/L, Alanine transaminase 468 IU/L. CA19-9 was 11783 IU/mL. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and β2-microglobulin were normal.

data.diagnosis: Primary pancreatic lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
data.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising predominantly in the pancreas, often presenting as a pancreatic head mass with biliary obstruction. Histology commonly shows diffuse sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with B-cell immunophenotypic markers.
symptoms_in_common: No significant prior medical history or systemic illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated CA19-9 level
Normal LDH
Normal beta2-microglobulin
Very short 1-week symptom duration

data.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, usually originating from ductal epithelium in the pancreatic head and causing obstruction of the common bile duct.
symptoms_in_common: Pancreatic head mass causing biliary obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Lack of abdominal or back pain
No weight loss or anorexia reported
No constitutional symptoms
Histology suggesting a diffuse lymphoid rather than gland-forming epithelial neoplasm

data.description: A tumor arising from pancreatic neuroendocrine cells that may be functioning or nonfunctioning. Larger nonfunctioning tumors can compress the bile duct and produce obstructive jaundice.
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked CA19-9 elevation
No hormone-related syndrome such as hypoglycemia, diarrhea, flushing, or peptic ulcer disease
Histology not typically showing classic nested or trabecular neuroendocrine architecture

data.diagnosis: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
data.description: A rare, usually low-grade pancreatic tumor with solid and pseudopapillary microscopic areas. It occurs predominantly in young women but can rarely occur in middle-aged men.
symptoms_not_in_common: Male sex
Age of 48 years
Marked CA19-9 elevation
Abrupt severe cholestatic jaundice is less typical
Histology not clearly demonstrating papillary or pseudopapillary structures

data.description: An inflammatory fibroimmune pancreatic disorder that can form a mass-like pancreatic lesion and mimic pancreatic cancer, often causing obstructive jaundice.
symptoms_in_common: Mass-like pancreatic enlargement or lesion on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked CA19-9 elevation
No reported elevated serum IgG4 level
No history of other IgG4-related organ involvement
Histology suggesting a neoplastic cellular infiltrate rather than lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.title: T-cell/histiocyte rich large B-cell lymphoma

data.description: 80-year-old woman with 6-month history of slowly increasing asymptomatic lumbar subcutaneous mass. History of chronic renal failure requiring dialysis three times weekly for 10 years. Poor compliance with phosphate-binding medications and dietary restrictions. Physical exam showed firm, immobile subcutaneous nodule measuring 9 cm in major axis. Laboratory findings: serum calcium 1.95 mmol/L (normal: 2.05-2.55), serum phosphorus 3.3 mmol/L (normal: 0.74-1.52), serum intact parathyroid hormone 142 ng/L (normal: 10-65), serum creatinine 787 μmol/L (normal: 53-106).
Massive periarticular or subcutaneous calcium-phosphate deposition occurring in patients with chronic renal failure, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
symptoms_in_common: Poor adherence to phosphate binders and dietary phosphate restriction
Elevated parathyroid hormone level consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Slowly enlarging painless firm subcutaneous mass
Large lobulated calcified mass on CT imaging
Subcutaneous location near the hip/pelvic region
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypocalcemia is less typical than normal or elevated calcium levels, although it can occur in dialysis-associated disease
No reported limitation of joint motion or pain

data.diagnosis: Calcinosis cutis due to metastatic calcification
data.description: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in otherwise normal skin and subcutaneous tissues due to systemic calcium-phosphate imbalance, often from renal failure.
symptoms_in_common: Firm subcutaneous calcified nodule or mass
symptoms_not_in_common: The 9 cm lobulated mass is unusually large for typical calcinosis cutis
No skin ulceration, chalky discharge, inflammation, or pain is reported
No multiple smaller skin lesions are reported

data.description: A severe dialysis-associated disorder involving calcification and thrombosis of small dermal and subcutaneous vessels, usually causing painful ischemic skin lesions and necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: End-stage renal disease with long-term dialysis
symptoms_not_in_common: Mass is painless
No livedo, purpura, skin necrosis, ulceration, or eschar
No severe cutaneous pain
Imaging shows a focal lobulated calcified mass rather than primarily vascular calcification

data.description: Chronic deposition of monosodium urate crystals forming firm nodules (tophi), which can occasionally calcify and is more common in patients with renal dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic renal failure is a risk factor for hyperuricemia and gout
Mass can be painless in chronic tophaceous disease
Calcification can occasionally be present in longstanding tophi
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of gout attacks or hyperuricemia is provided
No joint pain, redness, or inflammatory arthritis is reported
Lesion location and extensive multilobulated calcification are more characteristic of tumoral calcinosis
Hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism strongly favor calcium-phosphate deposition instead

data.description: Abnormal bone formation in soft tissues, usually after trauma, surgery, neurologic injury, or prolonged immobilization; it may present as a firm calcified mass.
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of trauma, surgery, neurologic injury, or local inflammation
Subcutaneous rather than intramuscular location
No described zonal bone formation or organized cortical/trabecular structure on imaging
Severe hyperphosphatemia and dialysis-associated mineral imbalance favor uremic tumoral calcinosis

data.description: 47-year-old female presented to emergency department after being hit while skiing by another skier at high speed from behind. Immediate pain and marked general swelling of the knee joint occurred after impact. Unable to bear weight. Physical exam showed neurovascularly intact limb with no broken skin. No relevant medical, family, or social history.
An intra-articular fracture of the lateral upper tibia, often caused by valgus force or axial loading, with fracture splitting and depression of the joint surface.
symptoms_in_common: Radiographic irregularity and depression of the lateral tibial plateau
symptoms_not_in_common: No open wound
Neurovascular status is intact

data.description: A more extensive intra-articular fracture involving both medial and lateral tibial plateaus, usually due to high-energy trauma and associated with substantial swelling and instability.
symptoms_not_in_common: Imaging appears to show predominantly lateral rather than clear bicondylar involvement
No reported gross deformity or instability
Neurovascular status is intact

data.description: An avulsion fracture of the tibial intercondylar eminence, often related to anterior cruciate ligament traction during twisting or high-energy knee trauma.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty or inability to bear weight
Possible fracture near the intercondylar region
symptoms_not_in_common: Radiographs more strongly suggest a lateral tibial plateau fracture
No reported knee instability or positive anterior drawer/Lachman findings
No twisting mechanism specifically described

data.diagnosis: Anterior cruciate ligament rupture with hemarthrosis
data.description: Tearing of the anterior cruciate ligament, commonly caused by pivoting, hyperextension, or high-energy trauma, producing rapid swelling from bleeding into the joint and instability.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid marked knee swelling consistent with hemarthrosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Visible proximal tibial fracture on radiographs is not typical of an isolated ACL rupture
No reported popping sensation
No reported giving-way sensation or ligamentous instability

data.description: Displacement of the patella, usually laterally, which can cause acute pain, swelling, inability to bear weight, and occasionally an associated osteochondral fracture.
symptoms_not_in_common: No described patellar deformity or lateral displacement
Radiographs demonstrate a tibial plateau fracture pattern rather than patellar dislocation
Mechanism is direct high-speed impact rather than typical twisting injury

diagnoses.name: Tibial plateau fracture
diagnoses.title: Fracture of lower end of tibia[Tibial Plateau]

data.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with complaints of anal pain, constipation, and tenesmus for 3 months before being referred to the hospital. There were no relevant prior illnesses. Rectal digital examination revealed a 6-cm smooth elastic mass on the rectal posterior left side 2 cm from the anal verge. Colonoscopy showed a rectal submucosal bulging. Computed tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the presence of a single 6-cm well-delimited mass, compressing and infiltrating the wall of the medium to low rectum.

A mesenchymal tumor arising from the gastrointestinal tract wall, usually composed of spindle cells and often presenting as a submucosal rectal mass. Larger tumors can infiltrate the muscular wall and produce obstructive symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Compression and infiltration of the rectal wall
symptoms_not_in_common: No gastrointestinal bleeding was reported
No weight loss or systemic symptoms were reported

data.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum that can form a deep intramural or submucosal mass. It may cause pain, bowel obstruction, and local invasion.
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesion is described as smooth and well-delimited, whereas leiomyosarcomas may be more irregular or necrotic
No bleeding was reported
No constitutional symptoms such as weight loss or fever were reported

data.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor arising from the muscularis mucosae or muscularis propria of the rectum. Large lesions may produce obstructive symptoms despite benign histology.
symptoms_in_common: Smooth elastic rectal mass on digital examination
symptoms_not_in_common: Imaging suggests infiltration of the rectal wall, which is less typical of a benign leiomyoma
A 6-cm lesion is relatively large for a benign rectal leiomyoma

data.description: A rare nerve-sheath tumor that may arise in the rectal wall and appear as a slowly growing, well-defined submucosal mass. Most gastrointestinal schwannomas are benign.
symptoms_in_common: Normal-appearing mucosal surface with submucosal bulging on colonoscopy
symptoms_not_in_common: Rectal-wall infiltration is less typical for a benign schwannoma
The lesion is relatively large
No prolonged history of slowly progressive symptoms was reported

data.diagnosis: Rectal adenocarcinoma with submucosal or intramural growth
data.description: The most common malignant rectal tumor, usually originating from mucosal glandular epithelium. It commonly causes altered bowel habits, tenesmus, obstruction, and local invasion, although it typically appears as a mucosal lesion rather than a smooth submucosal mass.
symptoms_in_common: Mass involving the medium to low rectum
symptoms_not_in_common: Smooth elastic submucosal mass is not the usual colonoscopic appearance
No rectal bleeding was reported
No anemia, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms were reported
The imaging description of a single well-delimited mass is less typical than an irregular annular lesion

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

data.description: Two-year-four-month-old female with intrauterine growth restriction at birth (39 weeks, cesarean delivery; birth weight 1850 g, length 44.5 cm, head circumference 31 cm, all <3rd percentile). In infancy, she had severe bilateral sensorineural hearing loss confirmed by ABR at 3 months and received hearing aids at 4 months. She showed persistent short stature and low weight, with normal psychomotor development (sitting at 8 months, walking at 14 months, talking at 13 months). Physical features included triangular face, prominent forehead, small chin, hypoplastic nasal alae, large mouth with thin downturned lips, low-set ears, deep-set eyes, delayed teething, microdontia, delayed bone age, thin wrinkled skin with visible vessels, and lipoatrophy. CNS MRI was normal. Genetic testing found a de novo heterozygous PIK3R1 variant c.1956dupT (p.Lys653*).

A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PIK3R1 variants, characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, postnatal short stature, partial lipodystrophy, characteristic facial appearance, delayed dentition, and often insulin resistance later in life.
symptoms_in_common: De novo heterozygous PIK3R1 c.1956dupT (p.Lys653*) variant
Intrauterine growth restriction with birth weight, length, and head circumference below the 3rd percentile
Persistent short stature and low weight
Triangular face with prominent forehead and small chin
Large mouth with thin downturned lips
Thin wrinkled skin with visible veins
Normal brain MRI and relatively preserved psychomotor development
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe bilateral congenital sensorineural hearing loss is not a classic core feature, although hearing impairment has been reported in some affected individuals

data.description: A genetic disorder with near-complete lack of subcutaneous fat from birth, resulting in a muscular appearance, prominent veins, metabolic complications, and often enlarged liver or heart.
symptoms_in_common: Marked lipoatrophy or reduced subcutaneous fat
Visible superficial veins through thin skin
Low body weight and lean appearance
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe intrauterine growth restriction is not typical
Persistent short stature is not typical
Triangular face with hypoplastic nasal alae and characteristic SHORT-like facial appearance is not typical
Delayed bone age is not typical
Delayed teething and microdontia are not typical
Severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss is not typical
No reported hepatomegaly, cardiomyopathy, acromegaloid appearance, or metabolic abnormalities
A pathogenic PIK3R1 variant supports SHORT syndrome rather than congenital generalized lipodystrophy

data.description: A premature-aging disorder, usually caused by a de novo LMNA variant, characterized by postnatal growth failure, loss of subcutaneous fat, thin skin, prominent veins, and an aged facial appearance.
symptoms_in_common: Thin wrinkled skin with visible veins
symptoms_not_in_common: Intrauterine growth restriction is less typical because affected infants are often normal at birth
Severe bilateral congenital sensorineural hearing loss is not typical
Triangular face with hypoplastic nasal alae and large downturned mouth is more suggestive of SHORT syndrome
Delayed bone age is not a defining feature
No alopecia, scalp-vein prominence, joint contractures, hip dislocation, or cardiovascular disease is described
The identified PIK3R1 variant is not the usual genetic cause

data.description: A growth-restriction syndrome most often related to abnormal methylation at 11p15 or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7, featuring prenatal and postnatal growth failure, relative macrocephaly, triangular face, and feeding difficulties.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent postnatal short stature and low weight
symptoms_not_in_common: Lipoatrophy with thin wrinkled skin and prominent visible veins is not typical
Hypoplastic nasal alae and a large mouth with thin downturned lips are not classic features
Microdontia and markedly delayed teething are not typical defining findings
Severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss is not typical
No body asymmetry, relative macrocephaly at birth, or feeding difficulty is reported
The de novo PIK3R1 variant supports SHORT syndrome rather than Russell-Silver syndrome

data.description: A severe autosomal recessive insulin-receptor disorder caused by biallelic INSR variants, characterized by profound fetal and postnatal growth restriction, loss of fat, distinctive facial features, and severe insulin-resistance-related metabolic disease.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent poor growth and low weight
Reduced subcutaneous fat or lipoatrophic appearance
Prominent forehead and abnormal facial appearance
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal psychomotor development and survival into early childhood without severe systemic illness are less consistent with classic Donohue syndrome
No severe hyperinsulinemia, hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, acanthosis nigricans, enlarged genitalia, or organ enlargement is reported
Triangular face, hypoplastic nasal alae, and downturned thin lips are more characteristic of SHORT syndrome
Severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss is not typical
The patient has a heterozygous PIK3R1 variant rather than biallelic INSR variants

data.description: 56-year-old Ethiopian male with prior type A thymoma resected 3 years earlier, admitted for persistent fever, chills, cough, night sweats, and weight loss. He also reported fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections intermittently responsive to antibiotics, and diarrhea associated with IBS-D symptoms. On admission he had low-grade fever with otherwise normal vital signs and room-air oxygen saturation. Labs showed lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 1,000/μL), mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL), and low albumin/protein. Extensive infectious workup was negative, but induced sputum on hospital day 2 was positive for Pneumocystis jiroveci and Moraxella catarrhalis. Cavitary lesion biopsy showed ulceration with acute and chronic inflammation, negative cultures, negative GMS staining, and no malignancy. He had absent antibody response to 14 pneumococcal serotypes, reduced lymphocyte proliferation to tetanus and candida, and lymphocyte subsets showed low CD3, CD4, and marked B-cell depletion (CD19 1/cmm).

A rare acquired immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, marked B-cell depletion, impaired T-cell function, and recurrent bacterial and opportunistic infections.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic cough and dyspnea on exertion
Low CD3 and CD4 T-cell counts
Reduced lymphocyte proliferation to tetanus and candida
symptoms_not_in_common: Cavitary pulmonary lesion is not a classic direct manifestation, although it can occur from recurrent or opportunistic pulmonary infection

data.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring primarily in patients with impaired cellular immunity, especially reduced CD4 T-cell function.
symptoms_in_common: Positive induced sputum for Pneumocystis jiroveci
symptoms_not_in_common: Cavitary lung lesion is unusual for classic PJP
Recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections are not explained by PJP alone
Marked B-cell depletion and absent pneumococcal antibody responses are not caused by PJP
Moraxella catarrhalis infection is a separate bacterial process

data.description: A primary antibody deficiency characterized by impaired antibody production, recurrent respiratory infections, and sometimes gastrointestinal disease and chronic lung damage.
symptoms_in_common: Absent protective antibody response to pneumococcal serotypes
Possible chronic airway changes on chest imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: History of thymoma strongly favors Good syndrome rather than CVID
Near-complete B-cell depletion is less typical of CVID
Marked CD4 T-cell reduction and Pneumocystis infection are less typical in uncomplicated CVID
Cavitary lung lesion is not a typical primary CVID finding

data.description: A chronic mycobacterial pulmonary infection that can cause constitutional symptoms and cavitary lung disease, particularly in patients with impaired cellular immunity.
symptoms_in_common: Origin from a region with higher tuberculosis prevalence
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative extensive infectious testing and negative lesion cultures argue against tuberculosis
Pneumocystis jiroveci positivity suggests an alternative opportunistic pulmonary infection
Profound B-cell depletion and absent pneumococcal antibody response are not explained by tuberculosis
Recurrent Moraxella and other sinopulmonary infections are not typical consequences of isolated tuberculosis

data.diagnosis: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection with advanced immunosuppression
data.description: HIV causes progressive CD4 T-cell depletion and predisposes to opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, constitutional symptoms, and recurrent infections.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior thymoma and severe B-cell depletion more strongly support Good syndrome
Absent pneumococcal antibody responses with near-absent CD19 B cells are not the usual dominant HIV pattern
No HIV-positive test result is reported
Cavitary lesion is not typical of PJP and would require another concurrent process if HIV were present

data.description: A 26-year-old man presented with a firm, nontender palpable lymph node in his left cervical area. The patient had no specific past medical history. On admission, his vital signs were stable with blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse rate 80/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and body temperature 36.5°C. Routine laboratory investigations showed a normal complete blood count, serum chemical tests, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Serologic tests for cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis of mycobacteria yielded negative results. Serum immunoglobulin levels were within normal ranges: IgG 1,680 mg/dL (normal 700-1,700 mg/dL), IgA 117 mg/dL (normal 70-400 mg/dL), IgM 129 mg/dL (normal 40-230 mg/dL), and IgE 33.8 IU/mL (normal 0-100 IU/mL). The patient had no history of fever during the clinical course.

A benign, self-limited inflammatory lymph-node disorder characterized by patchy necrosis with abundant histiocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, most commonly affecting cervical lymph nodes in young adults.
symptoms_in_common: Normal complete blood count and inflammatory markers can occur
Histology compatible with necrotizing lymphadenitis containing histiocytes
symptoms_not_in_common: Nontender lymph node
No fever during the clinical course
Mediastinal lymph-node involvement on imaging
Normal ESR

data.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that commonly presents with persistent painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; diagnosis requires identification of Reed-Sternberg cells in an appropriate inflammatory background.
symptoms_in_common: Normal blood counts may be present in early disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or other B symptoms
Normal ESR
Histology showing necrotizing lymphadenitis with numerous histiocytes rather than Reed-Sternberg cells
No reported weight loss or night sweats

data.description: Mycobacterial infection of lymph nodes, usually causing chronic cervical lymph-node enlargement with granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis; mediastinal nodal disease may coexist.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic firm lymph-node enlargement can be nontender
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative mycobacterial PCR
No fever
Normal ESR
Normal routine laboratory findings
Histology lacking typical caseating granulomas and acid-fast bacilli

data.description: Autoimmune lymph-node inflammation that can resemble Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease histologically, sometimes with necrosis, hematoxylin bodies, and vascular immune-complex changes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Male sex
No fever
No rash, arthritis, oral ulcers, serositis, or renal symptoms reported
Normal ESR
No reported autoimmune serologic abnormalities

data.diagnosis: Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy)
data.description: A nonmalignant histiocytic disorder that typically produces painless cervical lymphadenopathy and may involve mediastinal or other extranodal sites; lymph-node histology classically shows S100-positive histiocytes with emperipolesis.
symptoms_not_in_common: No massive bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy described
No fever
Normal ESR
Histology suggestive of necrotizing lymphadenitis rather than prominent sinus histiocytosis with emperipolesis

data.description: 26-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks’ gestation with monochorionic diamniotic twins. History of childhood asthma, obesity, anxiety, depression, gestational diabetes, polyhydramnios in one fetus, and two prior uncomplicated pregnancies. Three weeks before presentation, after her children had ear infection and sore throat, she developed conjunctival erythema with green discharge, followed by nonproductive cough, sore throat, ear pain, and new leg edema. One week before admission, she developed progressive right leg pain. At first hospital, she had pitting leg edema without erythema or warmth, tachycardia, and hypotension. Five days later, she developed left leg tenderness with worsening bilateral edema, severe coughing episodes, and expiratory wheezes. She then had sudden severe crushing chest pain, became unresponsive and pulseless, and was found to have monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, leading to cardiac arrest.

Acute inflammatory injury of the heart muscle, often following a viral respiratory illness, which can rapidly cause severe ventricular dysfunction, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and cardiac arrest.
symptoms_in_common: Recent upper respiratory illness with sore throat, cough, ear pain, and conjunctivitis
Pulmonary edema and pleural effusions on chest imaging
Apparent absence of obstructive coronary disease on angiography
symptoms_not_in_common: Green conjunctival discharge is not a typical cardiac manifestation
Progressive unilateral right leg pain is not a classic myocarditis feature
Pregnancy with monochorionic diamniotic twins is a risk context but not a direct myocarditis symptom

data.description: Pregnancy-associated systolic heart failure occurring late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery, characterized by reduced left-ventricular function, fluid overload, arrhythmias, and possible cardiogenic shock.
symptoms_in_common: Presentation during late pregnancy at 32 weeks' gestation
Twin pregnancy, which increases hemodynamic stress and risk
Cough and wheezing that may reflect pulmonary congestion
Pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions on imaging
Severe cardiac decompensation with ventricular tachycardia and arrest
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent conjunctivitis, sore throat, ear pain, and respiratory viral prodrome are not typical features
Sudden crushing chest pain is less typical than progressive dyspnea and fatigue
Initial unilateral leg pain is not characteristic
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia can occur but is not the most common initial presentation

data.description: Acute obstruction of the pulmonary arterial circulation by thrombus, commonly arising from deep venous thrombosis; pregnancy, obesity, and immobility are important risk factors.
symptoms_in_common: Pregnancy and obesity, both major thromboembolic risk factors
Progressive right then left leg pain and bilateral leg edema, which could suggest deep venous thrombosis
symptoms_not_in_common: A three-week infectious prodrome with conjunctivitis, sore throat, and ear pain is not typical
Pulmonary edema and pleural effusions are less typical than acute right-heart strain findings
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is less typical than pulseless electrical activity or severe hypoxemia-related arrest
No pulmonary arterial embolus is described on the provided CT imaging

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome due to spontaneous coronary artery dissection
data.description: A nontraumatic tear or intramural hematoma in a coronary artery that can cause myocardial infarction; it occurs disproportionately in pregnant and postpartum women and may provoke ventricular arrhythmias.
symptoms_in_common: Late pregnancy, a recognized risk period for pregnancy-associated spontaneous coronary artery dissection
symptoms_not_in_common: The preceding respiratory and conjunctival illness is not typical
Progressive edema and pulmonary congestion before the chest pain are not the usual initial presentation
Bilateral leg pain and edema are not characteristic
Coronary angiography does not appear to show an obstructive coronary lesion or dissection

data.description: Inflammation involving both the myocardium and pericardium, usually viral, which may cause chest pain, electrocardiographic changes, impaired ventricular function, arrhythmia, and occasionally fulminant shock.
symptoms_in_common: Pulmonary edema consistent with severe myocardial involvement
No clear obstructive coronary explanation for the cardiac event
symptoms_not_in_common: The chest pain is described as crushing rather than pleuritic or positional
No pericardial friction rub is reported
No clear pericardial effusion is described
Progressive leg pain is not a typical myopericarditis manifestation

data.description: 73-year-old man with confusion and irritability that worsened over 2 days, preceded by weakness, lethargy, chills, diarrhea, decreased oral intake, reduced responsiveness, near-catatonia, recurrent epistaxis, and chest/left arm pain. Past history: diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, diastolic heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, prior exudative pericardial effusion (resolved), recurrent epistaxis since childhood, hyperlipidemia, pancytopenia, obstructive sleep apnea, GERD, and headaches. Family history notable for recurrent epistaxis in mother and daughter. On examination: somnolent but arousable, oriented with waxing and waning attention, dry mucous membranes, dried blood around nares, multiple telangiectasias on face/lips/torso, nonblanching cherry angiomas on chest, irregularly irregular heart rhythm, palpable liver edge 2 cm below the right costal margin, and chronic venous insufficiency changes in the legs.

An autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and arteriovenous malformations in organs such as the liver, lungs, brain, and gastrointestinal tract. The imaging is compatible with hepatic vascular malformations/shunting.
symptoms_in_common: Family history of recurrent epistaxis in mother and daughter
Multiple telangiectasias on the face, lips, and torso
Possible hepatic vascular malformations on Doppler ultrasound and CT
History of heart failure and pulmonary hypertension, which can occur from high-output cardiac failure due to hepatic shunting
Pancytopenia, potentially related to chronic bleeding or portal hypertension
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute diarrhea
Chills
Dry mucous membranes and decreased oral intake
Acute waxing-and-waning confusion
Chest and left arm pain

data.diagnosis: Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due to HHT
data.description: Abnormal direct connections between hepatic arteries, portal veins, and hepatic veins that can cause high-output heart failure, portal hypertension, biliary ischemia, or portosystemic shunting. Doppler findings of turbulent high-flow vascular channels support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal hepatic vascular flow/shunting on ultrasound and CT
Confusion or reduced responsiveness, potentially due to portosystemic shunting
Telangiectasias and recurrent epistaxis suggesting underlying HHT
symptoms_not_in_common: Diarrhea
Chills
Dried blood around the nares
Near-catatonia
Chest and left arm pain

data.description: A neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by impaired clearance of neurotoxins, commonly ammonia, when portal venous blood bypasses the liver through cirrhosis-related or congenital/acquired portosystemic shunts. Hepatic vascular malformations can produce clinically significant shunting even without classic cirrhosis.
symptoms_in_common: Possible hepatic vascular shunting on imaging
Dehydration and decreased oral intake, which may precipitate encephalopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent epistaxis since childhood
Facial and lip telangiectasias
Chills
Diarrhea
Chest and left arm pain

data.diagnosis: Delirium due to dehydration and acute infectious gastroenteritis
data.description: Acute delirium in an older adult can be precipitated by volume depletion, poor oral intake, electrolyte abnormalities, or infection. Diarrhea, chills, lethargy, and dry mucous membranes suggest an acute systemic illness with dehydration.
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent lifelong epistaxis
Family history of epistaxis
Multiple telangiectasias
Abnormal hepatic vascular shunting on imaging
Palpable liver edge

data.diagnosis: High-output heart failure secondary to hepatic arteriovenous shunting
data.description: Large hepatic arteriovenous shunts can substantially increase cardiac output and eventually cause heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, atrial arrhythmias, hepatic congestion, and fatigue. This complication is particularly associated with hepatic involvement in HHT.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable liver edge, possibly reflecting hepatic congestion
Underlying features of HHT, including epistaxis and telangiectasias
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute diarrhea
Chills
Dry mucous membranes
Dried blood around the nares
Near-catatonia and acute fluctuating confusion

data.description: A 7-month-old female infant presented with a 2-month history of brown macules on the back and thighs, without prodromal erythema or trauma. Her birth history was unremarkable, and her growth and development were normal. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed 7 sharply marginated, irregularly shaped, polymorphic hyperpigmented macules of 10 to 15 mm in diameter, without scales, on the back and thighs. The hyperpigmented macules were of orange hue, with unevenness of the pigmentation. Vital signs were normal. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory test results, including complete blood cell count, liver function tests, and renal function, were normal.
A benign non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of infancy that can rarely present as flat orange-brown macules rather than the more typical yellow-red papules or nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Sharply demarcated lesions on the trunk and thighs
Normal blood count and liver and renal function tests
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions are flat macules rather than typical papules or nodules
Irregular polymorphic shape rather than round dome-shaped lesions
No yellow coloration described

data.description: A mast-cell proliferation in the skin, usually presenting during infancy or childhood with multiple tan, brown, or red-brown macules and papules that may urticate after rubbing.
symptoms_in_common: Normal systemic examination and laboratory testing can occur in skin-limited disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported itching, flushing, blistering, or urtication
No reported Darier sign after rubbing
Lesions are relatively large at 10 to 15 mm
Orange hue and irregular polymorphic borders are less typical
Only seven lesions are present, whereas mastocytosis often causes numerous lesions

data.description: Benign, flat, uniformly light-brown pigmented patches that may be isolated or, when numerous, associated with genetic disorders such as neurofibromatosis type 1.
symptoms_in_common: Normal development and family history do not exclude isolated lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions developed during infancy rather than being clearly present from birth
Orange-brown hue rather than uniform light brown color
Uneven pigmentation
Irregular polymorphic shapes rather than smooth oval patches
Back and thigh distribution without other classic neurofibromatosis findings

data.description: A self-limited non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of infancy characterized by asymptomatic red-yellow to red-brown papules, usually beginning on the head and spreading to the upper body.
symptoms_in_common: Asymptomatic reddish-brown to orange-brown skin lesions
Normal physical examination apart from skin lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions are macules rather than papules
No facial or scalp involvement
Thigh involvement is less characteristic
Lesions are hyperpigmented brown macules rather than red-yellow papules

data.description: A clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells that can affect infants and may produce papules, crusted lesions, seborrheic-like eruptions, or purpuric lesions; systemic involvement must be assessed.
symptoms_in_common: May initially be limited to the skin
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions are flat, non-scaly hyperpigmented macules rather than papules, crusts, erosions, or purpura
No scalp, flexural, or diaper-area predominance
No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly
Normal blood count and liver function tests
No constitutional symptoms or growth impairment

data.description: A 17-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with constipation and bloodless vomiting for 3 weeks. The vomiting worsened after food ingestion. The patient was exhausted and underweight, although she did not suffer abdominal pain. At admission, the patient had unwillingly lost 10 kg over 2 years, resulting in a body mass index of 14. During this period, she started prevention medicine due to a loss of menstruation. The patient had no prior medical or surgical history. Blood tests revealed an increased sed rate (ESR) of 33 (normal range: 2-20) as the only outlier. A contrast-enhanced CT was ordered based on the acute exacerbating of vomiting and constipation, with ileus as the tentative diagnosis.

Compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, usually after substantial loss of retroperitoneal fat from weight loss. The imaging demonstrates a markedly narrowed aortomesenteric angle and distance with gastric/duodenal dilatation.
symptoms_in_common: Marked underweight status with BMI of 14
Amenorrhea associated with low body weight
Imaging findings of reduced aortomesenteric angle/distance and proximal gastrointestinal dilatation
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain

data.diagnosis: Anorexia nervosa or severe malnutrition-related eating disorder
data.description: An eating disorder characterized by inadequate caloric intake and very low body weight, often causing amenorrhea, constipation, fatigue, delayed gastric emptying, and risk of secondary superior mesenteric artery syndrome.
symptoms_not_in_common: No stated fear of weight gain, body-image disturbance, food restriction, bingeing, or purging behavior
Acute obstructive imaging findings are not explained by an eating disorder alone

data.description: Delayed gastric emptying due to impaired stomach motility, producing nausea, vomiting after meals, early satiety, poor nutritional intake, and weight loss.
symptoms_in_common: Vomiting that worsens after food ingestion
symptoms_not_in_common: No diabetes, neurologic disorder, medication trigger, or prior gastric surgery
No abdominal pain
CT evidence of focal duodenal compression and narrowed aortomesenteric anatomy is not typical of primary gastroparesis

data.diagnosis: Peptic ulcer disease with gastric outlet obstruction
data.description: Inflammation or ulcer-related scarring at the pylorus or proximal duodenum can obstruct gastric emptying, causing postprandial vomiting, dehydration, and weight loss.
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal or epigastric pain
No gastrointestinal bleeding
No reported history of ulcer disease or NSAID use
Imaging indicates compression at the third part of the duodenum rather than pyloric obstruction

data.description: A partial or complete blockage of intestinal transit can cause vomiting, constipation, abdominal distension, and inability to tolerate oral intake. In this case, duodenal obstruction from superior mesenteric artery compression is a more specific mechanical cause.
symptoms_in_common: Weight loss and exhaustion from poor intake
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain
No prior abdominal surgery or other stated risk factor for adhesions
Three-week gradual course and severe low BMI favor superior mesenteric artery syndrome over a nonspecific acute bowel obstruction

data.description: 41-year-old man with morbid obesity, hyperlipidemia, prior cholecystectomy, and remote Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Eight years after surgery, he developed epigastric and left upper quadrant abdominal pain (5/10) worsened by eating, with abdominal tenderness on exam and normal basic labs. He later developed foul-smelling watery diarrhea 6–7 times daily with visible food particles, pale floating stools, increased flatus, and daily feculent eructation. Over 4 months, he developed progressive weakness, myalgias, muscle cramps, and significant weight loss from 95.3 kg to 72.6 kg, and appeared cachectic and chronically ill with dry mucous membranes, feculent breath, and decreased skin turgor.

data.diagnosis: Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastric pouch and transverse colon
data.description: An abnormal connection between the stomach/gastric pouch and colon, allowing recently ingested food to pass directly into the colon. This can occur as a rare late complication after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and causes severe diarrhea, malnutrition, and feculent belching. The contrast study demonstrates communication between the gastric pouch and transverse/descending colon.
symptoms_in_common: Visible undigested food particles in stool
Postprandial epigastric and left upper quadrant pain
Weakness, myalgias, and muscle cramps from malnutrition and electrolyte loss
Dehydration signs including dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor
Imaging showing a fistulous connection from the gastric pouch to the transverse colon
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal basic laboratory studies early in the course

data.description: Excessive growth of bacteria in the small intestine, often related to altered anatomy after gastrointestinal surgery. It can cause malabsorption, bloating, foul gas, diarrhea, and nutritional deficiencies.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness and muscle cramps related to malabsorption
Prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, which predisposes to altered intestinal bacterial colonization
symptoms_not_in_common: Feculent eructation
Visible food particles in the stool due to rapid gastric-to-colonic transit
Pale floating stools as a dominant feature
Imaging evidence of a direct gastric pouch-to-colon fistula
Profound cachexia developing over only several months is more suggestive of a high-output fistula

data.description: Insufficient secretion of pancreatic digestive enzymes, resulting in fat malabsorption and steatorrhea. It may cause pale, greasy, floating, foul-smelling stools, weight loss, and nutritional deficiency.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness, myalgias, and muscle cramps related to malnutrition
symptoms_not_in_common: Feculent eructation and feculent breath
Visible undigested food particles in watery diarrhea
Severe postprandial watery diarrhea 6–7 times daily
History of Roux-en-Y bypass is not by itself a typical cause of pancreatic insufficiency
Imaging demonstrating a gastric pouch-to-colon fistula
No reported history of chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic surgery, or pancreatic disease

data.diagnosis: Dumping syndrome after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
data.description: Rapid delivery of hyperosmolar gastric contents into the small bowel after gastric surgery, causing postprandial cramping, diarrhea, bloating, and sometimes vasomotor symptoms. Chronic symptoms can contribute to weight loss.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness that may occur with poor intake or nutritional compromise
symptoms_not_in_common: Feculent eructation
Feculent breath
Visible food particles in stool
Pale floating stools suggesting malabsorption
Severe progressive cachexia and dehydration
Late onset eight years after surgery without typical flushing, palpitations, diaphoresis, or dizziness
Imaging evidence of a gastric pouch-to-colon fistula

data.diagnosis: Clostridioides difficile infection or other infectious enterocolitis
data.description: An infection of the colon that commonly causes frequent watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, dehydration, and systemic illness. C. difficile is especially associated with recent antibiotic exposure or healthcare contact.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness and weight loss during prolonged illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Feculent eructation and feculent breath
Visible undigested food particles in stool
Pale floating stools
Chronic progressive malnutrition and cachexia over four months without reported fever or leukocytosis
No reported antibiotic exposure or healthcare-associated trigger
Imaging showing a direct fistulous tract between the gastric pouch and colon

data.description: A 20-year-old woman with a history of asthma presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath and sharp pains in her chest and neck. The pain worsened on deep inspiration. She had a cough producing small amounts of whitish sputum. She had experienced several previous asthma exacerbations and had not been using her inhalers regularly. On examination, her airway was patent with a generalized moderate wheeze in her chest, but no other obvious clinical signs. She could speak in full sentences and had normal oxygen saturations and temperature. She was mildly tachycardic and appeared slightly anxious. Blood tests showed a mild neutrophilia and elevated C reactive protein.

Air in the mediastinum, often caused by alveolar rupture during coughing or an asthma exacerbation; it can produce chest pain radiating to the neck and may be visible as mediastinal air on chest radiography.
symptoms_in_common: History of asthma with likely increased intrathoracic pressure from coughing/wheezing
Chest radiograph appearance suggestive of mediastinal air
symptoms_not_in_common: Whitish sputum production
Mild neutrophilia
Elevated C-reactive protein

data.description: Acute worsening of reversible lower-airway obstruction causing wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and breathlessness, often precipitated by poor adherence to inhaled treatment or respiratory infection.
symptoms_in_common: Normal oxygen saturation can occur in a mild-to-moderate exacerbation
symptoms_not_in_common: Sharp chest pain worsened by deep inspiration
Neck pain
Radiographic suggestion of mediastinal air

data.diagnosis: Acute bronchitis or viral lower respiratory tract infection
data.description: Inflammation of the bronchi, usually viral, causing cough, sputum production, wheeze, and chest discomfort; it can trigger an asthma exacerbation.
symptoms_in_common: Normal temperature may occur, particularly with viral infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Sharp pleuritic chest pain radiating to the neck
Chest radiograph appearance suggestive of mediastinal air
No fever or systemic infectious symptoms

data.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, commonly presenting with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and sometimes cough or hemoptysis.
symptoms_in_common: Sharp chest pain worsened by deep inspiration
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized wheeze with a history of poorly controlled asthma
Cough producing whitish sputum
Neck pain
Normal oxygen saturations
Chest radiograph appearance suggestive of mediastinal air
No stated thromboembolic risk factors

data.description: Infection of the lung parenchyma that may cause cough, sputum production, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, fever, and raised inflammatory markers.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
Normal oxygen saturation
No focal crackles or focal chest examination findings
Generalized wheeze is more consistent with asthma
No focal consolidation apparent on the chest radiograph
Neck pain and mediastinal air are not typical

data.description: 47-year-old homeless man with 1 month of intermittent bilateral leg pain and pins-and-needles sensation, starting in the toes and gradually spreading to the shins. History includes 33 years of intravenous heroin use (current user), hepatitis C infection, hypertension, heavy smoking, and rare alcohol use; no family history of neuropathy. Exam: afebrile, hypertensive (170/110 mmHg), chronically ill-appearing, with normal cardiac/pulmonary/abdominal/skin findings, normal strength and reflexes, no cranial nerve deficits, but unsteady gait, limited ambulation due to pain, and decreased pinprick, light touch, and temperature sensation in both lower extremities.

A nutritional deficiency disorder causing photosensitive dermatitis, gastrointestinal symptoms, and neurologic manifestations including cognitive changes and peripheral neuropathy. The images are suggestive of photosensitive dermatitis with a Casal necklace pattern on the neck.
symptoms_in_common: Painful bilateral distal leg paresthesias beginning in the toes
Decreased pinprick, light-touch, and temperature sensation
Chronically ill appearance and homelessness suggesting malnutrition risk
Photosensitive/scaly dermatitis of the neck and forearms shown in the images
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported diarrhea
No reported dementia, confusion, or cognitive decline
Normal strength and reflexes

data.description: Pyridoxine deficiency can occur with poor nutrition, substance use, or certain medications and may cause a painful length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy; dermatitis may also occur.
symptoms_in_common: Distal symmetric pins-and-needles sensation in both legs
Burning or painful neuropathic leg symptoms
Sensory loss involving pain and temperature sensation
Gait instability related to sensory dysfunction
Risk of poor nutritional intake related to homelessness and chronic substance use
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent photosensitive neck and forearm dermatitis is not a classic isolated pyridoxine-deficiency finding
No reported oral inflammation, glossitis, or cheilosis
Normal reflexes despite clinically significant sensory symptoms

data.description: Thiamine deficiency can produce painful symmetric peripheral neuropathy, sensory loss, weakness, and gait difficulty, particularly in people with malnutrition or substance-use disorders.
symptoms_in_common: Leg pain with distal sensory loss
High risk of nutritional deficiency due to homelessness and chronic heroin use
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported weakness or muscle wasting
Reflexes are normal, whereas dry beriberi often causes reduced reflexes
Photosensitive dermatitis of the neck and forearms is not typical
Rare alcohol use, whereas thiamine deficiency is often associated with heavy alcohol use

data.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, which may produce painful peripheral neuropathy, purpura, arthralgias, renal disease, and skin lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Pins-and-needles sensation and reduced pinprick/temperature sensation
Possible scattered skin lesions on the forearms
symptoms_not_in_common: The sensory symptoms are symmetric and length-dependent rather than clearly asymmetric or mononeuritic
No palpable purpura, arthralgias, renal symptoms, or systemic vasculitic symptoms reported
Photosensitive scaly neck rash is not typical of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
Normal skin examination in the written examination conflicts with classic vasculitic skin findings

data.description: HIV infection, especially in advanced disease or with certain antiretroviral therapies, can cause a painful distal symmetric sensory polyneuropathy. Intravenous drug use increases HIV exposure risk.
symptoms_in_common: Distal symmetric paresthesias beginning in the toes
Progression of sensory symptoms upward toward the shins
Reduced pain, temperature, and light-touch sensation
Gait impairment due to sensory symptoms
Intravenous drug use as a risk factor for HIV acquisition
symptoms_not_in_common: No known HIV diagnosis or reported immunosuppressive symptoms
No reported weight loss, recurrent infections, fever, or lymphadenopathy
Photosensitive dermatitis with a Casal-necklace-like distribution is not typical of HIV neuropathy
Normal reflexes may be present early but are less typical in more advanced distal polyneuropathy

data.description: 8-month-old male born at term, from a non-consanguineous family, with no relevant family history. He had two prior admissions for bronchitis at 3 and 6 months of age; during one episode, severe neutropenia was noted and resolved without treatment. He presented with respiratory distress, fever, and fatigue. Examination showed no palpable lymph nodes or tonsillar tissue, bilateral lung crackles, and diminished breath sounds. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral infiltrates without pleural effusion. Laboratory tests showed low IgG and IgM, and IgA <10 mg/dL.

data.diagnosis: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agammaglobulinemia) due to BTK mutation
data.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked BTK gene, resulting in arrested B-cell maturation, profoundly reduced or absent mature B cells, and very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes. The displayed BTK c.494G>A (p.Cys165Tyr) variant and absent/reduced BTK expression strongly support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Male infant with onset of recurrent respiratory infections after early infancy
Current pneumonia with fever, respiratory distress, crackles, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates
Transient severe neutropenia can occur during severe bacterial infections in X-linked agammaglobulinemia
symptoms_not_in_common: No major atypical symptoms; the presentation is highly characteristic

data.description: A heterogeneous antibody-deficiency disorder characterized by low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM, impaired antibody responses, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. It usually presents later in childhood or adulthood and typically has circulating B cells.
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation at 8 months of age is unusually early for CVID
Absent tonsils and lymph nodes are more typical of profound B-cell absence than CVID
BTK mutation is not a cause of CVID
Male X-linked pattern and reduced BTK expression favor X-linked agammaglobulinemia

data.description: A group of severe inherited immunodeficiencies with major T-cell dysfunction, often accompanied by B-cell and/or NK-cell abnormalities, causing severe recurrent bacterial, viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections in infancy.
symptoms_in_common: Pneumonia with respiratory distress and bilateral infiltrates
Absent or poorly developed lymphoid tissue may occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported opportunistic, persistent viral, or fungal infections
No chronic diarrhea or failure to thrive is described
No severe persistent lymphopenia is reported
The BTK mutation specifically indicates a B-cell maturation defect rather than SCID
Transient neutropenia is not a defining feature of SCID

data.diagnosis: Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency or related disorder)
data.description: A primary immunodeficiency in which defective immunoglobulin class-switch recombination causes low IgG and IgA with normal or elevated IgM. Patients may have recurrent respiratory and opportunistic infections.
symptoms_in_common: Male infant with recurrent respiratory infections
Neutropenia can occur in some forms of hyper-IgM syndrome
symptoms_not_in_common: IgM is low rather than normal or elevated
Absent tonsils and lymph nodes suggest absent B cells, whereas B-cell numbers are usually normal in hyper-IgM syndrome
No opportunistic infections are reported
BTK mutation and reduced BTK expression support X-linked agammaglobulinemia instead

data.description: A temporary prolongation of the physiologic decline in maternally acquired IgG, causing low IgG and sometimes recurrent respiratory infections in infancy; endogenous immunoglobulin production generally normalizes with time.
symptoms_in_common: Respiratory distress, fever, crackles, and bilateral infiltrates during acute infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Low IgM and profoundly low IgA are less typical
Absent tonsillar tissue and nonpalpable lymph nodes are not typical
Severe recurrent infections are more suggestive of a major primary immunodeficiency
BTK mutation and reduced BTK expression are not compatible with a transient developmental delay in immunoglobulin production
Transient severe neutropenia is not typical

data.description: A 35-year-old patient presented to A&E with complaints of sudden onset pain in scrotum extending to perineum, scrotal swelling, loss of penile erection following sexual intercourse. On examination the patient had scrotal swelling and bruising at the base of the penis and scrotum, but no penile swelling.

data.diagnosis: Penile fracture with rupture of the right corpus cavernosum
data.description: Acute tear of the tunica albuginea surrounding an erect corpus cavernosum, usually during sexual intercourse, causing bleeding and soft-tissue hematoma. The MRI demonstrates a defect in the tunica albuginea near the penile base with adjacent hematoma extending into the scrotum.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden onset pain during or immediately after sexual intercourse
Bruising at the base of the penis and scrotum
Imaging evidence of tunica albuginea defect and corpus cavernosum injury
symptoms_not_in_common: No visible penile swelling

data.diagnosis: Isolated scrotal hematoma secondary to genital trauma
data.description: A collection of blood within scrotal soft tissues after trauma, which may result from direct scrotal injury or blood tracking from a more proximal penile or perineal injury.
symptoms_in_common: Ultrasound and MRI evidence of scrotal soft-tissue hematoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden loss of erection following intercourse
Imaging evidence of a tunica albuginea defect in the corpus cavernosum
No reported direct scrotal impact

data.description: Tear of the superficial or deep dorsal penile vein during intercourse, producing penile or scrotal bruising and hematoma; it can clinically resemble penile fracture but generally lacks a tunica albuginea tear.
symptoms_in_common: Acute genital pain after sexual intercourse
Scrotal swelling due to tracking blood
symptoms_not_in_common: Immediate loss of erection is less typical
MRI evidence of a corpus cavernosum tunica albuginea defect
No penile swelling

data.description: Twisting of the spermatic cord that compromises testicular blood flow and causes an acute scrotum; it is a time-critical urologic emergency.
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset following sexual intercourse
Bruising at the base of the penis and scrotum
Perineal hematoma
Loss of erection
Imaging evidence of a tunica albuginea defect of the corpus cavernosum
No described testicular abnormality

data.description: Inflammation or infection of the epididymis and sometimes the testis, usually producing gradually progressive unilateral scrotal pain, tenderness, and swelling.
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt onset immediately after intercourse
Bruising at the penile base and scrotum
Loss of erection
Perineal soft-tissue hematoma
Imaging evidence of traumatic tunica albuginea rupture
No reported fever, urinary symptoms, or infectious symptoms

data.description: 8-year-5-month-old male with severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. He was born at full term by normal vaginal delivery to consanguineous parents, birth weight 2.5 kg. He never achieved head control or independent sitting, learned to roll at age 5, and cannot speak or communicate. Physical examination showed myopathic facies, high-arched palate, nystagmus, generalized muscle weakness, marked hypotonia, absent deep tendon reflexes, contractures of both knees and ankles, and positive right Babinski sign with possible left Babinski sign. Serum CK was 1514 U/L.

An autosomal-recessive congenital muscular dystrophy caused by abnormal alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation, characterized by severe developmental delay, hypotonia, elevated CK, eye abnormalities, and structural brain malformations.
symptoms_in_common: Severe global developmental delay and profound intellectual disability
No head control or independent sitting
Generalized muscle weakness and marked hypotonia
Brain MRI abnormalities including ventriculomegaly/hydrocephalus and cortical/white-matter abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive Babinski signs may indicate prominent upper motor neuron involvement, which is less typical than the peripheral hypotonia and areflexia

data.description: A severe congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy with congenital brain malformations, eye abnormalities, profound developmental impairment, hypotonia, and elevated muscle enzymes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Survival to 8 years is less typical because classic Walker-Warburg syndrome often causes death in infancy or early childhood
No clearly described severe congenital eye malformation such as microphthalmia, retinal detachment, or cataract
No reported seizures

data.description: An alpha-dystroglycan-related congenital muscular dystrophy causing early hypotonia, weakness, intellectual disability, elevated CK, contractures, and brain developmental abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Early and severe motor developmental impairment
Contractures of the knees and ankles
Structural brain abnormalities and ventriculomegaly on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Nystagmus and major ocular involvement are less prominent than in muscle-eye-brain disease or Walker-Warburg syndrome
The very profound absence of head control and communication is more severe than many typical Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy presentations
Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy is most common in Japanese populations, although it can occur elsewhere

data.description: A dystroglycanopathy due to FKRP variants that can cause congenital muscular dystrophy with weakness, high CK, contractures, and, in severe cases, brain and eye involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound intellectual disability and absent communication are not typical in many FKRP-related muscular dystrophy cases
Nystagmus is not a usual prominent feature
Major structural brain abnormalities with marked ventriculomegaly are uncommon except in the most severe dystroglycanopathy spectrum
Positive Babinski signs are not typical of a predominantly muscular dystrophy

data.diagnosis: LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystrophy (merosin-deficient congenital muscular dystrophy)
data.description: An autosomal-recessive congenital muscular dystrophy characterized by severe neonatal or infantile hypotonia, profound weakness, absent reflexes, contractures, elevated CK, and characteristic diffuse cerebral white-matter abnormalities.
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound intellectual disability and complete absence of communication are less typical, as cognition is often relatively preserved
Nystagmus is not a classic feature

data.description: 15-year-old girl with 6 weeks of lower abdominal pain, initially midline, sharp/crampy, worse with movement and relieved by lying down, shifting to the right within 24 hours. Initial exam showed mild bilateral lower abdominal tenderness, greater on the right, with a soft nondistended abdomen and no rebound or guarding; labs showed leukocytosis, anemia, and mildly elevated CRP. She was discharged with presumed ruptured ovarian cyst. Six weeks later, she returned with recurrent similar pain and inability to attend school, plus increased waist size over 2 weeks and difficulty fitting into pants. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, and vaginal bleeding/discharge. She had no significant past medical history, no medications, no allergies, normal growth and development, and had not yet had menarche. Exam then showed a firm, distended right lower abdomen with mild tenderness and Tanner stage 4 pubertal development. Labs showed worsening leukocytosis, anemia, and markedly elevated CRP.

An aggressive high-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can rarely present as a rapidly enlarging ovarian or pelvic mass in children and adolescents. Histology often shows a 'starry-sky' pattern due to numerous macrophages among rapidly proliferating tumor cells.

Absence of vaginal bleeding or discharge

data.description: 32-month-old Korean boy presented with irritability and fever. Born at 40 weeks gestation with 2.9kg birth weight via normal vaginal delivery to a healthy 28-year-old G3P2 mother. Had flexion deformity of both middle fingers at birth. Showed mild general hypotonia in early infancy with weak cry and poor sucking. History of epileptic seizures 6 times since age 15 months. Developmental delay: raised head at 7 months, sat at 26 months, not yet standing. Physical exam showed prognathism, low-set ears, small crashed nose, widely spaced incisors, round back. Demonstrated repeated stereotyped behavior like hitting chin with palm. Neurologic exam showed decreased muscle tone (grade IV/IV bilaterally) but normal deep tendon reflexes, no spasticity or pathologic reflexes, normal sensory function, and no meningeal signs.

data.diagnosis: Alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual disability syndrome (ATR-X syndrome)

Marked motor delay, including inability to stand at 32 months

Congenital flexion deformities of the fingers
Blood-smear findings compatible with hemoglobin H inclusions

Facial features that can include a wide mouth and widely spaced teeth

data.description: A previously healthy 58-year-old male presented with two weeks of lumbar pain and fever, accompanied by asthenia, anorexia, and recent weight loss of 3kg. He was a non-smoker with no drug abuse, recent travel, or animal contact history. On examination, he had a fever of 39.3°C with hemodynamic stability, bilateral painless swollen legs, and respiratory crackles on the right side. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 116 g/l, leukocyte count 33.3*109 cells/l, C-reactive protein 114.6mg/l, creatinine 56 μmol/l, elevated liver enzymes (AST 174 U/l, ALT 209 U/l, ALP 406 U/l, GGT 517 U/l), total bilirubin 76 μmol/l, conjugated bilirubin 66 μmol/l, and INR 1.38. Serology for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Urinary sediment was unremarkable.

data.description: A 67-year-old man with advanced alcoholic cirrhosis presented with progressive dyspnea. Physical examination after thoracentesis revealed right lung crackles, and the patient developed coughing, tachypnea, and tachycardia. His oxygen saturation was 82% while breathing ambient air.

data.description: 52-year-old woman with exertional right buttock and thigh pain that resolves within 2 minutes of rest. Exercise tolerance worsened over past year, now limited to several blocks. Previously able to run 5-6 miles per day. Recently diagnosed hypertension controlled with lisinopril (5 mg daily). No other cardiovascular risk factors. Physical exam shows blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg bilaterally, high-pitched systolic bruit over right subcostal region and umbilicus, normal peripheral pulses. Ankle brachial index (ABI) at rest borderline normal (0.91) on right and normal (1.03) on left. Remainder of examination normal.

data.description: A 66-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with episodes of palpitations, dizziness, and near fainting that had lasted for a few hours. Her medical history included removal of a left atrial myxoma 15 years ago, after which she experienced recurrent atrial tachycardia managed with modified release verapamil 240 mg once daily. She had recently started sotalol 120 mg twice daily in addition to verapamil and underwent direct current cardioversion for persistent atrial tachycardia one week prior to presentation. Initial workup showed normal urea and electrolytes including magnesium. An echocardiogram revealed normal left ventricular systolic function with no recurrence of left atrial myxoma.

data.diagnosis: Torsades de pointes (drug-induced polymorphic ventricular tachycardia)

Normal magnesium and other electrolytes, supporting a drug-related rather than electrolyte-related cause
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior left atrial myxoma
Persistent atrial tachycardia requiring cardioversion

data.description: 18-year-old pregnant woman. Healthy with no history of smoking, drug abuse, or family history of chromosomal disease or encephalodysplasia. Experienced mild flu-like symptoms during first month of pregnancy that resolved after three days without medication.
