data.description: A male full-term neonate was admitted to the hospital 4 hours after birth for ecchymosis and petechiae. The infant was delivered by cesarean section at 40+5 weeks gestation due to failed induction, with birth weight 4000g and Apgar scores of 10. Physical examination revealed stable vital signs, weight 3850g, length 52cm, head circumference 35cm. The infant was alert and responsive with no special facial features. Skin examination showed large areas of ecchymosis on the chest, back, and upper limbs, with ecchymosis at the hepatitis B vaccine and vitamin K1 injection sites, and scattered pinpoint hemorrhages on the buttocks and lower limbs. The umbilical cord ligation site showed no bleeding, and cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurological examinations were normal.
Maternal antibodies against fetal platelet antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal platelets, causing severe thrombocytopenia with petechiae, purpura, and bleeding shortly after birth.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae present within hours of birth
Extensive ecchymoses on the chest, back, and upper limbs
Bleeding/bruising at hepatitis B vaccine and vitamin K injection sites
Otherwise well-appearing full-term neonate with normal vital signs and normal physical examination
symptoms_not_in_common: No umbilical cord bleeding
No reported intracranial hemorrhage or other major internal bleeding

data.description: A rare inherited bone-marrow failure disorder, often caused by MPL gene variants, characterized by severe thrombocytopenia beginning at birth due to markedly reduced or absent megakaryocytes; it may later progress to pancytopenia.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and widespread ecchymosis in the neonatal period
Normal appearance and stable condition at birth
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported anemia, neutropenia, or other cytopenias
No reported recurrent infections or later bone-marrow failure findings

data.description: An inherited platelet adhesion disorder caused by defects of the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex. It produces thrombocytopenia with giant platelets and mucocutaneous bleeding manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Excessive bruising or bleeding after injections
Bleeding manifestations apparent early in life
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported mucosal bleeding such as epistaxis or oral bleeding
No reported giant platelets or thrombocytopenia on laboratory testing
No known family history of a platelet bleeding disorder

data.description: An X-linked disorder in boys characterized by thrombocytopenia, classically with small platelets, eczema, immunodeficiency, and bleeding that can begin in infancy or the neonatal period.
symptoms_not_in_common: No eczema
No recurrent or severe infections
No reported small platelets or immune dysfunction
No gastrointestinal bleeding

data.description: X-linked deficiencies of coagulation factor VIII or IX that cause impaired clot formation and bleeding, especially after trauma, procedures, or injections; affected newborn boys may have bruising after delivery.
symptoms_in_common: Bruising or bleeding at intramuscular injection sites
Possible bleeding after birth-related trauma or procedures
symptoms_not_in_common: Petechiae are not typical of hemophilia and more strongly suggest thrombocytopenia
Scattered pinpoint hemorrhages are atypical
No prolonged bleeding from the umbilical cord or other deep-tissue bleeding has been reported

data.description: 50-year-old man presented with 2-week history of constant worsening headache affecting the whole head. No history of head trauma, but reported headbanging at a Motörhead concert 4 weeks prior to presentation. Medical history was unremarkable and patient denied substance misuse. Neurological examination and laboratory studies, including coagulation screening, were normal.
A slowly accumulating collection of old blood beneath the dura, often occurring weeks after minor or repetitive head trauma and commonly presenting with progressive headache.
symptoms_in_common: Progressively worsening constant headache for 2 weeks
Recent repetitive head movement/headbanging that could cause minor bridging-vein injury
Delayed presentation several weeks after the potential traumatic event
Normal neurological examination can occur in chronic subdural hematoma
symptoms_not_in_common: No focal neurological deficits
No reported confusion, drowsiness, gait disturbance, or seizures

data.description: A chronic subdural blood collection with more recent rebleeding, which can cause worsening headache and imaging with mixed-density subdural collections.
symptoms_in_common: History of repetitive minor head trauma from headbanging
Symptoms beginning weeks after the inciting activity
Normal coagulation studies do not exclude traumatic subdural bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: No acute loss of consciousness
No vomiting, seizure, focal weakness, or declining level of consciousness

data.description: A collection of cerebrospinal fluid in the subdural space, often following minor trauma; it may produce headache and can resemble a chronic subdural hematoma on CT.
symptoms_in_common: Possible preceding minor repetitive head trauma
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressively worsening severe headache is more suggestive of a hematoma with mass effect
No reported symptoms of raised intracranial pressure such as vomiting or reduced consciousness

data.description: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space after trauma, typically causing sudden severe headache and sometimes neurological symptoms depending on the amount and location of bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Potential traumatic mechanism from vigorous headbanging
symptoms_not_in_common: Headache was gradual and progressive rather than sudden thunderclap onset
No neck stiffness
No vomiting
No loss of consciousness
No focal neurological deficits

data.description: Thrombosis of intracranial venous sinuses that can cause persistent progressive headache, intracranial hypertension, venous infarction, or hemorrhage.
symptoms_in_common: Normal initial neurological examination can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent headbanging provides a more direct traumatic explanation for a subdural collection
No seizures
No focal neurological deficits
No visual disturbance or papilledema reported
No known prothrombotic risk factors reported

data.description: A 35-year-old woman presented to the emergency room with a clinically incarcerated umbilical hernia. Fourteen days after the initial hernia repair surgery, she developed strong pain in the right lower abdomen and complained of umbilical secretion. Physical examination revealed the patient was afebrile. Blood analysis showed a slight elevation in leukocyte count at 11.05 × 10^9/L, while other parameters were unexceptional. Ultrasound of the abdominal wall detected a semisolid infraumbilical mass with a diameter of 5.5 cm. Initial histologic examination of the resected omental fat from the hernia repair revealed malignant cells with neuroendocrine differentiation. Immunohistochemical analysis was positive for synaptophysin and protein gene product 9.5. Fluorescent in situ hybridization revealed a rearrangement of the EWSR1 gene.

data.diagnosis: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor (pPNET)
data.description: A malignant small round-cell sarcoma arising in soft tissue rather than bone. It commonly shows neuroectodermal differentiation and an EWSR1 gene rearrangement, most often involving an EWSR1-FLI1 fusion.
symptoms_in_common: Painful right lower abdominal/abdominal wall mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Umbilical secretion
Presentation shortly after umbilical hernia repair
Mild leukocytosis

data.description: An aggressive small round-cell sarcoma that typically arises in the abdominal or pelvic peritoneum of young people. It is usually driven by an EWSR1-WT1 fusion and often presents as an intra-abdominal mass or peritoneal disease.
symptoms_in_common: Malignant small round-cell-type tumor with an EWSR1 rearrangement
symptoms_not_in_common: Female sex is less typical because the disease has a strong male predominance
Isolated small abdominal-wall lesion rather than widespread peritoneal masses
Synaptophysin and protein gene product 9.5 positivity are not the classic immunophenotype
Umbilical secretion
Presentation as an incarcerated umbilical hernia

data.diagnosis: Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue
data.description: A rare malignant soft-tissue tumor, sometimes called melanoma of soft parts, often associated with EWSR1-ATF1 or EWSR1-CREB1 rearrangements. It usually occurs in tendons or aponeuroses of the extremities and commonly expresses melanocytic markers.
symptoms_not_in_common: Abdominal wall or omental location is unusual
Neuroendocrine-marker positivity is not typical
No reported melanocytic-marker positivity
Umbilical secretion
Acute postoperative presentation

data.diagnosis: EWSR1-rearranged myoepithelial carcinoma of soft tissue
data.description: A malignant myoepithelial neoplasm that can arise in soft tissue, including the trunk and abdominal wall. A subset has EWSR1 rearrangements, but tumors generally show epithelial and myoepithelial marker expression rather than a purely neuroendocrine phenotype.
symptoms_in_common: Possible occurrence in a young or middle-aged adult
symptoms_not_in_common: Synaptophysin and protein gene product 9.5 positivity without reported cytokeratin, EMA, S100, or myoepithelial-marker expression
Marked neuroendocrine differentiation is not typical
Umbilical secretion
Presentation as an incarcerated hernia

data.diagnosis: Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma metastatic to the abdominal wall or omentum
data.description: A high-grade epithelial malignancy with neuroendocrine differentiation that can involve the peritoneum, omentum, or abdominal wall, usually as metastasis from a gastrointestinal, pancreatic, pulmonary, or gynecologic primary tumor.
symptoms_not_in_common: EWSR1 gene rearrangement is not typical
Age 35 is younger than typical for most high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas
No known visceral primary tumor or metastatic disease is described
Umbilical secretion
Presentation as an incarcerated umbilical hernia

data.description: 60-year-old Japanese woman presented with a black nodule on the right postauricular area. Initial staging after radical resection and sentinel node biopsy was pT3aN0M0 stage IIA. At 19 months post-surgery, imaging detected right jugular lymph node and lung metastases. Seven courses of pembrolizumab treatment later, evaluation showed further lung metastasis and new liver metastasis. Tumor harbored BRAF V600E mutation. Thirteen days after starting dabrafenib/trametinib, patient developed fever and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, increased liver enzyme levels, and coagulation abnormalities.

A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T lymphocytes, often associated with malignancy, infection, or medications. It commonly causes fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and markedly elevated ferritin.
symptoms_not_in_common: Rapid onset 13 days after dabrafenib/trametinib specifically suggests a drug trigger rather than idiopathic HLH
Progressive lung and liver metastases are not direct manifestations of HLH

data.description: Drug-induced HLH is a severe immune-mediated adverse reaction in which a medication triggers excessive macrophage activation and systemic inflammation. BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy can rarely precipitate this syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Symptoms began 13 days after starting dabrafenib/trametinib
symptoms_not_in_common: Pre-existing pulmonary and hepatic metastatic lesions are due to melanoma progression rather than the drug reaction
No medication-specific atypical symptoms are described

data.description: HLH can occur as a rare immune-related adverse event after immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment, including pembrolizumab. It may develop during therapy or, less commonly, after treatment has been discontinued, and can be difficult to distinguish from malignancy- or drug-triggered HLH.
symptoms_not_in_common: The close temporal relationship to initiation of dabrafenib/trametinib is more suggestive of targeted-therapy-induced HLH
No symptoms are reported as beginning during pembrolizumab treatment
Progressive metastatic disease is not itself a typical immune-related adverse event

data.diagnosis: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome
data.description: DRESS is a severe delayed drug hypersensitivity reaction characterized by fever, widespread rash, internal-organ involvement, and hematologic abnormalities. Liver involvement is common, although eosinophilia and lymphadenopathy are often expected.
symptoms_in_common: Recent introduction of a new systemic medication
symptoms_not_in_common: Pancytopenia is less typical than eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis
Marked hyperferritinemia strongly favors HLH
Coagulation abnormalities are more suggestive of severe systemic inflammation, liver failure, or HLH
No eosinophilia, facial edema, or lymphadenopathy is reported

data.description: Severe infection can produce systemic inflammation, fever, thrombocytopenia, liver injury, and coagulation abnormalities. Sepsis may also trigger secondary HLH, particularly in patients with advanced cancer or immunomodulatory treatment exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced metastatic cancer, which increases infection risk
symptoms_not_in_common: Hepatosplenomegaly is less typical of uncomplicated acute sepsis
Marked hyperferritinemia is more characteristic of HLH
No infectious source, positive culture, hypotension, or shock is reported
The onset shortly after dabrafenib/trametinib favors a treatment-related inflammatory syndrome

data.description: 14-year-old boy presented to trauma unit with gunshot wound to left eye. Alert and hemodynamically stable, blind in left eye, no CSF rhinorrhea. Pubertal status: Tanner stage S3, height: 1.7m (75th percentile). Laboratory findings: 8am serum cortisol 28 nmol/L (normal 171-536), thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.63 mIU/L (normal 0.27-4.20), free thyroxine 13.5 pmol/L (normal 13.6-23.2), luteinising hormone 0.7 IU/L (normal 1.3-9.8), insulin-like growth factor 1 19.4 nmol/L (normal 28.8-127.3), prolactin 13.04 pmol/L (normal 174-660.9), testosterone undetectable <0.1 nmol/L (normal 1-38.5).

data.diagnosis: Traumatic panhypopituitarism from sellar/pituitary stalk injury
data.description: Deficiency of multiple anterior pituitary hormones caused by penetrating craniofacial trauma, likely involving the sella turcica or pituitary stalk; the retained bullet is located near the sellar region.
symptoms_in_common: Low free thyroxine with inappropriately non-elevated TSH
Delayed or incomplete pubertal progression relative to age
Penetrating head/orbital trauma with retained projectile near the pituitary region
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute blindness of the left eye
Gunshot wound directly involving the left eye
Hemodynamic stability at presentation
Absence of CSF rhinorrhea

data.description: Inadequate ACTH stimulation of the adrenal glands due to pituitary or hypothalamic damage, resulting in deficient cortisol production.
symptoms_in_common: Other evidence of pituitary hormone deficiencies
symptoms_not_in_common: Left-eye blindness
Low free thyroxine
Low luteinising hormone and undetectable testosterone
Low insulin-like growth factor 1
Low prolactin
No reported hypotension, vomiting, hypoglycemia, fatigue, or hyperpigmentation

data.description: Hypothyroidism caused by insufficient pituitary TSH secretion or hypothalamic TRH stimulation, rather than primary thyroid gland disease.
symptoms_in_common: TSH that is inappropriately low-normal rather than elevated
Associated deficiencies of other pituitary hormones
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute unilateral blindness from eye trauma
Very low morning cortisol
Undetectable testosterone
Low insulin-like growth factor 1
No reported cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, bradycardia, or dry skin

data.diagnosis: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to pituitary injury
data.description: Failure of hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotropin production causing low LH and testosterone and impaired pubertal development.
symptoms_in_common: Tanner stage S3 at age 14, compatible with delayed or interrupted pubertal progression
Low insulin-like growth factor 1 suggesting broader pituitary dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute left-eye blindness
Very low morning cortisol
Low free thyroxine
Low prolactin
No reported reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia, or infertility

data.diagnosis: Growth hormone deficiency secondary to traumatic hypopituitarism
data.description: Reduced growth hormone secretion from pituitary injury, often reflected by low IGF-1 and potentially accompanied by other anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.
symptoms_in_common: Penetrating trauma near the pituitary region
Pubertal development that may be impaired by combined pituitary hormone deficiency
symptoms_not_in_common: Height at the 75th percentile rather than short stature
Acute blindness of the left eye
Very low morning cortisol
Low free thyroxine
Undetectable testosterone
No reported poor growth velocity, increased body fat, or recurrent hypoglycemia

data.description: 14-month-old girl with a 3-month history of recurrent episodic vomiting beginning at 11 months of age, with four episodes lasting 3–5 days and associated lethargy, decreased oral intake, and intermittent diarrhea. Over the same period, she had developmental regression, stopping attempts to walk and crawling unsteadily with occasional falls. Parents reported brief morning episodes of symmetric shaking movements without loss of consciousness. On examination, she was alert and interactive but had frontal bossing, a full fontanelle with visible pulsations when supine, head circumference 51.5 cm, decreased tone in the legs, brisk 3+ patellar reflexes, and flexor plantar responses. Eye movements were normal, with reactive pupils and no nystagmus or gaze limitation. Born full-term without complications.

data.diagnosis: Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus
data.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct blocks cerebrospinal-fluid flow from the third to fourth ventricle, producing triventricular hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Imaging is consistent with marked enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles with obstruction at the aqueduct.
symptoms_in_common: Loss of walking attempts and unsteady crawling
Brief abnormal shaking episodes that may reflect increased intracranial pressure or seizures
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent diarrhea
Normal eye movements without gaze limitation or nystagmus

data.diagnosis: Tectal plate glioma with aqueductal obstruction
data.description: A low-grade tumor of the tectal region can compress the cerebral aqueduct and cause slowly progressive obstructive hydrocephalus. Such lesions often present primarily with symptoms of raised intracranial pressure rather than focal neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Macrocephaly with rapidly increasing head circumference
Ventricular enlargement consistent with obstructive hydrocephalus
symptoms_not_in_common: No vertical gaze palsy or other eye-movement abnormality
No nystagmus
Intermittent diarrhea
No persistent focal cranial-nerve deficit

data.diagnosis: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to an aqueductal web or membranous aqueductal obstruction
data.description: A thin congenital membrane or web within the cerebral aqueduct may cause partial obstruction that becomes clinically apparent during infancy as cerebrospinal-fluid production exceeds drainage capacity.
symptoms_in_common: Marked lateral and third ventricular enlargement on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent diarrhea
Brief symmetric shaking without loss of consciousness
No sunsetting eyes or impaired upward gaze

data.description: Prior meningitis or ventriculitis can produce scarring of the aqueduct or other cerebrospinal-fluid pathways, resulting in progressive hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure.
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of neonatal infection, meningitis, or febrile neurologic illness
Born full-term without complications
Intermittent diarrhea without systemic infectious features
No fever or neck stiffness described

data.description: Dandy-Walker spectrum disorders are congenital posterior-fossa developmental abnormalities that can impair cerebrospinal-fluid circulation and cause hydrocephalus, macrocephaly, vomiting, and developmental delay.
symptoms_in_common: Delayed gross motor development and unsteady crawling
symptoms_not_in_common: Imaging pattern is more suggestive of aqueductal obstruction than a posterior-fossa cystic malformation
No described enlarged posterior fossa or cerebellar vermis abnormality
Brisk reflexes are less characteristic than truncal hypotonia and ataxia
Intermittent diarrhea

diagnoses.name: Aqueductal stenosis
diagnoses.title: Stenosis of the aqueduct of Sylvius

data.description: 31-year-old man with sleep apnea and a 20 pack-year smoking history, referred for newly diagnosed hypertension. Blood pressure remained persistently elevated at 170/128 mm Hg, 164/110 mm Hg, and 173/110 mm Hg. He reported 6 months of lethargy and intermittent headaches. On examination, heart rate was 106 bpm and BMI 34; no cushingoid features, hyperpigmentation, renal or carotid bruits, or fine tremors were present. Full blood count, urea, and electrolytes were normal, and renal artery Doppler showed no renal artery stenosis.
Chronic high blood pressure without a single identifiable secondary cause; it is common in people with obesity, smoking exposure, and family or lifestyle risk factors.
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age at presentation (31 years), which warrants evaluation for secondary causes
Tachycardia (heart rate 106 bpm)

data.description: Obstructive sleep apnea causes recurrent nighttime airway obstruction, intermittent low oxygen levels, and sympathetic activation, contributing to resistant or severe hypertension.
symptoms_not_in_common: Tachycardia is not a defining feature
No reported snoring, witnessed apneas, or daytime sleepiness in the current history

data.description: A catecholamine-secreting tumor, usually arising from the adrenal glands, that can cause severe or episodic hypertension with headaches, palpitations, sweating, and tachycardia.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported episodic palpitations
No excessive sweating
Blood pressure appears persistently elevated rather than clearly episodic
No tremor

data.description: Excess aldosterone production, commonly from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, causing hypertension and often low potassium levels.
symptoms_in_common: Headaches may occur due to hypertension
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal electrolytes, with no documented hypokalemia
No muscle weakness, cramps, or excessive urination reported
Tachycardia is not typical

data.description: A disorder of excess cortisol production that may cause hypertension, weight gain, glucose intolerance, muscle weakness, mood changes, and characteristic physical features.
symptoms_not_in_common: No cushingoid features on examination
No reported proximal muscle weakness
No easy bruising, purple striae, diabetes symptoms, or mood changes
Tachycardia is not a typical primary feature

data.description: 46-year-old woman who experienced chest pain before having an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Pre-arrest rhythm strip showed sinus tachycardia. Initial troponin I was 5.9 μg/L (normal: 0-0.04 μg/L). Medical history included similar chest pain episode one year prior after taking sumatriptan for migraine, with transient inferior and lateral ST elevation on ECG but negative troponin at that time. Previous coronary angiography showed normal left coronary system and dominant right coronary artery with minor ostial spasm and slow flow. Negative bubble study for right to left shunting. Current medications: oral diltiazem, nicorandil, lansoprazole, and beclometasone inhaler. Patient was a former smoker.

data.diagnosis: Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic/Prinzmetal angina) causing acute myocardial infarction
data.description: Transient intense constriction of an epicardial coronary artery can cause severe ischemia, ST-segment elevation, myocardial infarction, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias despite otherwise normal coronary arteries.
symptoms_in_common: Transient ST-segment elevation during the prior chest-pain episode
Previously documented minor right coronary ostial spasm
Previously normal or near-normal coronary angiography
Current ECG with marked anterior ST-segment elevation consistent with acute transmural ischemia
Former smoking history, a risk factor for coronary vasospasm
symptoms_not_in_common: Sinus tachycardia before arrest is nonspecific rather than characteristic
The current episode is not explicitly reported as occurring at rest or nocturnally, which is common in vasospastic angina

data.description: Triptans can cause coronary vasoconstriction through serotonin receptor activity and may rarely trigger coronary spasm, ST-elevation myocardial infarction, ventricular arrhythmia, or cardiac arrest.
symptoms_in_common: Previous chest pain occurred after taking sumatriptan
Previous transient inferior and lateral ST-segment elevation after sumatriptan exposure
Previous angiography showed no significant obstructive coronary disease
Evidence of coronary spasm on prior angiography
Current chest pain, marked troponin elevation, and ST-segment elevation are compatible with ischemic injury from spasm
symptoms_not_in_common: No sumatriptan use immediately before the current cardiac arrest is reported
The current ECG changes are predominantly anterior rather than the prior inferior and lateral distribution
Cardiac arrest is a rare complication of triptan-associated vasospasm

data.diagnosis: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (anterior STEMI)
data.description: An anterior STEMI is acute myocardial necrosis from severe reduction or interruption of blood flow in the left anterior descending coronary artery territory; it may result from thrombosis, spasm, embolism, or dissection.
symptoms_in_common: Marked ST-segment elevation in the anterior precordial leads, especially V1 through V4
Troponin I of 5.9 μg/L, indicating myocardial injury
Cardiac arrest, a possible complication of acute STEMI
Sinus tachycardia, which can occur during acute myocardial ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior coronary angiography did not show obstructive coronary artery disease
The prior episode had transient ST elevation with negative troponin, favoring episodic spasm rather than fixed coronary obstruction
Age 46 and female sex are less typical for plaque-rupture STEMI, although STEMI remains possible

data.diagnosis: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
data.description: MINOCA refers to myocardial infarction occurring without obstructive coronary artery disease on angiography. Potential causes include coronary vasospasm, plaque erosion, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, coronary embolism, and microvascular dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Previous angiography showing normal left coronary arteries and only minor right coronary abnormalities
Female sex and relatively young age
Potential vasospasm as an underlying mechanism
symptoms_not_in_common: MINOCA cannot be confirmed without coronary imaging during or after the current infarction
Cardiac arrest is possible but is not present in most MINOCA cases
The ECG pattern suggests a localized anterior ischemic territory, whereas MINOCA has multiple possible mechanisms

data.description: SCAD is a nontraumatic tear or intramural hematoma within a coronary artery that causes acute coronary obstruction. It is an important cause of myocardial infarction in younger and middle-aged women with few traditional atherosclerotic risk factors.
symptoms_in_common: Anterior ST-segment elevation consistent with acute coronary ischemia
Cardiac arrest can occur as a complication of SCAD
Limited traditional atherosclerotic risk factors apart from former smoking
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior transient ST elevation after sumatriptan and observed coronary spasm more strongly support vasospasm
Previous angiography did not describe coronary dissection
Recurrent brief episodes with normal troponin are less typical of SCAD than of episodic coronary vasospasm

data.description: A 44-year-old woman with cerebral palsy and multiple sclerosis (diagnosed at age 16) presented to the emergency department with four days of acute constipation and vomiting. She had a history of chronic constipation due to neurogenic bowel dysfunction secondary to her underlying conditions, initially managed with laxatives. Her constipation had become severe enough to warrant insertion of a sacral anterior root stimulator in the last year. On examination, her abdomen was markedly distended, diffusely tender, with absent bowel sounds. There was no guarding, rigidity, or previous incisions, and all hernia orifices were intact. Vital signs showed tachycardia (140 beats/min), tachypnea, normal blood pressure (130/60 mmHg), and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Laboratory findings revealed normal pH of 7.36, hypocapnea (PCO2 29mmHg), hyperlactataemia (20 mg/dL), normal PO2 (), white blood cell count of 10,500 cells/mm3 (73% neutrophils), and elevated C-reactive protein of 3.25 mg/dL.

Functional obstruction of the colon causing marked colonic dilatation without a mechanical blockage, often occurring in patients with neurologic disease, severe illness, or impaired autonomic bowel control.
symptoms_in_common: Neurogenic bowel dysfunction from cerebral palsy and multiple sclerosis
Dilated bowel with multiple air-fluid levels on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Hyperlactataemia suggesting possible bowel ischemia
Imaging evidence concerning for pneumatosis or free intraperitoneal air
Elevated inflammatory markers

data.diagnosis: Stercoral colitis with impending or actual colonic perforation
data.description: Inflammation, pressure necrosis, ischemia, and possible perforation of the colon caused by severe fecal impaction, usually in patients with chronic constipation or neurologic impairment.
symptoms_in_common: Long history of severe chronic constipation
Fecal loading visible on CT imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No guarding or rigidity despite concern for perforation
Only mild leukocytosis
Normal blood pressure despite possible advanced intra-abdominal complication

data.diagnosis: Acute megacolon due to severe neurogenic constipation
data.description: Massive dilation of the colon resulting from longstanding impaired colonic motility and fecal evacuation, which can occur in multiple sclerosis, cerebral palsy, and other neurologic disorders.
symptoms_in_common: Recent need for sacral anterior root stimulation
Markedly dilated colon on radiographs and CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Hyperlactataemia
Elevated C-reactive protein
Possible free intraperitoneal air or bowel-wall gas on CT
Acute tachycardia of 140 beats/min

data.description: Mechanical obstruction of the distal colon caused by a large mass of impacted stool, producing proximal colonic dilatation, pain, vomiting, and risk of ischemia or perforation.
symptoms_in_common: Fecal material in the distal colon on CT
Proximal bowel dilatation and air-fluid levels
symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable rectal fecal mass is described
Possible pneumatosis and free air suggest a more advanced ischemic or perforated complication
No previous abdominal surgery or hernia to explain obstruction

data.diagnosis: Ischemic colitis with colonic pneumatosis and perforation secondary to massive distension
data.description: Compromised blood flow to an overdistended colon can cause bowel-wall ischemia, pneumatosis intestinalis, necrosis, and perforation, particularly when severe constipation or pseudo-obstruction produces high intraluminal pressure.
symptoms_in_common: Possible free intraperitoneal air on CT
Underlying severe constipation and neurogenic bowel dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: No guarding or rigidity
Normal pH
Normal blood pressure
Only mild leukocytosis
No reported bloody diarrhea or rectal bleeding

data.description: 64-year-old man with 5 months of cough with thin yellow sputum, exertional dyspnea, chest tightness, and wheezing, followed 10 days before presentation by lethargy, myalgias, chills, headaches, anorexia, and night sweats. At presentation he had dyspnea, wheezing, cough, headaches, neck stiffness, and photophobia. He was febrile and tachycardic, appeared mildly ill, and had inspiratory crackles bilaterally, neck stiffness, and mild synovial thickening in the hands consistent with chronic arthritic changes. Past history included fibromyalgia, L5 radiculopathy with foot drop, carpal tunnel syndrome, knee and neck osteoarthritis, cervical spondylosis, sleep apnea, and peptic ulcer disease. He worked in a healthcare facility and had recent travel to Florida and Europe/Caribbean.

data.diagnosis: Disseminated cryptococcosis with pulmonary cryptococcosis and cryptococcal meningitis
data.description: Infection with Cryptococcus species that can cause subacute pulmonary disease and spread to the central nervous system, producing meningitis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals but occasionally in apparently immunocompetent hosts.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral pulmonary nodular or infiltrative CT abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent wheezing
Thin yellow sputum production
Chest tightness

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause chronic pulmonary symptoms with constitutional features and, when disseminated, meningeal inflammation causing headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse small pulmonary nodules or infiltrates on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Wheezing
Chest tightness
Acute tachycardia as a prominent feature

data.diagnosis: Disseminated histoplasmosis with central nervous system involvement
data.description: Histoplasma capsulatum is an endemic fungal infection acquired by inhalation; it may cause pulmonary nodules or diffuse infiltrates and can rarely disseminate to the meninges.
symptoms_in_common: Pulmonary nodular or diffuse infiltrative abnormalities
Possible meningitis symptoms including neck stiffness and photophobia
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent wheezing
Chest tightness
Thin yellow sputum

data.description: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes an opportunistic pneumonia characterized by subacute cough, progressive hypoxemic dyspnea, fever, and diffuse bilateral ground-glass or interstitial lung abnormalities; fluorescent respiratory staining can identify the organism.
symptoms_in_common: Constitutional symptoms including lethargy and anorexia
symptoms_not_in_common: Thin yellow sputum production
Neck stiffness
Photophobia
Severe headache
Night sweats
Prominent wheezing

data.diagnosis: Legionnaires' disease due to Legionella pneumonia with neurologic involvement
data.description: Legionella infection produces an atypical pneumonia with fever, cough, dyspnea, myalgias, headache, and sometimes altered mental status or meningeal symptoms; exposure can occur during travel or through water systems.
symptoms_not_in_common: Five months of preceding respiratory symptoms
Neck stiffness
Photophobia
Night sweats
Prominent wheezing
Thin yellow sputum

data.description: 47-year-old woman admitted with left lumbar pain and macroscopic hematuria. Past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, she had pale skin, no peripheral edema, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, and diuresis of 1000 mL/day. Laboratory tests showed moderate normocytic anemia. Autoimmune serologies, antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-GBM antibodies, cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor, hepatitis B/C, HIV, and serum protein electrophoresis were all negative.

A microvascular occlusive disorder causing endothelial injury, arteriolar/arterial intimal thickening, glomerular ischemia, and thrombosis; it may occur without the full systemic hemolytic uremic syndrome picture.
symptoms_in_common: Renal biopsy appearance consistent with vascular endothelial injury and chronic thrombotic microangiopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal blood pressure
No peripheral edema
No reported thrombocytopenia
No reported acute severe renal failure

data.description: A complement dysregulation disorder causing thrombotic microangiopathy, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury; some cases are predominantly renal.
symptoms_in_common: Findings suggestive of thrombotic microangiopathy on renal pathology
No evidence of autoimmune disease or infection as an alternative trigger
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported thrombocytopenia
No documented biochemical evidence of hemolysis
No documented acute kidney failure
Macroscopic hematuria and focal lumbar pain are less typical presenting features

data.description: Severe hypertension can injure renal arterioles and glomeruli, producing fibrinoid vascular injury, onion-skin arteriolar thickening, ischemic glomeruli, hematuria, and anemia.
symptoms_in_common: Renal vascular lesions compatible with thrombotic microangiopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure is not severely elevated (130/80 mmHg)
No history of hypertension
No peripheral edema
No reported hypertensive emergency symptoms such as headache, visual disturbance, or neurologic deficits

data.description: Renal small-vessel thrombosis and chronic vascular lesions caused by antiphospholipid antibodies, often manifesting with hypertension, hematuria, proteinuria, and impaired kidney function.
symptoms_in_common: Renal vascular and glomerular lesions that can resemble chronic thrombotic microangiopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Antiphospholipid antibody tests are negative
No history of venous or arterial thrombosis
No pregnancy morbidity history reported
Normal blood pressure

data.diagnosis: Renal infarction due to renal arterial thrombosis or embolism
data.description: Acute interruption of renal arterial blood flow causes flank pain, hematuria, and ischemic renal injury; segmental or small-vessel infarction may result from thrombotic disease.
symptoms_in_common: Anemia may occur with significant hematuria
Renal ischemic vascular injury may be present
symptoms_not_in_common: No known atrial fibrillation or cardiac embolic source
No documented vascular thrombosis or embolic risk factor
No reported elevated lactate dehydrogenase
Biopsy findings of diffuse thrombotic microangiopathy would be less typical than a focal infarct

data.description: A 31-year-old female, G3P2, came in with 5-day history of severe menorrhagia. She was treated medically and discharged. She was readmitted 2 days later with menorrhagia and anaemia (haemoglobin of 77). The patient had suffered a spontaneous miscarriage a few months earlier.
An abnormal high-flow connection between uterine arteries and veins, which may be acquired after pregnancy loss, curettage, or other uterine trauma and can cause life-threatening uterine bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent bleeding despite initial medical treatment

data.description: Persistence of placental or fetal tissue in the uterus following miscarriage, often causing prolonged or heavy vaginal bleeding and sometimes infection.
symptoms_in_common: History of spontaneous miscarriage a few months earlier
symptoms_not_in_common: Very delayed presentation several months after the miscarriage is less typical
No reported pelvic pain, fever, uterine tenderness, or foul-smelling discharge

data.description: Abnormal proliferation of placental trophoblastic tissue, including molar pregnancy or persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which can present with abnormal bleeding after a pregnancy event.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported persistently positive or elevated beta-hCG
No reported enlarged uterus, hyperemesis, pelvic mass, or symptoms of metastatic disease

data.diagnosis: Subinvolution of the placental implantation site
data.description: Failure of the uteroplacental vessels at a previous implantation site to regress normally after pregnancy termination, causing delayed and sometimes severe uterine bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Severe anaemia due to blood loss
History of miscarriage preceding the bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation months after miscarriage is less common than bleeding in the early post-pregnancy period
No reported uterine enlargement or pelvic pain

data.diagnosis: Uterine leiomyoma (fibroid), especially a submucosal fibroid
data.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor of the uterus; submucosal fibroids can distort the endometrial cavity and cause marked heavy menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia.
symptoms_in_common: Anaemia associated with heavy menstrual blood loss
symptoms_not_in_common: The close temporal association with a recent miscarriage is not specifically typical
No reported chronic history of heavy periods, pelvic pressure, enlarged uterus, or urinary symptoms

data.description: 28-year-old man with abdominal pain and diarrhea (10–12 watery stools/day) after completing azithromycin for pneumonia. Six weeks later, after symptoms resolved and bowel habits returned to baseline, he developed 3 weeks of abdominal discomfort relieved by bowel movements with increased stool frequency to 4–5 stools/day. At the second presentation, vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable; laboratory testing showed positive Clostridium difficile PCR with normal white blood cell count, hemoglobin, platelets, and albumin.
A recurrence of toxin-producing C. difficile colitis after an initial episode, often occurring within weeks after apparent clinical resolution and commonly associated with recent antibiotic exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Initial episode of frequent watery diarrhea (10–12 stools/day)
Recurrent increased stool frequency six weeks after symptoms resolved
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal white blood cell count
Normal albumin
Relatively mild recurrent diarrhea (4–5 stools/day)
Abdominal discomfort relieved by bowel movements

data.description: A functional bowel disorder that can develop after infectious gastroenteritis or colitis, causing recurrent abdominal discomfort associated with bowel movements and altered stool frequency or consistency.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal discomfort relieved by bowel movements
Symptoms beginning after a prior diarrheal intestinal infection
Normal white blood cell count, hemoglobin, platelets, and albumin
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive Clostridioides difficile PCR
Initial severe watery diarrhea of 10–12 stools per day after antibiotic treatment
Recent azithromycin exposure as a direct trigger

data.diagnosis: Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic Clostridioides difficile colonization with another cause of diarrhea
data.description: C. difficile can be present in the colon without causing active toxin-mediated colitis; PCR detects the organism's genetic material but does not by itself prove active infection.
symptoms_in_common: Mild recurrent increase in stool frequency
symptoms_not_in_common: Abdominal discomfort and diarrhea may indicate active gastrointestinal disease rather than asymptomatic colonization
Prior episode of severe watery diarrhea (10–12 stools/day)
Recent antibiotic exposure associated with symptomatic C. difficile infection

data.diagnosis: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea not caused by Clostridioides difficile
data.description: Diarrhea resulting from disruption of normal intestinal flora during or after antibiotic therapy, usually mild and self-limited and not necessarily due to C. difficile toxin-mediated disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive Clostridioides difficile PCR
Severe initial stool frequency of 10–12 watery stools per day
Recurrence six weeks after bowel habits had returned to baseline

data.diagnosis: Inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease
data.description: Chronic immune-mediated inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract that can cause recurrent diarrhea and abdominal pain, although objective inflammatory findings are often present during active disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms closely followed antibiotic exposure and a likely infectious episode
Abdominal discomfort relieved by bowel movements
Normal white blood cell count
Normal hemoglobin
Normal albumin
No reported blood in stool, fever, weight loss, or abnormal physical examination
Positive Clostridioides difficile PCR provides an alternative explanation
